# Warcraft III races and campaigns as a data mod for Age of Mythology: Retold

> The four Warcraft III races (Humans, Orcs, Undead, Night Elves) are playable cultures in AoM: Retold, each with
> three major gods (WC3 heroes), minor gods, units and buildings converted from the WC3 SD models, WC3 voices
> and an AI. Two Reign of Chaos campaigns (21 missions) are rebuilt as AoM scenarios with XS trigger scripts and
> cinematics. Everything is additive data in local mods. It runs in the real game: each change is checked by
> launching to the main menu and reading the game's merged data dump, then playtested.

## Setup
- **Game:** AoM: Retold on Steam, Windows 11. Local mods live in
  `%USERPROFILE%\Games\Age of Mythology Retold\<steamid>\mods\local\<Mod name>`.
- **Debug dump:** add `DebugOutputGameData` to `<profile>\config\user.cfg`. At every launch the game writes the
  data it really merged (base + every active mod) as UTF-16 XML under
  `%LocalAppData%\Temp\Age of Mythology Retold\Data\game\data\` (`gameplay\proto.xml`, `techtree.xml`,
  `tactics\*.tactics`...). Errors go to `<install-or-user>\temp\Logs\MythLog.txt`.
- **Tools:** CryBar.Cli (BAR archives, `glb-to-tmm`, XMB, `xs-to-xml`), stormex (reads the WC3 3.0 CASC storage),
  Blender (previews and portraits only), Python for everything else.
- **Source assets:** an installed Warcraft III Reforged (read-only). Nothing from either game is redistributed;
  the mod is personal. Its models, icons and voices are Blizzard's, so the built mod stays on this PC: no upload to
  the AoM: Retold mod site or Nexus, and it isn't handed to other players for a multiplayer match. A shareable
  version would need original art and audio.

## Route and why
A pure **data mod**: proto/techtree/culture/civ XML through `*_mods.xml` merge files, new art (TMM/TMA models,
DDT textures), sounds, UI pages and scenarios. Bang is native code with no supported plugin loader, and data
covers everything needed: new cultures, gods, AI personalities, triggers. No DLL, no hook.
- The Bang engine's additive merge (`mergeMode`) and `DebugOutputGameData` are documented officially for Age of
  Empires III: DE, with different file names there (`protomods.xml`):
  [Additive Data Mods](https://support.ageofempires.com/hc/en-us/articles/360062106732-Additive-Data-Mods).
- The other new-civilization data mod in the KB is
  [San Franciscans for AoE II DE](../age-of-empires-ii-de/san-franciscans-civ.md) (Genie engine, units rendered
  from 3D). Another Blizzard-asset port kept private is the
  [StarCraft II character in SWBF2](../star-wars-battlefront-ii-2005/porting-a-skinned-starcraft-ii-character-onto-the-swbf2-2005.md).

## How the game works (what we had to learn)
- **Merge files:** each data file has a `*_mods.xml` twin (`proto_mods.xml`, `techtree_mods.xml`,
  `civs_mods.xml`, `cultures_mods.xml`, `minorgods_mods.xml`, `unitfunctiondata_mods.xml`, `unittransforms_mods.xml`,
  `protounitcommands_mods.xml`, `powers_mods.xml`, `simdata_mods.xml`...). Elements carry `mergeMode="add"`
  (or `remove`). Several local mods stack by priority and their merge files merge too.
- **A new culture = a cloned culture.** Copy the data graph of a base culture (its own techs, units, buildings,
  gods), rename every id with a prefix, then re-wire what is shared: train lists of shared buildings,
  `<animfile culture="x">` on shared protos, unit functions, transforms, unit commands, god picker and tech
  tree XAML pages. Age-up techs of cloned minor gods only show if added with the trick the community
  [Major God Builder](https://forums.ageofempires.com/t/major-god-builder/287709) uses:
  `CommandRemove SecretsOfTheTitans`, `CommandAdd <age tech> row=2 column=0` on `AbstractTownCenter`, then
  `CommandAdd SecretsOfTheTitans`, all in the culture's start tech.
- **What an attack is:** a proto's `<protoaction>` (HandAttack, RangedAttack, ChargedRangedAttack...) only works
  if the proto's `<tactics>` file declares that action. The tactics `rate` decides what the action may target
  (`greek_hero.tactics` gives heroes a RangedAttack that only hits `AbstractFlyingUnit`). The animation played is
  the one named in the tactics action (`<anim>RangedAttack</anim>`), looked up in the unit's animfile.
  Projectiles are protos too: the look is the projectile proto's animfile, launched from the `LaunchPoint`
  attach point. A mod can add its own `.tactics` files under `game\data\gameplay\tactics\`: they load (they show
  up in the dump).
- **Models:** `glb-to-tmm` (CryBar) turns one glTF into a TMM plus one TMA per animation. `.material` and the
  simdata (bounds, attach points, animation durations and tags) are written by hand. Materials are
  `opaque_lit` with BaseColor, Normals, Masks (AO, roughness, metal) and Masks2 (R = player colour);
  alpha cut-out is the `ALPHA_CUT_OUT` permutation plus a threshold. The MDX side is in the technique note
  [Converting Warcraft III Reforged SD models](../../techniques/converting-warcraft-iii-reforged-sd-models-mdx-v1800-to-skin.md).
- **The model manifest has a hard limit** (see Gotchas): the base game has about 12,800 entries in
  `intermediate\modelcache\modelManifest*.xml`, and the game crashes after loading data when the total passes
  about 14,460. That leaves about **1,650 TMM + TMA entries for all active mods together**.
- **Sounds:** additive soundsets (`game\sound\soundsets_<x>.soundset`) with 48 kHz mono PCM16 WAV work without
  touching `soundmanifest.xml`. WC3 animation sound events (`SNDx` event objects in the MDX) map to
  `ui\soundinfo\animsounds.slk` and become `SpecificSoundSet` tags.
- **Icons and portraits:** PNG under `game\ui_myth\resources\...`, referenced as `resources\...png`.
- **Skirmish AI:** a personality in `game\ai\personalities\personalities_mods.xml` pointing to a copy of the
  standard AI script with the culture's units; list every culture's personality in that one file, or the last
  mod copied overwrites the others.
- **Scenarios and triggers:** a `.mythscn` scenario can include XS files (`<Script name="campaign\...\x.xs"/>` in
  its `<Triggers>`), searched under `game\trigger\`. `crybar convert xs-to-xml` turns XS rules into a trigger
  block. Missions were generated from Python scripts into XS with a shared library (camera shots, dialogue with
  subtitles and voice, unit staging, waves from destructible buildings).

## Build steps
1. Extract the base game data from the BAR archives (CryBar) once, for reference and cloning.
2. For each WC3 unit: one JSON config (MDX path, sequence to AoM animation map, attach points, icon, voice set),
   converted MDX → glTF → TMM/TMA (`glb-to-tmm`), plus `.material` and simdata written by the build.
3. For each race: one culture config (base culture, gods, unit slots, overrides, techs), cloned into
   `*_mods.xml` files.
4. Write everything into `mods\local\<Mod>` from scratch at every build (never edit the mod folder by hand).
5. Launch to the menu (`um win launch --steam 1934680`), then read the dump and `MythLog.txt`.
6. Split models into separate mods (skirmish pack, one per campaign) to stay under the manifest limit.

## Verification
- **Oracle 1, the merged data dump:** after each build, launch to the main menu only. The dump shows what the
  engine really merged. Static audits run on it: unit stats against WC3, ranged units really ranged with a
  fitting projectile, animations present in the animfile, tech effects aimed at existing actions, manifest count.
- **Oracle 2, the game's log:** `MythLog.txt` shows load errors.
- **Oracle 3, playtests and screenshots:** skirmish games and full campaign missions, by the human and by the
  agent (game window capture with `um win shot --exe AoMRT_s.exe`, menus driven by computer use, debug builds of
  missions that play themselves). Ordinary screenshots of a fullscreen game only see the desktop.
- **Offline staging check of cinematics:** a simulation of each scripted scene flags actors too close to talk,
  attacks with no enemy in reach, and animations missing from a model.
- **Not verified:** multiplayer, and whether TMAs can be left out of the manifest.

## Gotchas
1. **The game crashes right after loading data, with no useful error.** **Cause:** the model manifest is over
   its limit (about 14,460 entries in total; the base game uses about 12,800), proven with dummy entries.
   **Fix:** share byte-identical TMAs between animations (Idle/CarryIdle/Birth on the same sequence), one variant
   per action, and split the models into separate mods. A campaign mod ships only the models its missions show.
2. **"Assertion Error" on TMM/TMA at launch.** **Cause:** the game was started while a build was rewriting the
   mod folder. **Fix:** never launch during a build.
3. **A unit set to ranged still walks into melee.** **Cause:** its tactics file has no ranged action for ground
   targets (Greek hero tactics only allow ranged against flyers), or the default attack is the hand attack.
   **Fix:** set `<tactics>` to a ranged tactics (`rangedattack.tactics`, `rangedattack_heal.tactics`,
   `rangedattack_chargedrangedattack.tactics`), remove the HandAttack, add the RangedAttack.
4. **Upgrades stop working after a melee/ranged swap.** **Cause:** cloned techs aim at an action by name
   (`action="HandAttack"`). **Fix:** retarget them, and check the dump for effects aimed at actions the proto no
   longer has.
5. **A projectile is invisible in one mod but not another.** **Cause:** the projectile's model sat in a mod that
   was not active (models were split per campaign). **Fix:** ship every projectile model a mod's units fire.
6. **A converted unit seems to hit the air.** Some base projectiles use an invisible animfile
   (`ball_of_fire_invisible`); the visible part (breath, swirl) is presumably on the base unit's own model or its
   spawned effects, which a converted model does not have. **Fix:** give such units a visible projectile (a clone
   of the same projectile proto with another animfile keeps its spawn on hit). Found by audit, not yet seen in game.
7. **Age II never appears for a new culture.** **Cause:** cloned minor-god age techs added to the Town Center
   proto do not show. **Fix:** the CommandRemove/CommandAdd trick above.
8. **Two personalities, only one AI loads.** **Cause:** each culture wrote its own
   `personalities_mods.xml`. **Fix:** one merged file.
9. **`um scan` says the game is .NET.** **Cause:** a .NET helper exe ships with the game. The engine is native
   Bang: use the data route.
10. **Base-game rank names rename your units** ("Medium Contarius"). **Cause:** cloned unit-line upgrade techs
    carry `SetName` effects. **Fix:** drop `SetName` effects whose new name is a base `STR_UNIT_` string.
11. **After a crash, Steam will not relaunch the game.** **Cause:** the crash reporter window stays open.
    **Fix:** close it, or start `AoMRT_s.exe` directly.
12. **A scenario test from the main menu shows a black background and no error.** **Cause:** the scenario was not
    loaded at all. **Fix:** test scenarios from the in-game editor (open, then play).
13. **Computer-use clicks miss the top-right corner of the game** (the main menu button). **Cause:** an invisible
    agent window covers it (`um win drive` reports the agent as foreground). **Fix:** use Escape in game, or ask the
    human for that one click.
14. **Python written through a Bash heredoc came out broken** (`\n` and `\b` turned into control characters).
    **Cause:** not Bash itself, which keeps `\n` and `\b` as two characters in any heredoc (a quoted one,
    `<<'EOF'`, changes nothing at all); a layer between the agent and the shell converted them. **Fix:** write code
    files with a file tool.

## Assets
All art and audio come from the user's own installed Warcraft III: SD models converted by script, SD command
button icons upscaled, original voices. Hero portraits are Blender renders of the WC3 portrait models from the
model's own camera. No generated art. Nothing from either game is shared, and the built mod stays private (see
Setup).

## Cost and time
About a week of agent sessions (2026-10-06 to 2026-10-13), local and cloud, with daily playtests by the human.
No API spend.

## Open questions
- Can TMAs be left out of the model manifest (the official docs only mention TMMs)? That would lift the main
  limit.
- Which of `cultures_mods.xml` / `culture_mods.xml` the game really reads (both were written; one culture
  appears).
- A fifth race needs either the reduced animation profile or a further split of the model mods.

# 60 fps + 16:9 + 64-bit rewrite: PFF, encryption, 3DO/JIM and a VoxelSpace renderer

> Armored Fist 3 (NovaLogic Voxel Space 32, 1999) was taken from a 4:3/30 fps
> engine to **60 fps with game speed unchanged** in the real game, using a Rust
> 32-bit launcher + injected payload (runtime hooks only; the on-disk game is
> never touched). That's verified at 1152x864 by counters/readback (loop
> 59.8/s, world renders 59.4/s, sim tick 30.25/s unchanged, 62% of one core,
> 60+ s soak); at 1920x1080 the 32-bit game is render-bound at about 42
> renders/s, with a 16:9 HUD fixed up. In parallel, a 64-bit program written
> from scratch in Rust reads the user's own PFF archives and renders the
> terrain plus the placed scenario objects in its own VoxelSpace renderer at
> 60 fps at 1920x1080, checked by rendered frames against the game's own.

## Setup

- Windows 11 x64, retail AF3 **v1.00.20** (Steam/retail; `AF3.EXE` 2,433,024
  bytes, SHA-256 `52ED80CC...7EA7`), complete install with `*.PFF` and the real
  `AF3INTRO.BIK` (336,378,083 bytes).
- The game is still sold on Steam (app 32710). The 1999 disc release had a
  simple disc check; PCGamingWiki lists v1.00.20 among its retail patches.
- The game is 32-bit, software-rendered, DirectDraw; no anti-cheat, no loader.
  It had NovaWorld online play; everything here was tested single-player,
  offline.
- Toolchain that worked:
  - Python 3.12 + `keystone-engine`/`capstone` (cave builders + probes).
  - `cdb.exe` x86 (Windows SDK Debuggers) for live readback.
  - Rust 1.99 `stable-x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` + targets `i686-pc-windows-gnu`
    and `x86_64-pc-windows-gnu`.
  - **MinGW linker:** rustc's `*-windows-gnu` targets need `libgcc`/`libgcc_eh`;
    LLVM-MinGW ships compiler-rt instead and **fails to link** rustc output.
    Use WinLibs GCC (real MinGW-w64): i686 build extracted locally, x86_64 via
    winget `BrechtSanders.WinLibs.POSIX.UCRT`. (Rust's separate
    `*-pc-windows-gnullvm` targets are the ones meant for LLVM-MinGW.)
  - `windows-mcp` (real mouse/keyboard; the game only reads input with the
    cursor inside its window) driven through its stdio JSON-RPC client.
  - Ghidra 12.1.3 + JDK 21 for static reading (read-only).
- Format references, credited: the Novahq-net community's
  [NovaResearch](https://github.com/Novahq-net/NovaResearch) docs (PFF, 3DO,
  AI, RTXT), [NHQTools](https://github.com/Novahq-net/NHQTools) (C# parsers and
  the SCR cipher), [Nova3di](https://github.com/Novahq-net/Nova3di) (3DI and AI
  composition, including the AF3 attachment tables), and
  [a post on NovaLogic's FMV formats](https://codecs.multimedia.cx/2024/08/looking-at-nova-logic-fmv-formats)
  (KDV). The mod's own code is in the author's private repo.

## Route and why

Two tracks:

1. **Runtime patcher + injected payload (32-bit).** AF3 has no loader and the
   existing project already proved byte patches + hand-assembled caves applied
   to a `CREATE_SUSPENDED` process. The new deliverable keeps that model but
   moves it to Rust: `af3full.exe` validates the EXE, spawns it suspended,
   applies the base byte patches and injects `af3full_payload.dll`, which
   installs a single frame-pacing hook. Nothing is written to disk in the game
   folder and the DLL lives beside the launcher.
2. **64-bit rewrite from scratch (`af3modern`).** The binary cannot be "ported":
   it is 32-bit machine code with self-modifying MMX and 32-bit pointers. The
   64-bit path reads the user's own archives (PFF/3DO/JIM/terrain) and renders
   with a modern Rust renderer. It also sidesteps the MMX rasterizer's cost at
   1080p+ (replacing that rasterizer inside the 32-bit game is still open).

Rejected: a proxy DLL (`winmm.dll` or a DirectInput DLL) in the game folder.
Loaded in-process, it would have the same access as the injected payload (and
Rust can build one), but the launcher keeps the game folder untouched. Also
rejected: patching the frame rate by halving the tick (it doubles game time —
measured, see Gotchas).

## How the game works (what we had to learn)

**Timing.** The engine is a 33 ms fixed-step loop. The tick rate is governed by
a synthetic clock constant (`add [0x5D1D00],0x21`, immediate at file
`0x16A03A`), not by the divisor at `0x569F71`: patching only the divisor does
nothing, and patching the clock constant to 16 doubles the tick rate **and
doubles tick-derived game time** (the displayed mission clock ran 2.09 s/s).
Keep the sim at 33 ms; raise only the render rate.

**Render pacing.** The render throttle compares `now - last_render` against 33
ms (`cmp eax,0x21` at VA `0x56A494`, immediate at file `0x16A496`); with the
stock loop period (~24 ms: `Sleep(11)` + ~13 ms render) terrain only redraws
~21/s against a 30/s simulation. The `Sleep(11)` helper at `0x40F51B` has
exactly **one caller: the main loop at `0x569CF0`**.

**Loading is timing-sensitive.** The main loop runs during mission load; making
it spin (Sleep 0/4, or even a wait that only engages when the loop is slow)
breaks the load with a `MEMMGR: Undefined Memory pointer` modal. A hook must
reproduce stock behavior until the mission is actually live. The frame counter
`[0x5D1CF4]` and the framebuffer pointer `[0x651838]` are both 0 through the
whole load and flip together at mission start — that pair is a reliable
"mission live" gate.

**Renderer.** World renderer entry `0x632930` → band generator `0x633FCD` →
MMX rasterizer `0x63472C` (~12.8 ms at 1152x864). The rasterizer is
**self-modified at runtime** (live code uses `shr eax,0x1e` and a per-run heap
table), so static disassembly of that address is stale; hook the indirect call
site `0x63460C` or read live memory. Band culling breaks when
`(height-1)*pitch*2048` overflows signed 32-bit (`0x6342C6`, `jns` → `jmp` when
it does).

**Archive format (PFF).** 20-byte header (header length, `"PFFx"`, entry count,
entry length, entry-table offset), data blobs, entry table, footer. Entries are
32 bytes (PFF3 variant 1: `DeadSpaceFlags, DataOffset, DataSize, Timestamp,
Name[16]`) or 36 bytes with a trailing CRC; PFF2 reuses the first dword as a
CRC. `AF3.EXE` uses PFF3 for TERRAIN/RESOURCE/MENUS/NORMAL/VOICE/AF3MED and
PFF2 for MISSIONS/CORE/MAPS. (NovaResearch and NHQTools list AF3 as PFF3 only
and describe PFF data as unencrypted, so the PFF2 archives and the pad below
are this note's own finding.)

**The encryption (the unlock for all mission data).** Every entry of a **PFF2
archive is XOR-padded with a fixed 32-byte repeating key**; PFF3 archives are
plain. The pad was derived from 170 files stored plain in RESOURCE and padded
in MISSIONS (identical sizes; every twin XORs to the same sequence) and
verified on all 1729 `3DO` entries in the padded archives (they decrypt to
`"3DO1"`), both KDV movies
(`"xVDK"` header) and all JIM files. Pad:
`00 78 2e 7c 70 07 c2 77 e7 80 3c 17 be 38 03 e1 bb f3 c0 1e 0b df 9c 01 f0 5d
f9 e0 0f 85 ef ce`. The NHQTools SCR/ARX cipher does **not** apply to AF3
(brute-forced all 2^32 keys — no match).

**Terrain.** Per map `<NAME>_D.R16` = `"R16a"` + u32 width + u32 height +
w*h u16 LE heightmap (1024x1024, heights ~2761..15958); `<NAME>_C.TGA` =
1024x1024 24bpp bottom-up colormap; `<NAME>_M.PCX` = 8bpp RLE material map;
`<NAME>_CM.CAL` = text class table (`Adt1`, `Cdt3`, `Ags3`, ...). The two
`MAPS.PFF` `KDV` blobs are not terrain: they are NovaLogic FMV videos
(decrypted header `"xVDK"`, 640x480).

**3DO models.** 92-byte header (`"3DO1"`, name, bbox, counts, offsets), then
textures (28 B), vertices (44 B), triangles (32 B), normals (16 B), mesh
entries (12 B), hardpoints (16 B). Triangle vertex/normal/texture references are
**byte offsets into their arrays**, not indices. Standalone models are shifted
left by 7 at load. Textures carry a 12-byte name, an alpha byte, a flat colour
and render flags. **Axes: z-up, x mirrored** — Nova3di's converter maps
`(-x, z, -y)` into its y-up OBJ space, i.e. `world = (-x, y, z)` for a z-up
renderer; the palm trunk / tank height run along z (check the vertex
distribution, not the header bbox). Mesh-entry offsets beyond the body's
bounding diagonal are sentinels and must be ignored, or AI composites grow
giant stray planes. AI parts are one LOD tier each (`_H*`/`_M*`/`_L*`); the
`_L` parts are coarse boxes, so pick a single tier.

**AI manifests.** ASCII: a type-id header line, then environment blocks
(`>G` green, `>D` desert, `>S` snow, `>N` night, `>R`/`>B` team) each listing
child `.3DO` parts, then `>IDOV` (id), a 5-line `>DATA` block (LOD cutoffs in
metres + collision flags) and an optional `>LEAF` count. Part names are **LOD
variants** (`..._L01/_H02/_L03/_H04` pairs + shared parts), not additive
pieces; composing a full vehicle needs the engine's per-type assembly tables
(solved later, see Open question 2 and the Update section). The first line may be a comment with the type on the next line
(`;TANKJACK` / `43 ;type`), and part lines can carry a trailing comment
(`TRAP_L.3DO ;SINGLE ?`).

**JIM missions.** After the PFF2 pad: 9-byte header (a start record), then fixed
9-byte records `[tag u8][x u16 LE][y u16 LE][value u8][00 00 00]`, zero
padding, then a NUL-separated ASCII object table. Tags: `0x7f` objectives
(the `value` indexes the numbered labels), `0x07` units, `0x11`/`0x12` spawns,
`0x01` start. `C6M7.JIM` resolves to `1-START POINT`, `2-CP ALPHA`,
`3-OBJ ACKERMAN`, `4-OBJ HAINES`, `5-CP BRAVO`, `6-RELEASE POINT` plus unit
records. All 85 missions parse (1569 records; `C2M9.JIM` is a 1-byte
placeholder). JIMs turned out to be mission-editor documents that the game
never loads (Open question 1); the game's missions are the BMS scenarios below.

**CORE.PFF** holds the same JIMs plus `.ORD` per-mission briefing text
(`>TEXT`-style markup) and per-map `.INF` info text (94 maps `MP01..MP94`) and
`.POS` binary position tables. Each scenario's map comes from its own TRN file
(`dg2_dy03.trn` -> `AFDG2`, Open question 1).

**BMS scenarios (the mission text/placement files).** `*.BMS` in MISSION.PFF /
UPDATED.PFF are **not** PFF2-padded: they are stored raw and end with a clear
`NoVa` tag. Decrypt with the NovaLogic 8-byte block transform (AF3.EXE VA
`0x570845`, mission manager): per 8-byte block `eax = rol(eax, 9)` (seed
`0xfade2bad`, `+0x1abb09` when the sign bit is set), `ebp = ror(ebp, 1)` (seed
`0xace4dead`), then `dword0 = xchg bh,bl(u32le ^ eax)` and
`dword1 = ror16(u32le ^ ebp)`; only `(len-4)/8` blocks are processed. The
payload is ASCII scenario text (`;v1.xx AF3MED`, `;Mission:`, `>WPNT`
waypoint lists, `{mission}` triggers, object placements) followed by a binary
trailer. Coordinates are 32-bit **21.11 fixed point**; the engine's HUD
formatter (`AF3.EXE` VA `0x5481a8`) divides the player's world position by
`0x280000` = 2^21 * 1.25, so the map is **1280 world units across** and the
heightmap pixel is `value / 2,621,440` (not `value / 2^21`; the HUD's second
number is the **negated** y, a UI flip only). Headings are 32-bit turn
fractions (`value * 360 / 2^32` degrees). Object lines are
`NAME.AI,variant,id,x,y,heading,...` (scenery omits the id); `stpl` lines are
route segments and `stid` labels the next unit. **v1.21 battle scenarios**
(UPDATED.PFF `F3RBGM*`/`F3CTFM*`/`F3TDMM*`) have **no `OBJECTS included`
marker**: their placements follow the trigger block directly after
`END`/`0,1`. Bare tokens (`stlm`, `sttk`, `STCN`, `stac`) are markers, not
models — only names with `.AI`/`.3DO` are placements. Sibling `*.BIN` briefings are
an `RTXT` container (stored plain) with the title and the in-game messages.
Sibling `*.INF` audio scripts use the **same block cipher** (raw + `NoVa`):
`>SC01` sections of `.SQUAK`/`.DELAY,N`/`<file>.wav ; radio line`; scenario
triggers reference them as `EVENT,14,SCxx` (kind 8 is the `MSxx` text message).
All 71 MISSION.PFF INF decode (some have `;Shipped Dialog For AF3` comment
headers and lowercase `.squak`).

**3DI v7 models (AF3MED.PFF scenery/units).** 124-byte header (`3DI\x07`,
12-byte name, `lod_count` at +0x14), `u32 texture_count`, then a 184-byte LOD
header (`lod_data_size` +0x14; vertex/normal/face counts at
+0x80/+0x88/+0x90; mesh/hardpoint/material/volume counts at
+0x98/+0xA0/+0xA8/+0xB0). LOD data order: vertices (8 B: i16 x,y,z + u16
mesh), normals (8 B), faces (72 B: `u[3]` i32 +4, `v[3]` i32 +16, `vi[3]` i16
+28, `ni[3]` i16 +34, material u32 +0x44), meshes (112 B), hardpoints (12 B),
volumes (140 B), materials (120 B: 12-byte name, flags +0x10, flat RGB +0x28).
Face `vi` are **mesh-relative**: resolve with the per-mesh vertex counts in
order. AF3 stores `texture_count = 0`; the **material names are the texture
names** (`FROND01` -> `FROND01H.PCX` in RESOURCE.PFF). Cut-out foliage uses
palette entry 0 as a color key (purple-ish); remap it to a sentinel and skip
those texels, or the trees render their key color.

## Build steps

32-bit (in the game folder, nothing installed into it):

```text
rust/build.ps1 full        # builds af3full.exe + af3full_payload.dll (i686)
rust/target/i686-pc-windows-gnu/release/af3full.exe
```

The launcher reads `AF3_GAME_DIR` (defaults to the repo folder), validates the
EXE bytes, patches, injects, resumes, prints the pid. `AF3_NO_PAYLOAD=1` skips
injection for A/B tests; `AF3_FRAME_WAIT_MS` (payload) sets the frame target
(default 16; 0 disables); `AF3_RENDER_GATE_MS` (launcher) sets the render gate
byte (default 0).

64-bit rewrite:

```text
rust/build.ps1 modern      # builds af3modern.exe (x86_64)
af3modern pff list <archive.pff>
af3modern terrain TERRAIN.PFF AFD1 --out preview.ppm
af3modern render TERRAIN.PFF AFD1 --x 300 --y 200 --follow --heading 90 --out frame.ppm
af3modern run    TERRAIN.PFF AFD1 --width 1920 --height 1080
af3modern model  MISSIONS.PFF BMP2B_M1.3DO --out model.ppm --obj model.obj
af3modern jim    MISSIONS.PFF C6M7.JIM
af3modern ai     RESOURCE.PFF MLRS.AI --out composite.ppm
af3modern scene  TERRAIN.PFF AFD1 MISSIONS.PFF BMP2B_M1.3DO --obj-x 330 --obj-y 200 --out scene.ppm
af3modern trn    MISSION.PFF DG2_DY03.TRN
af3modern bms    MISSION.PFF F3C01M01.BMS --text
af3modern 3di    AF3MED.PFF PALM.3DI
af3modern run    TERRAIN.PFF AFDG2 --scenario MISSION.PFF F3C01M01.BMS \
                 --models MISSIONS.PFF --med AF3MED.PFF --resource RESOURCE.PFF \
                 --tex RESOURCE.PFF --trn MISSION.PFF DG2_DY03.TRN \
                 --font NORMAL.PFF AF3FNT8.FNT
af3modern bench  TERRAIN.PFF AFD1 --width 1920 --height 1080
```

Verification harness (Python, in the private repo's `AF3_Mod/scripts/`): `AF3_VerifyMode.py` (the
27-assertion acceptance gate), `AF3_TimeProbe.py` (sim tick / render stamp /
accumulator), `AF3_RustStats.py` (named-mapping stats from the payload),
`AF3_DriveToMission.py` (menus → mission via windows-mcp), `AF3_LoadWatch.py`
(load-state timeline).

## Verification

- **32-bit, mode 6 (1152x864), 60+ s soak:** payload hook calls 59.8/s, world
  render stamp 59.1-59.4/s, sim tick `[0x5D1CF4]` 30.25-30.34/s (unchanged),
  62% of one core, process responsive, no modal, no access violation.
- **A/B:** with `AF3_NO_PAYLOAD=1` the same launcher reaches a mission, proving
  the patch set is byte-identical to the old Python launcher's.
- **Render gate:** with the gate left at 16 ms the loop (16.7 ms) only rendered
  39.5/s (2 of 3 loops); gate 0 gives ~59-60/s.
- **64-bit:** headless bench 1.72 ms/frame at 960x540, 3.79 ms at 1920x1080;
  the interactive window reports **60 FPS at 1920x1080** in its title; the
  numeric gate `AF3_ModernVerify.py` sustains min 56-57 / mean 59.5 fps at
  1080p (render 7-10 ms + copy ~1 ms + present ~1 ms). 2560x1440 is
  render-bound (18.6-21.9 ms -> ~42 fps).
- **32-bit at 1080p with the Rust payload:** 41.7 world renders/s (render-bound;
  the frame-wait hook rarely sleeps). RDTSC pass profile of the world entry
  (~24 ms): **terrain draw `0x633417` = 76.5% (18.35 ms)**, sprite/object pass
  `0x56ED20` = 23.5% (5.64 ms), everything else ~0. That 18.35 ms is the exact
  target for real-game 60 fps at 16:9.
- **Formats:** PFF parse validated by re-reading every archive (entry counts,
  live byte coverage ~100%); the pad by decrypting all 1729 3DOs to `"3DO1"`;
  3DO/JIM/AI parsers have unit tests plus real-file round-trips (OBJ export,
  wireframes, scene renders, material histograms).
- **Later sessions (see Update):** vehicle composition from the typed AI
  manifests (wireframes for M1A2, BMP, BRDM, OLIFANT and 2S6M), and the 16:9
  HUD in the 32-bit payload (window fit, strip text, minimap) with the 4:3 mode
  gate still 27/27.
- **NOT verified:** 60 fps at 1080p in the 32-bit game (about 42 renders/s, see
  above); 2560x1440 in the 32-bit payload; 3DO/3DI scale against the engine's
  world units (Open question 3).

## Gotchas

1. **Halving the tick doubles game time.** The synthetic clock constant
   (`add [0x5D1D00],0x21`) governs the tick rate; setting it to 16 raised sim
   ticks to 62.5/s and the mission clock to 2.09 s/s. **Fix:** keep 33 ms and
   raise only the render rate. (The old project's two-site `AF3_TICK_MS` knob
   only changed the divisor, so it silently did nothing.)
2. **A frame-wait hook that engages during loading breaks the load** with
   `MEMMGR: Undefined Memory pointer`. The loader needs the stock loop cadence.
   **Fix:** a hand-built stub that calls the original `Sleep(11)` helper unless
   `[0x5D1CF4] != 0 && [0x651838] != 0` (mission live), then waits to the
   16.6 ms target; preserve all registers with `pushfd/pushad`.
3. **The render gate must be 0** (or well under the loop period): a 16 ms
   threshold against a 16.7 ms loop skipped every third render (39.5/s).
4. **The PFF2 XOR pad is per-archive-version, not per-file:** PFF2 archives
   (MISSIONS/CORE/MAPS) are padded, PFF3 are not. Apply
   `plain[i] = cipher[i] ^ PAD[i % 32]`.
5. **3DO references are byte offsets** (vertex 44 B, normal 16 B, texture 28 B);
   dividing by the stride is required, and out-of-range refs must be rejected.
6. **JIM record scanning must stop at printable ASCII**, otherwise the `Player`
   string parses as a bogus record (tag `0x50`); also handle the 1-byte
   placeholder mission.
7. **KDV is a video**, not a terrain/map blob (NovaLogic FMV, 4x4 block modes).
8. **Hot-loop integer division is the killer:** `rem_euclid` per sample made the
   renderer ~30x slower; power-of-two bitmask wrapping plus hoisted span
   strides took 960x540 from 32 fps to ~580 fps headless.
9. **`Sleep(1)` is 15.6 ms** until the process calls `timeBeginPeriod(1)`; 60
   fps pacing needs it (and an absolute per-frame schedule).
10. **rustc GNU targets + LLVM-MinGW do not link** (`-lgcc`/`-lgcc_eh` missing).
    Use real MinGW-w64 (WinLibs) for both i686 and x86_64.
11. **The MMX rasterizer's static bytes are stale** (self-modified at runtime):
    always read the live code/table before touching it.
12. **`AF3INTRO.BIK` is load-bearing** for the wrapper's validation; the intro
    spawns a `BINKPLAY.EXE` child that can zombie and hang the boot wait — kill
    it by its exact PID (`um win kill`), never by image name.
13. **At 16:9 the engine still draws its own strip text** at 640-space x~0
    (clipped left), coloured by whatever palette entries the mod last wrote.
    The glyph cave's band guard (cursor y >= 429*pitch/640) does not catch the
    message row. The mod's own strip is the centred 2.25x copy; skip-engine
    variants are unreliable.
14. **Some AI-shared 3DO parts store coordinates relative to a ±2^29 origin**
    (e.g. `MLRX_L` y ~ -2^29 + real); shift the whole axis back when the
    bounds are all beyond ±2^28 or the composite collapses to a dot.
15. **BMS scenarios are the trap:** neither raw nor pad-removed bytes are text,
    and XOR of two BMS files looks *text-like* (their shared header cancels),
    which reads like a shared stream cipher. It is really the weak 8-byte
    block transform above; the give-away is that the ciphertext XOR of two
    files stays text-like everywhere, and the derived "keystream" only agrees
    while the plaintexts agree.
16. **AI manifests use lowercase `>g`/`>d`/`>s` markers**, and HUT/PALM-style
    files declare all environments first and then list **one shared parts
    list** (`>g >d >s` then parts, terminated by `<<`); M1A2-style files list
    per-environment parts separated by `<`. Infantry (`INFENM/INFUS`) parts
    are animation frames, so use one part, not the LOD grouping.
17. **Scenario object names are editor aliases** (`TREPALM`, `Bana1`, `SHACK7`,
    `infenm`, ...). Resolve them by hand: 3DI in AF3MED.PFF (`PALM.3DI`,
    `BANA1.3DI`, `OLIFANT.3DI`, `BMP-2.3DI`, `SSIGN2.3DI`, ...), else AI/3DO in
    MISSIONS.PFF (`PALM1.AI`, `AFSHK7.AI`, `ELEPHANT.AI`, ...), else
    RESOURCE.PFF (`INFENM.AI`, shared AI parts). The `;NN` comment on each
    line is an editor type index, not a filename.
18. **PCX textures can be non-square and color-keyed** (64x256 trunks); the
    key is palette entry 0 and its RGB varies per texture
    ([141,22,181], [95,42,122], [128,0,128]), so detect it by "red and blue
    dominate green", not a fixed color.
19. **The live scenario buffer is the ground truth for cipher work:** the
    decrypted text of the running battle can be dumped from process memory
    (scan for `;Owner` / `;v1.`), and its fixed-point placements match the
    engine's globals byte-for-byte. `AF3_ScanScenario.py` does the scan.
20. **Scenario coordinates are not `value/2^21` map pixels:** the engine HUD
    divides by `0x280000` (2^21*1.25), i.e. the map is 1280 world units across
    with 1.25 units per heightmap pixel. Using 2^21 places every object 25%
    too far out (and pushed some past the 1024 map edge). The HUD's y is
    negated for display only; the terrain/renderer y is not flipped.
21. **With hundreds of placed objects the object pass dominates at 1080p**
    (41 ms single-threaded before culling). Per-object frustum culling,
    backface culling, hoisted barycentric reciprocals and a power-of-two
    texture-wrap mask take it to ~20 ms; splitting the frame into horizontal
    bands with one thread each (disjoint row writes into the same frame/zbuf)
    takes it to ~7 ms — the full scenario then runs at 60 fps at 1920x1080.

## Assets

No new art yet. The rewrite reuses the game's own terrain textures (TGA/R16)
and 3DO models; the model previews and scene renders are generated PPM/PNG.
`um fal` was not needed.

## Cost and time

One long session (~6 h). Toolchain installs: rustup + WinLibs + gh via winget
(~200 MB). All measurements are in the project `MODLOG.md`.

## Open questions

1. ~~Mission→map association and the JIM world-unit → map-pixel scale~~ —
   **resolved: JIMs are mission-editor documents, not game data.** `AF3.EXE`
   has no `.JIM` literal; live scans of a running campaign (briefing and
   in-mission) find neither the file bytes nor its string table; a 2-point
   RANSAC similarity fit (rotation/reflection allowed, scale 0.2..1.6) between
   JIM records and every fixed-point coordinate pair in the compiled scenario
   never reaches 4 inliers. JIM overlays are now normalized over their own
   bounding box (relative layout only). The mission→map association comes from
   the scenario's own TRN (`dg2_dy03.trn` -> `AFDG2`).
2. ~~Full vehicle composition~~ — **solved via the engine's per-type assembly
   tables.** The *typed* manifests live in `RESOURCE.PFF` (header number, e.g.
   `BMP.AI` type 4, `M1A2.AI` type 1, `BRDM.AI` type 20); `MISSIONS.PFF` copies
   are editor documents (no type, but plot routines like `tank,0,10` /
   `2sa6,5,32` / `1prt,8`). The per-type attachment table (Nova3di
   `af3_assemblies`, extracted from the engine) is implemented with its exact
   semantics: slot/parent/mesh index, `mesh -1/-2/-3`, body-diagonal sentinels,
   first-attachment-per-slot offsets, per-part LOD substitution
   (`BMP2B_L1` -> `BMP2B_H1`), X (destroyed) part splitting and flat
   shadow/decal skipping. Plot-routine manifests compose through the routine
   tables with their `base_part` offsets.
3. 3DO/3DI model orientation/scale calibration against the engine's world
   units (the rewrite normalises each model to a per-name target size).
4. 16:9 in the 32-bit payload: **window fit and the doubled strip text are
   done**, and so is the minimap (see the Update section); the SSE2 /
   multi-threaded terrain rasterizer for the 32-bit path is still open (18.35 ms
   at 1080p).
5. The rewrite's HUD/cameras/simulation and mission loading from JIM (moot now
   that JIMs are editor-only).
6. ~~Animated materials/texture frames~~ — **moot**: all 4140 3DO models
   (27,112 texture entries) have `frame_count == 0`; AF3 animates effects and
   model parts, never texture frames. The engine's exact object render flags
   remain open.

## Update (later sessions)

**AI composition (RESOURCE typed manifests).** See open question 2 above; the
implementation lives in `af3full-core/src/ai.rs` (attachment tables + plot
routines + X-split + LOD helpers) and `af3modern` (`compose_ai_model`).
Verified wireframes for M1A2/BMP/BRDM/OLIFANT (typed) and 2S6M (plot routine).

**32-bit wide HUD.**

- **Window fit**: the Rust payload (`af3full_payload.dll`) now runs a watcher
  that converts the game window to borderless topmost at the monitor origin
  when the mode exceeds the desktop work area (1080p mode + taskbar), sizing
  from the engine's framebuffer globals (`[0x65188C]`/`[0x651890]`) so the 1:1
  blit survives; restores the saved style when a smaller mode fits.
  `AF3_WINDOW_FIT=0` disables.
- **Doubled strip text fixed**: the glyph cave now scales by `height/480`
  (was `pitch/640`) including the advance helpers, and the strip band guard
  threshold is `429*height/480` (the old `429*pitch/640` computed 1287 px at
  1080p and never fired). At 4:3 both are mathematical no-ops. The 4:3 gate
  stays 27/27.
- **Minimap fixed at 16:9**: the wide HUD layout is an element-id grid at
  `[0x613200]` with dims `[0x613224]x[0x613228]`, set to pitch x height at
  mode init (`0x412C39`/`0x45ECD0`); element rects are the bounding boxes of
  each id (`0x56F680`/`0x56F818`, written into the slot struct by `0x5416FE`).
  The grid zones are the native 640x480 zones scaled x*pitch/640,
  y*height/480 - the anisotropy every wide element inherits. The minimap is
  id `0xF7`, its bbox computed at call site `0x542614`, written to slot
  `+0xFC`. A 100-byte cave (`build_minimap_rect.py`, `patch_minimap_rect`)
  hooks that call, preserves CF, and rewrites x as
  `x*(4*height)/(3*pitch) + (3*pitch-4*height)/6`; at 4:3 it is a
  mathematical no-op. Verified: the minimap moves from `(12,686,580,261)` to
  `(249,686,435,261)` - square, at the pillarbox edge; mode gate 27/27.
  (The grid itself is decoded from a resource by `0x612FC2 -> 0x404A46`; the
  per-element rect transform avoids touching that pipeline.)

**Batch tooling.** `AF3_Mod/scripts/AF3_ScenarioSheet.py` renders the showcase
mission list headlessly (terrain map auto-resolved from each TRN prefix) and
builds a titled `contact_sheet.png` in one command; verified on 8 missions
(148-378 objects each, 5 different maps).

# A visible, driven second character in AC4 single-player (co-op ghost avatar)

> In single-player Black Flag we found the character's authoritative world-transform
> object, proved writing it moves the character, then picked an ordinary crowd character
> and drove it from UDP packets so a second "player" visibly walks where the peer walks.
> Verified in-game: a fake peer script made an NPC circle the player, and the NPC
> returned to its own AI when the packets stopped.
>
> A rendered second body can also be spawned instead of hijacked: build it from the local player's own
> cached `EntityBuilder` (Kamzik123's [AC4Coop](https://github.com/Kamzik123/AC4Coop) route). The
> [spawn-route note](spawning-a-real-second-player-in-ac4-black-flag-the-working-.md) has it.

## Setup

- Game: Steam AC4BFSP.exe, x86, pinned build above (fixed RVAs; image base 0x400000).
- Plugin: an ASI loaded by the 32-bit Ultimate ASI Loader (dinput8.dll), hooked at the
  camera update and running per frame on the game thread.
- Analysis: Ghidra 12.1.4 (20 GB heap for the 43 MB x86 exe), Cheat Engine 7.5 for
  breakpoint hunting, plus custom PowerShell scripts that attach as a WOW64 debugger
  for INT3 captures and hardware watches.

## Route and why

- Chose `native-hook` + fixed addresses over pattern scanning: single pinned build, and
  all addresses are re-resolved live anyway (heap objects move per session).
- The avatar here is not spawned: it's a *hijacked crowd character* whose transform is overwritten
  each frame. A rendered second body can also be spawned, from the local player's own cached
  `EntityBuilder` (`PlayerProgression` → `EntityBuilder::BuildEntityWithSelector` →
  `World::AddEntity`, plus a `PlayerPadManager::GetUnusedPadID` hook so it doesn't take the player's
  pad). That route is Kamzik123's ([AC4Coop](https://github.com/Kamzik123/AC4Coop)) and was verified
  live on 2026-10-11 (two Edwards on the Havana dock); the
  [spawn-route note](spawning-a-real-second-player-in-ac4-black-flag-the-working-.md) has the steps.
  The [dead-ends note](spawning-a-new-character-in-ac4-black-flag-single-player-dea.md) records the
  spawn paths that didn't work.
- A crowd body is still a usable body source: it already carries a walk skeleton, so mirroring bones
  animates it. A body spawned from the cached builder has no walk children (`c14+0x134 == 0`), so a
  bone mirror does nothing there; AC4Coop animates its puppet by action replication (`SetTargetAction`
  and the `SimpleAnimBlender<46>` blend tree) instead.
- Networking is the plugin's own: each copy of AC4BFSP.exe sends and receives 72-byte pose packets over UDP,
  peer to peer (tested over Radmin VPN between two PCs). Nothing goes through Ubisoft Connect, Ubisoft's servers
  or AC4BFMP.exe.

## How the game works (what we had to learn)

**Camera -> target chain.** The camera manager global (`0x02ABE588`) -> `+0x4C` -> holder
-> camera object -> `+0x68` -> a camera-target block. The block's `+0x174` points at a
per-target "provider" object whose `+0x100` is a quaternion and `+0x110` the target's
feet position. The block's `+0x50` is a smoothed "eye" copy (feet + ~1.2 m). All of this
is *derived*: writes there snap back.

**The character root node.** The provider copies from a single source object per
character: class vtable `0x01E4CE90`, allocation size exactly `0x100` bytes.
Layout (fixed, offsets < 0x100):

- `+0x00` vtable, `+0x04` id (a global allocation counter, not a type)
- `+0x08` player-only identity-matrix pointer (null on every civilian)
- `+0x10` 4x4 matrix; row 3 (`+0x40`) is the **feet position** — write this to move them
- `+0x60` children array pointer, `+0x66` child count (= the rig), `+0x68` handle marker
  constant `0x04DD5F8C`, `+0x7C` exactly `-0.50` for humanoids
- `+0xC8` per-character object, `+0xE8` behavior-controller object (different classes for
  player vs civilian)
- Everything at `>= 0x100` belongs to *neighbouring heap objects*, not this object.

**Which bodies are real.** Class instances come in flavours: the player (rig 27 parts), real
crowd characters (rig 18-20), and inactive proxies (rig 1, or 8-14) that exist in memory but
never render. Writing an inactive proxy moves nothing visible. Filter: `f7c == -0.50` AND
child count >= 16 AND within reach of the target position; exclude anything within ~2.5 m of
the local player so you never grab the player's own body.

**Writing the body each frame.** In-process per-frame writes (from a hook) win the render
frame; the puppet's own AI keeps running and takes back over the moment writes stop. Add
yaw by rewriting matrix rows 0/1 as a Z-rotation from the peer's quaternion.

## Build steps

1. Read the local player's feet (provider `+0x110`) and facing (`+0x100`) every frame in an
   existing per-frame hook; publish over UDP with a small envelope+payload protocol.
2. Receive the peer sample (same protocol, binary, 72-byte packets).
3. In the same hook: if peer data is fresh (< 2 s), scan for a drivable body (incremental
   scan, a few MB per frame), smoothing the body toward the peer position (lerp ~0.3/frame,
   hard snap past ~20 m), and release on timeout.
4. Config in an ini; the plugin reloads it live (sockets re-bind on the fly).

## Verification

- **Oracle 1 (self):** captured the smoother's breakpoint (INT3 at the instruction copying
  the source transform) and confirmed the captured source object's matrix translation equals
  the camera-chain feet within 0.04 m.
- **Oracle 2 (eye-witness):** a write of +20 m to the matrix X made the player character
  visibly teleport — user-confirmed ("watched him teleport").
- **Oracle 3 (eye-witness):** a scripted fake peer circled the real player's position; an
  NPC visibly teleported in and walked the circle, and was released (walked off) when packets
  stopped ("yup he's circling"). Loop counter: 2,839/2,839 UDP packets both ways.
- **Oracle 4 (two machines, eye-witness, 2026-10-06):** real Radmin VPN run between two PCs
  (~105 ms ping). Both players saw each other's driven crowd body in-game; log showed
  `peer=1 body=1@<addr> fresh=1 d=13.8..18.9` with the body picked 61.5 m from the peer and
  tracked while walking. Facing replica confirmed ("he turns to match") — validates the +Y
  forward convention used for both placement and body yaw. Both sides hit a stuck UDP port
  (bind 10048, a dead process owning it); changing LocalPort and mirroring RemotePort fixed it
  live (the ini hot-reload re-binds without restart). Watch items: tracking slightly choppy
  (20 Hz + latency + the crowd AI); peer climbs show as vertical teleports (no animation/parkour
  linkage yet).
- Not verified: animations/parkour events and true model replacement.

## Gotchas

1. **Debugger-attached game dies on a breakpoint that looks unknown.** 64-bit debuggers
   receive WOW64 breakpoints as `0x4000001F` (STATUS_WX86_BREAKPOINT), not `0x80000003`;
   returning it to the app as "not handled" terminates it. **Fix:** treat both codes as
   breakpoints, continue with DBG_CONTINUE, and always restore the patched byte plus fix EIP.
2. **A hardware write breakpoint on the visible position never fires.** The visible value is
   a derived copy; its writer only runs when the source updates. **Fix:** watch the true
   source, or find the writer via the breakpoint on the copy routine itself.
3. **Fields past the object's allocation size are other objects.** Reads at `+0x110`/`+0x170`
   looked like vtables and were neighbours. **Fix:** get the allocation size from the
   constructor's allocator call (here `0x100`) and ignore everything beyond it.
4. **Writes snap back when the character is moving.** The movement system rewrites the
   transform while it has velocity. **Fix:** write per frame from in-process; it wins the
   render and the AI takes over when you stop.
5. **Quiet-looking bodies that accept writes but never render.** Inactive proxies share the
   class. **Fix:** child-count + `f7c == -0.50` filter.
6. **A game that "pauses" the world when unfocused.** Any scan while the chat window has
   focus sees a frozen world and a zeroed camera. **Fix:** poll until the player position
   actually changes before sampling.
7. **Kernel-held UDP ports.** Some crashed sessions leave a dead process still owning the
   bound UDP port (bind fails with 10048 even after the process is gone). **Fix:** use a
   fresh local port per session, or reboot — worth doing before any two-machine test. If the
   plugin opens its socket in `DllMain`, a process from AC4's launch chain can be the owner:
   gotchas 1-2 of the [co-op note](coop-two-player-udp-bind-in-the-live-game.md) have the cause
   and the fix (open the socket on the first in-world frame).
8. **PowerShell name collisions broke our scripts repeatedly**: `rd`, `rp`, `rm`, `dir` are
   aliases; short helper names must be avoided in Windows-focused tooling.

## Assets

None — v0.1 hijacks an existing crowd character. Model replacement needs the multiplayer
"skin"/morph system (see below).

## Cost and time

One long session: recon of the transform chain, breakpoint capture, class census, body
picker, plugin write path, and a working loopback demo.

## Open questions

- **True model swap (make the ghost look like the protagonist).** The world puppet is a
  0x100-byte node whose rig (children) is built per model by the animation/graphics system;
  SP only has outfits *for the player*. The runtime character-model swap exists in the
  engine but in `AC4BFMP.exe` (`CharacterSkinsComponent`, `ActionSwapSkin`, `HIJACK_SKIN`,
  morph events). Next step: port that apply-skin path, or call SP's graphic factory
  (table-registry driven) for a puppet with the protagonist's definition. Spawning from the
  player's cached builder (spawn-route note) gives a second Edward directly, so it sidesteps the skin
  swap for a protagonist-looking body.
- Animation/parkour event replication is next (the two-machine link is done — see Oracle 4). AC4Coop
  does it by action replication (`SetTargetAction`, `ActivateCharacterActionSet` and the
  `SimpleAnimBlender<46>` blend tree) rather than per-bone writes; see the
  [spawn-route note](spawning-a-real-second-player-in-ac4-black-flag-the-working-.md).

# Working two-player co-op in AC4 Black Flag: spawn a peer puppet, and bind UDP in the live game

> Kamzik123's AC4Coop gives genuinely working two-player co-op inside AC4 *single-player*: each client
> spawns a **puppet** for the peer (built from the local player's own cached entity builder) and drives it
> by **action replication**, so the peer's body walks, runs and climbs instead of teleporting. The one
> thing that stopped it working over a VPN was not gameplay at all — it was **Winsock**. AC4's launch
> chain starts several processes that all load the ASI, a transient one grabbed the UDP port and died, and
> the live game's `bind()` then failed with `WSAEADDRINUSE` so it had **no net at all**. Starting the net
> on the first in-world frame (and pairing that with `SO_REUSEADDR`) fixed it. Verified: two real machines
> over Radmin VPN, both puppets spawn and animate.

## Setup

- Game: Steam `AC4BFSP.exe`, 32-bit, pinned build above (fixed RVAs, image base `0x400000`).
- Two copies, offline. Each player runs their own copy of the game on their own PC (AC4Coop's same-PC
  two-instance mode is only for testing on one machine). Ubisoft Connect has to be running for
  `AC4BFSP.exe` to start; with the plugin installed, put Ubisoft Connect in offline mode and don't use the
  game's online features. The only co-op traffic is the plugin's UDP between the two PCs, and
  `AC4BFMP.exe` is never run.
- Prior art: **Kamzik123/AC4Coop** — a community ASI plugin (the reference implementation; full credit to
  Kamzik123). It is the thing that already "works"; this note is about the one transport bug that kept it
  from working on a real two-machine link, plus the co-op design worth reusing. AC4Coop has no license
  file, so its code is all rights reserved: build it for yourself, offer fixes upstream, and ask Kamzik123
  before sharing a modified build.
- Loader: 32-bit Ultimate ASI Loader (`dinput8.dll`). The plugin runs its hooks on the game thread.
- Link: peer-to-peer UDP between two PCs over a private **Radmin VPN** subnet.
- Our build of the fixed source (not published), SHA-256:
  `FDF433D3AD6DD094E1CA47556AE1E741A16F6CEF446FE048EFD98296F8F5E2C5`.

## Route and why

- `native-hook` is the whole route: no game data is edited, the plugin installs hooks and calls engine
  functions in-process. See the sibling notes for the internals we mapped on the same build: the
  [spawn-route note](spawning-a-real-second-player-in-ac4-black-flag-the-working-.md) (the cached-builder
  spawn AC4Coop uses, with addresses), the
  [dead-ends note](spawning-a-new-character-in-ac4-black-flag-single-player-dea.md) and the
  [transform note](reading-the-player-s-world-transform-and-body-position-in-ac.md).
- Our earlier co-op attempt (the [ghost-avatar note](coop-ghost-avatar.md)) avoided spawning and
  *hijacked a crowd character*, overwriting its transform each frame. That works but looks like a ghost:
  no real animation. Kamzik's route is strictly better and is what this note endorses — **spawn a real
  puppet and replicate the player's actions**, not just the pose.
- No engine networking is used. AC4's own multiplayer (`AC4BFMP.exe`) is never touched; the coherence is
  the plugin's own UDP protocol.

## How the game works (what we had to learn)

**The peer puppet is a real entity, built from the local player's own cached builder.** The plugin does
not invent a character definition. It reads the local player's `PlayerProgression`, hands its cached
`EntityBuilder` to `EntityBuilder::BuildEntityWithSelector`, and inserts the result into the world with
`World::AddEntity`. A hook on `PlayerPadManager::GetUnusedPadID` tells the game which input pad the new
body belongs to. That is how you get a *second* real, renderable, animatable humanoid in single-player
without the model-swap project the ghost-avatar route was blocked on.

**The puppet is animated by action replication, not by moving a matrix.** The peer's body is driven by
calling `SetTargetAction` with the action the remote player is performing. That action feeds a **46-slot
locomotion blend tree** (the same tree the player's body uses), combined with the local player's
`CharacterActionSet`, a blend-in descriptor, and a **phase seek** (where in the clip to start) so a
mid-stride peer does not snap to the start of the animation. "Move the character's matrix each frame"
looks like a sliding puppet; "set the same action, with the same blend and phase" looks like a player.
With AC4Coop's shipped `AC4Coop.ini` (`HybridLoco=1`), the puppet's own state machine animates it on the
ground from replicated ground data, and action replication runs everywhere else; `HybridLoco=0` uses
action replication everywhere (AC4Coop's README).

**Ambient spawns are suppressed** (`DisableSpawns`) so the game does not keep populating the world around
the puppets while a co-op session runs.

**The launch chain is the trap.** AC4 does not boot as a single process. Its launcher/updater chain starts
*several* processes, and each of them loads the ASI in `DllMain`. Any of those transient processes can
reach the plugin's socket startup before the process that actually becomes the live game. That is the root
of the bug below.

## Build steps

1. Build AC4Coop from source as x86 (VS2022/MSBuild, `AC4Coop.sln`, Release|Win32; pass
   `/p:PlatformToolset=v143` if the v145 toolset isn't installed), so you can apply the three transport
   changes. The gameplay side (puppet build + action replication) is unchanged.
2. **Change 1 — do not start the network in `DllMain`.** Remove the `Net::Init()` call from module load
   (the `DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH` branch in `src/dllmain.cpp`).
3. **Change 2 — start the network on the first in-world frame.** Only the live game ever reaches a player
   frame (a transient launcher process does not). Initialise the net from a hook that runs once the world
   has a player, guarded so it happens exactly once.
4. **Change 3 — set `SO_REUSEADDR` on the socket before `bind()`**, so a lingering owner from a patched
   build does not turn the bind into `WSAEADDRINUSE`. This only helps when paired with change 2 — see the
   warning in Gotchas.
5. Copy the ASI and `AC4Coop.ini` next to `AC4BFSP.exe`. For two PCs, set `PeerIP` to the other PC's VPN
   address and `PeerPort=47801` (the same as `LocalPort`) on both, as the ini's comments say. Start both
   games and let each client reach the in-world frame.

## Verification

- **Two real machines, eye-witness, 2026-10-12 (the oracle for "it works").** A two-player session over
  **Radmin VPN** between two PCs: each side saw the other player's **puppet spawned and animated**
  (walking/running matched, not a sliding ghost). This is an in-game, eyeball check — the weakest oracle
  class, said so honestly — but it is a real two-machine link, not loopback. It is also an end-to-end
  check of AC4Coop's animation sync on a cached-builder puppet, which the spawn-route note lists as not
  driven from our own plugin.
- **The netstat symptom is itself a check.** `netstat -ano | findstr 47801` on the live machine before the
  fix showed the co-op port held by a PID that was **not** the live `AC4BFSP.exe` (the live game held only
  its native `9103`). After the fix, the live game is the process bound to `47801`. That turns a vague
  "no net" into a one-command diagnosis.
- **Direct UDP test:** before blaming the game, a standalone UDP send/receive between the two machines over
  Radmin succeeded, which pinned the fault on the plugin/socket, not the tunnel.
- Not verified: animation fidelity across packet loss, more than two players, long-session stability, and
  which launch-chain process took the port.

## Gotchas

1. **Puppet spawns but never moves; the live game has no net at all.** The plugin's UDP port is held by a
   PID from AC4's launch chain that is no longer running. **Cause:** the plugin called `Net::Init()` in
   `DllMain`; every process the launch chain starts loads the ASI, a throwaway one bound UDP `47801` and
   exited, and the port stayed bound, so the live game's later `bind()` failed with
   `WSAEADDRINUSE (10048)`. A socket normally closes when its process exits; it survives only while another
   process holds a handle to it, and Winsock sockets are inheritable by default, so a child process that
   inherited the handle is the likely holder (`netstat` keeps showing the creator's PID). That mechanism
   isn't confirmed here. **Fix:** don't init in `DllMain`; init on the first in-world frame (only the live
   game gets there) — see changes 1–2 above. Creating the socket with `WSA_FLAG_NO_HANDLE_INHERIT` (or
   clearing `HANDLE_FLAG_INHERIT` with `SetHandleInformation`) should also stop it leaking into child
   processes; untested.
2. **First fix attempt made it worse — and this is the important one.** Adding only `SO_REUSEADDR` and
   leaving the early init regressed: now the transient process *also* binds successfully, and its leftover
   socket **got the incoming datagrams** the live game should have received. **Cause:** `SO_REUSEADDR`
   lets both sockets bind, and Microsoft documents which one then receives as indeterminate
   ("Using SO_REUSEADDR and SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE"); a leftover socket never reads them. **Fix:** keep
   `SO_REUSEADDR` **paired with the deferred init**. With the deferred init no transient binds, so the live
   game is the port's only owner; `SO_REUSEADDR` then only gets it past a socket left over from an earlier
   launch, and delivery is undefined again in that case, so check with `netstat` that the live game is the
   only owner (or use a fresh port). Don't ship `SO_REUSEADDR` without the deferred init. Also, on current
   Windows a second `SO_REUSEADDR` bind to the wildcard address succeeds only if the socket already holding
   the port set `SO_REUSEADDR` too; against one bound without it (an unpatched build) it fails with
   `WSAEACCES` (the same Microsoft page, "Enhanced Socket Security").
3. **`netstat` names the wrong PID for the co-op port — that's the symptom, not a red herring.** A PID
   that is not `AC4BFSP.exe` holding `47801` is exactly the leftover-socket case. **Fix:** use it as the
   diagnostic; after the fix the live game holds `47801`.
4. **"Ping works" proves nothing about the link.** A successful ICMP ping between the two machines does
   **not** mean UDP gets through — different protocol, and firewalls/VPNs treat them differently.
   **Fix:** test UDP directly (a tiny send/receive pair), not with ping.
5. **Windows Firewall had to allow the game on the VPN's network profile.** A rule for `AC4BFSP.exe` that
   covered only some profiles left the tunnel blocked; the rule that worked applied to all profiles.
   Windows usually puts an unidentified network, such as a VPN adapter, on the Public profile. **Fix:**
   allow the game on the profile the VPN adapter is on, or on all profiles.
6. **Radmin VPN does carry the co-op UDP.** Once the socket was right, the link worked over Radmin — useful
   to know that the tunnel is not the suspect here. **Fix:** verify the socket/process first, the tunnel
   second (see the direct UDP test in Verification).

## Assets

None. The puppet is a runtime entity built from the player's own cached `EntityBuilder`; no new models or
textures are shipped.

## Cost and time

The co-op implementation itself (spawn + action replication) is Kamzik123's prior work. This session's cost
was almost entirely the transport bug: reading the launch chain, reproducing the leftover socket with
`netstat`, and finding that the obvious `SO_REUSEADDR` fix regresses on its own until it is paired with the
deferred init.

## Open questions

- Which launch-chain process loads the ASI and takes the port. Ultimate ASI Loader as `dinput8.dll` loads
  into any process from the game folder that loads `dinput8.dll`; Process Monitor's process tree during a
  launch would name it. Whether the deferred init can be made even more robust (e.g. bind only once a
  world with a player exists, and retry on failure).
- Animation fidelity under real packet loss and jitter (the session ran over a low-latency Radmin link).
- Whether the same deferred-bind pattern is needed for the sibling AC Rogue/other AnvilNext titles that
  share the launch-chain behaviour.

- **Kamzik123/AC4Coop** (<https://github.com/Kamzik123/AC4Coop>) — the co-op implementation: puppet spawn
  via the local player's cached `EntityBuilder`, action replication, and spawn suppression. The transport
  fix in this note is small and built entirely on that work.

# Reading the player's world transform and body position in AC4 Black Flag (native x86 ASI)

> Goal: a co-op replication layer for AC4 Black Flag — two players in one world. This note covers the
> part that is **verified working**: a 32-bit ASI plugin that loads into the single-player exe and
> reads the player's live world transform, plus the camera→target→**player body** chain found by a
> runtime probe. The second, drivable character is covered by the
> [spawn-route note](spawning-a-real-second-player-in-ac4-black-flag-the-working-.md) (a body built
> from the player's cached `EntityBuilder`) and the [ghost-avatar note](coop-ghost-avatar.md) (a
> hijacked crowd body).

## Setup
- **Game:** Assassin's Creed IV Black Flag, Steam (appid 242050), single-player exe **`AC4BFSP.exe`**
  — **x86 (32-bit)**, MD5 `2058342866688F780C8B34526A65BC35`, 45,056,040 bytes. AnvilNext engine
  ("scimitar" family — the same engine as AC Rogue). No anti-cheat; offline only.
- **Loader:** Ultimate ASI Loader **v9.7.4, x86** as `dinput8.dll` (**must be the 32-bit build**; a
  plugin for Rogue or any x64 title will not work). The plugin lives in `plugins\`.
- **Framework:** AC.PatchFix (SafetyHook + registry + config). It was **x64-only**; see Gotchas for
  the four files that had to be ported to build x86.
- **Analysis:** Ghidra 12.1.4 headless. **`AC4BFSP.exe` needs a large heap — 8 GB OOMs the x86
  analyzer; 20 GB works.** Dump helpers: functions/strings/string-refs + targeted decompiles.
- **Launches:** the game needs **Ubisoft Connect (`upc.exe`) running**, otherwise it silently exits
  without ever starting. No launch wedges were observed on this title.

## Route and why
Native hook (ASI + SafetyHook mid-hooks). There is no scripting layer and no modding SDK; the
engine's task scheduler is reachable by fixed RVA because the build is pinned. This mirrors the
approach that worked for AC Rogue, applied to the x86 Black Flag binary.

## How the game works (what we had to learn)
**Task-graph scheduler, same as Rogue.** Registrars build named task nodes:
- `FUN_00470b00` — engine-frame registrar; `FUN_00663590` — AI-world registrar.
- **`Ai::UpdateCamera` = `0x0063bbb0`** — a safe per-frame mid-hook target (its first callee,
  `FUN_0063ba70`, is the real camera update).

**Camera manager and its ring.** The manager global is **`0x02abe588`** (loaded in `FUN_0063ba70`
as `mov ecx,[0x02abe588]`). Its transform ring works like Rogue's:
- frame counter at `manager+0x130`, `% 5`;
- slot accessor `FUN_004ee120` → `manager + 0xE0 + idx*0x10` = **orientation quaternion**;
- the **position** ring is `manager + 0x90 + idx*0x10` — confirmed by its *writer* `FUN_005062e0`
  (advances the counter, copies the transform into `(idx+9)*0x10`).
- Globals: camera position `vec4` at **`0x02abe530`** and `0x02abe540` (produced by `FUN_0040bea0`).

**Camera object → player body.** `FUN_00417650` writes the camera position from the camera object:
`camobj = **(u32**)(manager+0x4C)`, with the camera position at `camobj+0x10` and orientation at
`camobj+0x20`. Following `camobj+0x68` gives the **camera target object**, whose `+0x50` holds the
**player's world body position** (see Verification).

**The reflection wall.** Engine type names (`EntityActor`, `AnimatedEntityComponent`,
`CameraTargetTracker`, `GetCharacterEntityOperator`, spawn types like `SpawnPlayerParams`) are
**reflection-table strings with no code xrefs** — you cannot grep from the name to the class. RTTI is
**partial** (mostly Havok/third-party), so classes must be identified by **vtable**, not by name.

## Build steps
1. Port the framework to x86 (see Gotchas), add a game target `ARCH x86` whose `exe_name` is
   `AC4BFSP.exe`, and hook `base + 0x23BBB0` (`Ai::UpdateCamera`).
2. Read the camera manager: `mgr = *(u32*)(base + 0x26BE588)`; then
   `idx = *(u32*)(mgr+0x130) % 5`; position `*(f32×3)(mgr+0x90+idx*0x10)`; quaternion
   `*(f32×4)(mgr+0xE0+idx*0x10)`.
3. Deploy `dinput8.dll` (x86 Ultimate ASI Loader) + `plugins\<Mod>.asi` (+ an INI; the framework
   watches it and hot-reloads).

## Verification
- **In-game, live:** the plugin loaded into `AC4BFSP.exe`, installed its hooks, and logged moving
  world coordinates with a valid unit quaternion:
  `pos=(-536.8,281.0,2.8) → (-490.3,358.7,3.3)`, `quat=(-0.019,-0.018,0.675,0.738)`.
- **Player body position confirmed by motion analysis.** A read-only probe logged the camera and the
  candidate field (`camobj+0x68 → +0x50`) at 4 Hz while the player walked then turned:
  - walking straight: the offset `candidate − camera` is **rock stable** at `(-0.3, -2.8, -0.6)`;
  - turning: the offset **rotates in the XY plane** (`(-0.3,-2.8) → (2.5,0) → (0.5,+2.3)`) — the
    camera orbits a **fixed world point**, which is the player's body.
- **NOT verified here:** anything to do with the multiplayer exe (`AC4BFMP.exe` was only
  string/reversed as a design reference, never run online).
- **Not covered here:** a second, drivable character. The
  [spawn-route note](spawning-a-real-second-player-in-ac4-black-flag-the-working-.md) builds one from the
  player's cached `EntityBuilder` (verified live, two Edwards), and the
  [ghost-avatar note](coop-ghost-avatar.md) drives a hijacked crowd body.

## Gotchas
1. **32-bit, always.** `AC4BFSP.exe` is x86 — the ASI loader, the plugin, and every address
   computation must be 32-bit. A 64-bit loader (e.g. one installed for a Rogue/x64 mod) will simply
   not load the plugin.
2. **RVA arithmetic: subtract the image base carefully.** The camera-manager global is
   `0x02abe588`; with base `0x400000` the RVA is `0x026BE588` (not `0x26ABE588`). The wrong value
   read a bogus address and failed *safely* (null manager, no crash) — but it silently produced no data.
3. **Ghidra heap on the x86 analyzer.** 8 GB OOM'd on the 43 MB exe; 20 GB completed. A failed run
   leaves a project marker (`*.gpr`) that blocks the retry — delete the project files before re-running.
4. **Reflection names have no xrefs.** `EntityActor`, `AnimatedEntityComponent`, `CameraTargetTracker`,
   spawn type names, etc. exist only in a reflection table. Don't plan a "grep to the class" path; use
   vtables (a runtime vtable dump) instead.
5. **`g_MainPlayerPosition` is a shader uniform**, not a CPU global — it appears next to
   `g_EyeDirection`, `g_DisolveFactor`, etc., and has no code xrefs. It looks tempting; it isn't the
   player position you want.
6. **The plugin log rotates at ~1 MB** — copy long captures out promptly or lose them.
7. **Ubisoft Connect must be running** or the game silently exits before the window appears.
8. **Use a read-only discovery pass before risky calls.** Dumping pointers/vtables/floats first (with
   every pointer `VirtualQuery`-guarded) tells you the layout; only then attempt writes.

## Assets
None. The plugin ships code only; no game files.

## Cost and time
Several sessions; the reconnaissance and the x86 framework port are the bulk. The in-game reads are
cheap once the addresses are pinned.

## Open questions
- Which **class** is the camera target object (the one holding the player body position at `+0x50`)?
  Next step: dump its vtable at runtime and identify it in Ghidra.
- The co-op gate, a second drivable character, is answered in the
  [spawn-route note](spawning-a-real-second-player-in-ac4-black-flag-the-working-.md): build it from
  the player's cached `EntityBuilder` (`EntityBuilder::BuildEntityWithSelector` → `World::AddEntity`,
  plus the `GetUnusedPadID` hook), Kamzik123's [AC4Coop](https://github.com/Kamzik123/AC4Coop)
  method. The BF MP exe's `NetPlayer` field-replication offsets (`0x80/0xe8/0x128/0x1f8/0x170`,
  move-mode `+0x398`) remain the design reference for *replicating* a body once it exists. For
  animation, AC4Coop replicates actions (`SetTargetAction` and the blend tree) rather than bones; a
  spawned body has no walk children (`c14+0x134 == 0`), so a bone mirror makes it glide.
- Cross-machine entity identity (64-bit entity ids appear in BF's debug strings).
