# Porting a skinned StarCraft II character onto the SWBF2 (2005) infantry skeleton

> A private, personal mod for Star Wars Battlefront II (2005, Steam): a StarCraft II "story mode" Marine model,
> read from the player's own SC2 install, replaces the basic clone trooper on a stock map, fully animated by the
> stock `human` animation bank. Route: data/addon (official mod tools + Blender), no game file modified.
> Verified in the real game (Instant Action, spawn screen and 3rd-person screenshots, running/strafing/aiming).
> No assets are shared here, only the method. The converted Marine is Blizzard's model and textures, so the addon
> stays on the user's own machine (see Assets).

## Setup
- SWBF2 Steam appid 6060, buildid 6217431 (`Galaxy.dll` present = the 2017 GOG Galaxy multiplayer update).
  `um scan` does not recognise the Zero Engine ("Unknown native engine") and proposes a native-hook route: ignore
  it, the community route is the official mod tools + `GameData\addon\<3-letter ID>\`.
- Mod tools: "SWBF2 Mod Tools SDK 2020" (ModDB, `BF2_ModTools.1.zip`, 562 198 681 bytes, MD5 published on the
  page). ModDB blocks scripted downloads (HTTP 403), a real browser works. Extract to `C:\BF2_ModTools` (no
  spaces, short path: the zip holds 18k files, 1.4 GB).
- Blender: `SWBF-msh-Blender-IO` 1.5.3 (Calrissian97 fork; it states Blender 5.0+ support) for .msh import/export.
  `m3studio` (no releases, use the repo) for StarCraft II .m3 import: **it does not run on Blender 5.x**
  (about 20 lines use `Action.fcurves`, which Blender 5.0 removed), so a portable Blender 4.5 LTS is needed for
  the m3 side.
- Reading SC2 data: CASC storage with an MNDX root. `CascView` is GUI-only; the .NET `CascLib` from
  WoW-Tools/CASCExplorer supports SC2 (`CASCGameType.S2`) and builds for net8.0 with
  `-p:TargetFrameworks=net8.0` (pass a NuGet source explicitly if none is configured).

## Route and why
Data/asset route. A new side lvl containing one class whose `ClassParent` is the stock clone class, loaded by a
custom mission (stock world + stock sides + the new side) registered from `addme.lua`. Everything lives in the
addon folder; nothing in `GameData\data` is touched. A native route makes no sense here: the toolchain already
does everything.

Other ports of a skinned character onto a host skeleton in the KB: the per-bone fit onto Risk of Rain 2's Commando
rig (`games/risk-of-rain-2/helldiver-survivor.md`) and Halo 3 characters rigid-skinned to their dominant bone
(`games/halo-3-mcc/halo-3-weapons-covenant-vehicles-and-maps-ported-into-minecr.md`).

## How the game works (what we had to learn)
- **Class inheritance across lvl files works at runtime.** `ReadDataFile("dc:SIDE\\scb.lvl", "<class>")` after
  `ReadDataFile("SIDE\\rep.lvl", ..., "rep_inf_ep3_rifleman", ...)`: a class whose `ClassParent` is
  `rep_inf_ep3_rifleman` inherits weapons, sounds, animation bank, etc. The side lvl only carries the odf, the
  .msh files and the textures (9 MB). Load the parent lvl first.
- **Infantry skeleton** (from `rep_inf_ep3trooper.msh`): 43 bones (`bone_root`, `bone_pelvis`,
  `bone_a_spine`/`b_spine`/`ribcage`, `bone_neck`/`head`, `bone_{l,r}_{clavicle,upperarm,forearm,hand,thigh,calf,
  foot,toe}`, `hp_weapons` + `root_*`/`eff_*` helpers). Bind pose is a **T-pose facing +Y** (in Blender after
  import), 2.08 m tall. The animations drive the bone translations too, so a new mesh must match the clone's
  proportions; you cannot ship a bigger skeleton for the `human` bank.
- **Skinning**: the clone mesh uses exactly one bone per vertex (21 vertex groups). The msh addon docs note that
  SWBF2 PC only appears to honour one weight; rigid skinning to the dominant bone works fine for armour.
- **Soldier .msh.option**: `-lodgroup soldier -nocollision` (the clone also has `-keepmaterial override_texture`).
  `GeometryLowRes` in the odf points to a second, low-poly msh.
- **Localization files** (`Common\Localize\<lang>.cfg`): nested `VarScope("...")` blocks with `VarBinary("key")`
  entries holding `Size(n)` and `Value("hex")` lines (64 hex digits per line). The payload is a 4-byte prefix
  followed by UTF-16LE text, `Size` counts both, and every byte is written as two hex digits **with the nibbles
  swapped** (0x53 -> "35"). What the prefix holds varies: this port found the first 4 letters of the top-level
  scope (`enti`, `mapn`, `leve`), while community cfg files (e.g. the Gametoast un-official patch's
  `CustomLVL/localize/English.cfg`) have `00000000` or small integers there. Keys: unit name
  `entity.<side>.<rest of class name>` (class `scb_inf_marine` -> `entity.scb.inf_marine`), map name
  `mapname.name.<map id>`, `mapname.description.<map id>`.
- **SC2 story-mode models** (`Assets/StoryModeCharacters/...`): control bones `<PREFIX>Ctrl_<Joint>_SkinPoint`
  (prefix varies per model, e.g. `MPT_` vs `MR3_`), up to 4 weights per vertex, ~0.8 units tall, A-pose. They do
  **not** share a facing (one looked down -Y, another down +X). Their diffuse **alpha is not team colour**: the
  material binds it as an ambient-occlusion layer read through the **second UV set (UV1)**. Normal maps store X
  in alpha and Y in green. The m3 importer adds an `EDGE_SPLIT` modifier on every mesh.

## Build steps
1. Copy `BF2_ModTools\data` to `data_<ID>` and the `TEMPLATE` folder into it, replacing `@#$` with the ID in file
   names and contents (what VisualMunge does). Fix the localization files (Gotcha 2).
2. Mission: copy the stock mission script you want (mod tools `assets\scripts\<world>\`), add the new side read
   and swap the class in `SetupTeams`. `Common\mission.req` lists it under `"lvl"`. `addme.lua` adds a
   `sp_/mp_missionselect_listbox_contents` entry and `AddDownloadableContent("<ID>", "<mission>", 4)`.
3. Side: `Sides\<ID>\odf\<class>.odf` (`ClassParent`, `GeometryName`, `GeometryLowRes`, movement tweaks),
   `req\<class>.req` (`"class"`), `<ID>.req` (`"lvl"`), msh + tga; `_BUILD\Sides\<ID>\munge.bat` =
   `@call ..\munge_side.bat <ID> %1`.
4. Character conversion in Blender 4.5 (scripted):
   - import the m3 with rig; keep the body pieces by their M3 material name, drop rifle/flare meshes;
   - rotate the rig so ankle->toe points +Y (snap to 90 degrees), scale ~2.5;
   - on the SC2 pose bones: `COPY_LOCATION` to the matching clone bone heads, `STRETCH_TO` (no volume) per limb
     segment, `inherit_scale = NONE` on every bone, shoulder pads without rotation inheritance, a `DAMPED_TRACK`
     on the wrists along the clone forearm; lift ankle/toe targets per side until each sole is at z = 0;
   - bake the evaluated meshes in world space, carry corner normals over as custom normals, assign each vertex to
     one BF2 bone from its dominant SC2 group (pads -> clavicle, fingers -> hand, helmet/visor -> head);
   - parent to the clone `skeleton`, delete the clone body and its `sv_` mesh, export with triangle strips on and
     modifiers off. Low LOD: decimate ~0.08, then re-rigidify the weights.
5. Textures: Cycles `EMIT` bake into UV0 of `diffuse.rgb(UV0) * diffuse.a(UV1)`, then multiply in a fixed key
   light computed from the normal map, put the specular map in alpha, 1024 x 1024 TGA.
6. Munge: `munge.bat /COMMON` and `munge.bat /SIDE <ID>` from `data_<ID>\_BUILD` (Gotcha 1), scriptmunge
   `addme.lua -platform pc`. Copy `addme.script`, `_LVL_PC\mission.lvl`, **`_LVL_PC\core.lvl`** and
   `_LVL_PC\SIDE\<id>.lvl` into `GameData\addon\<ID>\` (+ `data\_LVL_PC\...`).

## Verification
- In Blender before munging: apply stock `.msh` animations (`human_0\human_rifle_stand_runforward.msh`, shoot,
  sprint) to the converted rig with the addon's "Import Animation(s)" and render frames. Control: the same
  harness on the stock clone msh, so a broken render is known to be our mesh, not the harness. Round-trip:
  re-import the exported .msh and animate it again.
- In game: retail exe windowed (`/win /resolution 1280 720`, or via `steam://rungameid/6060`), Instant Action,
  screenshots of the spawn screen (front view) and of 3rd-person running/strafing. The new map name and the
  French UI strings were read off the screenshots.
- Not verified: performance with many units on screen beyond a short playtest, multiplayer, shadow volumes,
  normal-mapped rendertypes on skinned soldiers.

## Gotchas
1. **`munge.bat` "is not recognized" although it exists.** **Cause:** the environment had
   `NoDefaultCurrentDirectoryInExePath=1`, so cmd does not run programs from the current folder and every nested
   `call munge.bat` fails. **Fix:** `cmd /c "set NoDefaultCurrentDirectoryInExePath=&& cd /d ...\_BUILD && munge.bat /COMMON ..."`.
2. **mission.lvl builds but does not contain your mission; log shows "Could not open munged\pc\core.files".**
   **Cause:** in the SDK 2020 repack, the six `Common\Localize\<lang>.cfg` files (english, french, german,
   italian, spanish, uk_english) lack the final closing `}`, localizemunge fails, core.lvl is not packed, and
   every mission levelpack that uses `-common core.files` is skipped. **Fix:** append `}` to each file (count the
   braces first).
3. **Re-munging does not fix a broken output.** **Cause:** `-checkdate` keeps the earlier failed outputs
   (8-byte core.lvl/common.lvl). **Fix:** delete `_BUILD\Common\MUNGED` and `_LVL_PC` (and the side's `MUNGED`)
   before rebuilding.
4. **Every text in an addon mission shows as raw keys (`ifs.SpawnDisplay.Spawn`, `0x1274B8E0`, `[NULL]`)** while
   stock maps are fine. **Cause:** the addon shipped no `core.lvl`; VisualMunge normally copies one.
   **Fix:** copy the munged `_LVL_PC\core.lvl` (it contains every language from the mod tools localization plus
   your own keys) to `addon\<ID>\data\_LVL_PC\` and add
   `ReadDataFile("..\\..\\addon\\<ID>\\data\\_LVL_PC\\core.lvl")` at the top of `addme.lua` for the menu.
5. **The mod tools' `BF2_modtools.exe` (debug console + `BFront2.log`) asks for "CD 1" with the Steam install.**
   We didn't work around the disc check: that would be a DRM bypass. **Fix:** test with the retail exe and
   screenshots instead. The game rewrites `GameData\bf2cmd.txt` with its command line on every
   launch (original content was a lone CRLF): restore it if you keep a manifest of the game folder.
6. **Launching `BattlefrontII.exe` directly sometimes exits silently** (Steam relaunch). **Fix:**
   `steam://rungameid/6060`; the window mode/resolution from a previous `/win` launch was remembered.
7. **Menus ignore synthetic mouse clicks.** **Cause:** DirectInput mouse with its own cursor. Relative moves
   (`rel dx dy`) move the game cursor 1:1 and a click only lands when the game cursor is already on the target;
   Enter works with scancode input. **Fix:** let the human click through Instant Action, or navigate with
   relative moves.
8. **Converted character animates with long spikes everywhere.** **Cause:** the m3 importer's `EDGE_SPLIT`
   modifier changes vertex count/order (2 758 -> 2 764, 245 -> 287), so dominant-bone lookups done on the source
   mesh indices were shifted. **Fix:** read the vertex groups from the **evaluated** mesh
   (`bpy.data.meshes.new_from_object(..., preserve_all_data_layers=True)` keeps the deform weights).
9. **"Camouflage" blotches on the armour in game.** **Cause:** the SC2 story-mode diffuse alpha was treated as a
   team-colour mask; it is ambient occlusion bound to UV1, so sampling it with UV0 makes random patches.
   **Fix:** bake `rgb(UV0) * alpha(UV1)` into UV0 (Cycles emission bake) and drop team colour. Also check the
   actual RGB before choosing a model: one story Marine was steel-grey, another blue.
10. **Model faces backwards after conversion.** **Cause:** SC2 story models are not all oriented the same way.
    **Fix:** compute the facing from ankle -> toe bone heads instead of a fixed 180 degree turn.
11. **Hands sink into the chest and the legs rub when running.** **Cause:** a bulky armoured mesh driven by the
    slim clone's animations. **Fix (partial):** flatten the front of the torso (~70 %), slim forearms/gauntlets
    across the limb axis (~85 %), slim only the inner half of each leg (~70 %) and push the legs outwards a few
    cm. Too much leg slimming made the legs look thin; small residual contacts remain.
12. **`git clone` / portable Blender fail in the agent's working folder** ("Filename too long", "$GIT_DIR too
    big", "side-by-side configuration is incorrect"). **Cause:** a desktop app's sandboxed scratch folder was
    redirected to a very long path. **Fix:** move the project to a short real path (e.g. under Documents).
13. **`um scan` misdetects StarCraft II as a .NET game** (because of a third-party campaign launcher in the
    folder). Harmless for read-only extraction.

## Assets
All art comes from the user's own StarCraft II install (read-only, never redistributed): one story-mode character
model and its body textures, converted as described above. No generated assets. The converted model and textures
are still Blizzard's, so keep the built addon private: don't upload it (ModDB, Nexus) or hand it to other players
for a multiplayer match. A shareable version needs original art in its place. Movement was tuned in the odf
(MaxHealth 550, MaxSpeed 6, MaxStrafeSpeed 4.5, MaxTurnSpeed 4, JumpHeight 1.1, Acceleration 30,
SprintAccelerateTime 0.6; stock values live in the mod tools' `data\Common\odfs\com_inf_default.odf`).

## Cost and time
About 4 h 35 for the first character including tool setup and three visual iterations; the pipeline is now
scripted.

## Open questions
- Weapon: the character still holds the clone rifle; a custom weapon msh and the grip pose are next.
- Shadow volume (`sv_`) and normal-mapped rendertypes on skinned soldiers were not tried.
- Converting the SC2 model animations into SWBF2 animation banks would remove the residual clipping and unlock
  non-humanoid creatures; not attempted yet.

# Starfield animation (.af/.rig) and physics (Havok 2019.02)

> Starfield splits its two "Havok-shaped" problems apart. **Physics/collision still uses Havok** —
> the 2019.02 chunked packfile format. **Animation does not**: BGS dropped Havok and ships custom
> `.af` (animation) and `.rig` (skeleton) formats. Animation tooling works as a Blender addon and
> needs no script extender.

## Setup

- **Game:** Starfield (Bethesda, 2023), Creation Engine 2, PC.
- **Animation:** BGS custom `.af` + `.rig`, handled by **CALUMI.Animation** (a conversion DLL,
  Calaverah, LGPLv3) and the **`sf_animation_io`** Blender addon (Deveris256, v1.0.0 2026-03-18)
  that wraps it. Works in **Blender 4.3**; **does not need SFSE** (Script Extender).
- **Physics/collision:** Havok **2019.02** chunked packfile (`SDKV="20190200"`, tags
  `TAG0/SDKV/DATA/TYPE/INDX/PTCH`). Parser: `StarfieldMeshConverter` (Blender 3.5/3.6 Geometry
  Bridge), whose scope is models, morph, geometry and physics — **not** animation.
- **Samples used:** `bipeda_skeleton.rig` (13.7 KB) plus four `.af` animations
  (`relaxed_walkforward_start`, `staggerbackwardmedium`, `threat_curious01`, `walkbackward`).

## Route and why

Asset-only, via existing open tools. Starfield's animation is not Havok, so no Havok SDK is involved;
the shortest path is the CALUMI DLL through the Blender addon. For physics, the chunked format is
self-describing enough that the 2019.02 parser reads it without an SDK (see the HKX technique note).

## How the game works (what we had to learn)

- **Animation was deliberately taken off Havok.** `.af`/`.rig` are BGS-custom containers; do not try
  to feed them to a Havok tool.
- **Physics stayed on Havok**, at 2019.02, in the newer *chunked tagfile* shape (not the FO4-era
  classic packfile). The chunk tags match the WDL 2017.2.0 family, so the same parser structure
  applies.
- **No SFSE dependency for animation** — the conversion is pure file I/O, so it runs as a Blender
  addon rather than an in-process game hook.

## Build steps

1. Install the `sf_animation_io` Blender addon (Blender 4.3); it bundles/uses CALUMI.Animation.
2. Convert `.af`/`.rig` samples to a Blender-importable form and inspect the skeleton/animations.
3. For physics/collision, use `StarfieldMeshConverter` (models/morph/geometry/physics) — not the
   animation addon.

## Verification

- Format identification is verified by inspection: `.rig`/`.af` are handled by CALUMI, and the
  physics chunk header decodes to `sdk_version="20190200"`.
- The parser repo (`StarfieldMeshConverter`) was confirmed up to date with upstream at the time
  (HEAD `00e5529`).
- **NOT verified:** in-game round-trip of an edited animation, and anything requiring SFSE. Treat this
  note as tooling/format knowledge, not a released mod.

## Gotchas

1. **Don't route animation through Havok tools.** **Symptom:** a Havok parser rejects a Starfield
   animation file. **Cause:** Starfield animation is BGS-custom, not Havok. **Fix:** use
   CALUMI.Animation / `sf_animation_io`.
2. **Physics and animation are separate pipelines.** **Symptom:** a "Starfield mesh" tool ignores
   animation. **Cause:** `StarfieldMeshConverter` is scoped to models/morph/geometry/physics.
   **Fix:** pick the tool by the data type.
3. **The 2019.02 chunk layout is not the FO4 layout.** **Symptom:** a classic-packfile parser fails on
   Starfield physics. **Cause:** 2019.02 is a chunked tagfile. **Fix:** use a chunked parser; the WDL
   2017.2.0 reference works.
4. **No SFSE assumption.** **Symptom:** you plan an in-game hook for a format task. **Cause:**
   assuming animation needs runtime access. **Fix:** it is offline file conversion; a Blender addon
   suffices.

## Assets

Not applicable — this note is about reading/converting existing game assets, not authoring new ones.

## Cost and time

Not recorded.

## Open questions

- In-game verification of an edited `.af`/`.rig` round-trip.
- A complete field-level spec of `.af`/`.rig` (CALUMI is the current de-facto decoder).
- Whether any Starfield physics path needs the Havok SDK, or whether chunked parsing is always enough.

# A custom fighter in Super Smash Bros. Melee: m-ex dat code, ISO patching and Dolphin verification

> Put a working custom fighter (a Naruto moveset) into an m-ex build of Super Smash Bros. Melee by
> repurposing Mario's slot: C code compiled by **MexTK** into the fighter's own `PlMr.dat` as an
> `ftFunction` symbol, patched into a **copy** of the ISO through its file system table, and proven in
> the running game from **Dolphin's OSReport log**. No DOL edits, no ISO rebuild. Verified end to end:
> an in-`OnLoad` marker fired at match start, and the patched DAT was read back out of the ISO and
> hash-matched to the build.

## Setup

- **Game:** Super Smash Bros. Melee, **NTSC-U 1.02** (`GALE01`, revision 2), GameCube, dumped from a disc
  you own; don't download disc images. Emulated in **Dolphin**. Record the MD5 of your own dump and keep one
  pristine ISO; build the mod on a **copy**, never the base.
- **Framework:** **m-ex** ("Melee EX") is the mod framework behind **Akaneia Build** and other m-ex
  builds — this note used **Akaneia Build v1.0.1**. Akaneia ships as a patch: its builder applies it to your
  own clean 1.02 ISO, and its README gives the MD5 of both the clean and the patched image. m-ex overloads
  fighters/items/stages at runtime; fighters remain plain HAL `Pl*.dat` files inside the disc's FST.
- **Toolchain (Windows):** **devkitPPC** from **devkitPro** (the `powerpc-eabi-*` toolchain) and
  **MexTK** (the DAT compiler, shipped with m-ex). **HSDRaw** for reading DATs. **MexManager** (GUI) if
  you need to build a whole ISO, add a fighter slot or edit menus. **doldecomp/melee** as the
  symbol/struct reference.
- **Safety:** no anti-cheat involved; offline/single-player only. Ship patches and tools, never an ISO
  or extracted assets. The built `PlMr.dat` starts from the game's own file, so it is a game file with your
  code attached: share the C source and the build steps (or a binary diff against the player's own file),
  not the DAT.
- **Related:** Melee's decompiled engine running as a native DLL inside Terraria, with Slippi Dolphin as
  the oracle:
  [the Melee-in-Terraria note](../terraria/super-smash-bros-melee-s-decompiled-engine-inside-terraria-a.md),
  [hosting a decompiled engine](../../techniques/hosting-a-decompiled-console-engine-as-a-native-dll-inside-a.md)
  and [bit-exact decomp ports](../../techniques/bit-exact-decomp-ports-reproduce-the-original-compiler-s-and.md).

## Route and why

`route: loader-api`. m-ex is the loader: you write C, MexTK compiles it and attaches it to a fighter
DAT as a **symbol**, and m-ex relocates that code into RAM at boot and installs it into the fighter's
function table. You never edit the DOL.

Alternatives considered:

- **A brand-new fighter slot** needs MexManager to build the ISO, add the slot and edit the CSS, plus
  work for the character-select entry. Repurposing an existing slot is far cheaper and inherits a
  complete, working fighter and its menu entry — so we took over Mario's slot.
- **Editing the DOL** to add a fighter fights the framework and gains nothing over the DAT route.

## How the game works (what we had to learn)

**Fighter files.** Two DATs per fighter matter:

- `Pl<Xx>.dat` — the fighter's **code**: function table, move logic, items, attributes, model.
- `Pl<Xx><costume>.dat` — the **model and textures** for one costume (`PlMrNr.dat` = Mario Neutral).

`Xx` is HAL's internal two-letter fighter ID (`PlMr` Mario, `PlFx` Fox, `PlPp` Popo, `PlNr` Nana,
`PlCa` Captain Falcon, …).

**m-ex code injection.** MexTK adds one of two DAT symbols:

- **`ftFunction`** — the fighter function table: `OnLoad`, `move_logic`, the special-move states, etc.
- **`itFunction`** — the fighter's **item** behaviours (fireball, cape…).

At boot, m-ex's `Init ftFunction` finds the symbol, copies the attached code into RAM, **relocates** it
against the DOL's symbols, and stores it in the fighter's function table. `Init itFunction` does the
same for items. The engine never sees a patched DOL.

**The two attribute fields.** In the `Fighter` struct (see `ft/types.h` in the decomp):

- `dat_attrs` (`fp + 0x2D4`; m-ex name `special_attributes`) — the pointer the move code reads its
  tunables through.
- `dat_attrs_backup` (`fp + 0x2D8`; m-ex name `special_attributes2`) — the real storage.

The engine **does not initialise `dat_attrs`** for you. The fighter's `OnLoad` must point it at the
storage. If it doesn't, the engine's built-in `LoadSpecialAttrs` copies the fighter's default
attributes *through a garbage pointer*.

**Items and MxDt.** Fighter items are declared with `itFunction` and resolved through **`MxDt.dat`**,
which maps `(fighter, item slot) → ItemDesc`. MexTK cannot write `MxDt`; MexManager does, when it
builds the ISO. If `itFunction` declares items the ISO has no `MxDt` entries for, m-ex aborts at match
load.

**ISO and FST.** Disc images are 2048-byte sectors. The file system table offset/size live at ISO
offsets `0x424`/`0x428`; each FST entry is 12 bytes (`typeAndNameOff`, `fileOff`, `fileLen`) with the
name table after the entry array. A DAT that grows can simply be appended to the image and the FST
entry repointed.

**Dolphin is the oracle.** OSReport output goes to `<profile>\Logs\dolphin.log`.

## Build steps

1. Install **devkitPPC** and get **m-ex + MexTK**. Make one junction at `C:\devkitpro` pointing at the
   real devkitPro tree, and always call MexTK through a small wrapper — on Windows it looks for the
   compiler at that literal path (`C:/devkitpro/devkitPPC/` in its `Compiling.cs`) and ignores
   `DEVKITPRO`/`DEVKITPPC` (it reads `DEVKITPPC` only on other OSes).
2. Start from a **working template** (m-ex ships `examples/mario/src/mario.c`). Copy its `OnLoad` body
   and edit around it — never hand-roll `OnLoad`.
3. Build **ft-only**, starting from the game's own `PlMr.dat` so the build's attributes/model survive:

   ```bat
   copy /Y "PlMr.orig.dat" "PlMr.dat"
   mex.cmd -ff -i "src\naruto.c" -s ftFunction -dat "PlMr.dat" -ow
   ```

   MexTK prints the function table with a mark per overridden entry — check the ones you meant to
   override actually got overridden.

4. Patch the DAT into a **copy** of the ISO through the FST. If it fits, write in place; if it grew,
   append and **pad the image to a 0x8000 (32 KiB) boundary**.
5. **Verify by hash**, not by timestamp: read the DAT back out of the ISO and compare MD5 with your
   build.
6. Launch Dolphin with a profile that logs OSReport output (`-u <profile> -e <iso>`) and read
   `Logs\dolphin.log`.

## Verification

- **Oracle: Dolphin's OSReport log on a fresh boot.** An `OSReport("ft...: OnLoad ran\n")` in `OnLoad`
  appeared when the character loaded and the match started — proof the dat code was relocated and
  executing. Per-state markers then prove an input routes into your code.
- **ISO round-trip:** the patched DAT read back out of the image was byte-identical to the build; the
  texture DAT was unchanged.
- **Not verified at the time of writing:** the full moveset under live match conditions, texture
  replacement, and custom item behaviours. A savestate must **not** be used to verify a DAT change —
  the code a state captured is already in RAM; always fresh-boot.

## Gotchas

1. **`Invalid write to 0x3f…, PC = 0x…` dialog at match start.** **Cause:** a minimal `OnLoad`
   replaced the vanilla one and dropped the attribute init, so `dat_attrs` was heap garbage and vanilla
   `LoadSpecialAttrs` wrote through it (the `PC` sits inside it). Dolphin treats it as a non-fatal MMU
   warning, but the fighter's attributes were never initialised. **Fix:** set `dat_attrs` in `OnLoad`
   (m-ex: `special_attributes = special_attributes2`); copy the working template's `OnLoad`.
2. **`error: MxDt does not contain any items for fighter N` / `assertion "0" failed in m-ex` at match
   load, not boot.** **Cause:** built `-s itFunction` (items) but the ISO's `MxDt.dat` has no entries
   for that fighter, and MexTK cannot write `MxDt`. **Fix:** build `-s ftFunction` only until you have
   `MxDt` entries (add them via MexManager); meanwhile have the move spawn a vanilla item by ID.
3. **`The disc could not be read` on boot after a patch.** **Cause:** the appended file left the image
   tail unaligned to 32 KiB, or the FST entry was written wrong. **Fix:** pad the image to
   `0x8000`; re-read the FST entry.
4. **An ISO edit "succeeded" but the game still runs the old code.** **Cause:** copying over an ISO a
   running Dolphin held open — Windows lets the copy succeed silently and preserves the source's
   timestamp, so the file's mtime lies; writers then fail later with "being used by another process".
   **Fix:** close the emulator first; replace; then read the file back and compare MD5.
5. **MexTK can't find the compiler, or gcc dies with `cannot execute 'cc1'`.** **Cause:** devkitPPC is
   not at the literal path MexTK expects (`C:\devkitpro\devkitPPC\bin`); the environment variables are
   ignored on Windows; when the compiler isn't there, MexTK tries the same path relative to the working
   directory, so a stray `devkitpro` folder in the cwd gets used instead. **Fix:** exactly one junction, at
   `C:\devkitpro`, nothing named `devkitpro` in the cwd, and a wrapper script.
6. **`MexTK.exe -h` crashes.** **Cause:** `-h` expects a command after it and reads past the end of the
   arguments without one. **Fix:** `MexTK.exe -h -ff` prints the fighter-function help; no arguments at
   all prints the general usage.
7. **A savestate "confirms" a DAT change.** **Cause:** the code is already in RAM. **Fix:** fresh boot
   for every verification.
8. **You can't see the emulator to read an error dialog.** **Fix:** OSReport markers plus the log;
   OCR a screenshot for menu/error text; ask the human.

## Assets

Not done yet. The plan is standard Melee costume work: edit the base costume DAT's textures by walking
the HSD tree **JOBJ → DOBJ → MOBJ → TOBJ**, replacing a TOBJ's image and re-encoding it to that
TOBJ's native GX format (nearest-neighbour resize to the TOBJ's own dimensions).

## Cost and time

Several sessions; the cost was almost entirely two surprises (the item `MxDt` assert and the
`dat_attrs` attribute trap), both diagnosed rather than stumbled past.

## Open questions

- Register the fighter's items in `MxDt.dat` (m-ex/MexManager format for the build in use) to unlock
  custom `ItemDesc`s, or keep mapping item slots to vanilla item IDs.
- Replace the cloned special moves with real ones.
- Do a truly new fighter **slot** via MexManager (menu/CSS work), rather than repurposing a slot.

# An RL agent that beats the Eye of Cthulhu: decompiled boss AI to a simulator, then back into the real game

> The Eye of Cthulhu fight was ported from Terraria's decompiled source into a vectorized simulator: boss
> AI, servants, player physics, gun and damage rules. A PufferLib PPO agent trained in it (99.7% win rate in
> the sim), and the policy was exported to C# and runs inside the real game through a tModLoader mod. Real
> traces were replayed against the sim until they matched.

## Setup
- **Decompiles:** Terraria 1.4.5.8 with `ilspycmd` into a folder outside the repo. tModLoader's 1.4.4.9
  base decompiled too. The two were diffed: the Eye's AI is identical, apart from refactors like
  `ClearTarget()` vs `target = 255`.
- **Training:** Python 3.12 with PufferLib 3.0.0, locally on an RTX 4090 and on fal serverless H100s.
- **In game:** a tModLoader mod builds an arena identical to the sim, runs fights back to back, and logs
  results plus per-frame traces.

## Route and why
The loader API for the in-game half. The interesting part is **reimplementation-as-simulator**: the real
game runs at 60 fps with rendering, far too slow for RL. A faithful port of just the fight runs about 170k
steps/s.

## How the game works (what we had to learn)
- **The Eye:** NPC aiStyle 4, two phases, dashes and hovers. Its servants use aiStyle 5.
- **Player movement:** acceleration, max speed, jump height/time and gravity all come straight from the
  player update code.
- **Damage:** variance, defense and crits, hurt immunity frames, knockback.
- **Gun:** Minishark + musket balls, fire rate, projectile speed.
- **Time:** the fight's state machine is driven by `ai[]` counters that tick per frame.
- **Obs/action space:** 52 floats. MultiDiscrete [move 3, jump 2, fire 2, aim 32].

## Build steps
1. Decompile, then read `NPC.AI` for aiStyle 4/5 and the player update. Write a vectorized numpy port;
   later a numba one, float32-exact with the numpy version.
2. Wrap it as a PufferLib env and train PPO (30M local steps → 35% wins; 150M → 99.7%).
3. Export the policy MLP to plain C# weights. The mod reads the same observation every 3 frames and drives
   the player's controls.
4. Record real fights and compare them to the sim with trace replay.

## Verification
- **Trace replay:** feed the real game's state at frame t and its action into the sim, then compare the
  sim's t+1 to the real t+1, per variable.
- **Sim-to-real:** win rate over many fights in the real game.

## Gotchas
1. **Trace replay disagreed on every dash.**
   - **Cause:** the action applied on frame t takes effect on t+1; the sim was applying it one frame early.
   - **Fix:** apply frame t+1's action. The Eye's velocity then matched 99.9%.
2. **The numba sim slowly diverged from the numpy one.**
   - **Cause:** `0.2` (float64) is not `0.2f`.
   - **Fix:** use float32 constants and literals everywhere, like the C# does.
3. **The player moved faster in the real game than in the sim.**
   - **Cause:** a hidden buff. Standing near sunflowers gives *Happy!*, which is x1.21 move speed.
   - **Fix:** block the buff in the arena. Replays find what reading the code misses.
4. **PufferLib 3.0.0's sdist wouldn't build.**
   - **Cause:** its bundled demo C environments fail to compile.
   - **Fix:** build a wheel with `NO_OCEAN=1` and a one-line `setup.py` fix. It pins numpy<2 and its torch
     ABI.
5. **Serverless training failed to start.**
   - **Cause:** the key in use was a model-API key without serverless permissions.
   - **Fix:** `fal auth login` (device flow, approved by the human).
6. **Recording from inside the mod leaked memory.** See the Fal Arsenal note: capture the window from
   outside instead.

## Assets
A fal-generated reskin of the Eye and servants (flux/dev → `um sprite`) for the video.

## Cost and time
Roughly two days of sessions (approximate), plus fal GPU time for the large runs.

## Open questions
- Expert mode, and other bosses (the port pattern generalizes).
- An LLM "coach" that writes tactics for the policy. A scaffold exists; it isn't evaluated.

# Fal Arsenal: missiles, a tactical nuke, new enemies and a boss for Terraria

> Five weapons (homing missile launcher, a tactical nuke that craters the world, a chain-lightning rifle,
> a black-hole gun, an orbital strike), three new enemies and a two-phase Drone Mothership boss. All
> sprites were generated with fal. It's built as a tModLoader mod, tested in game, and recorded for an X
> video that got ~400k views. Code: `examples/terraria-tmodloader`.

## Setup
- **Loader:** tModLoader, the free Steam app **1281930**. It must be in the Steam library or it won't start.
  The GitHub build was used, with an isolated save folder.
- **Reference source:** `ilspycmd -p` on `Terraria.exe`, into a folder outside the repo.
- **Art:** fal `flux/dev` → `um sprite` (cutout, fit, sheet).

## Route and why
**Loader API.** tModLoader exposes everything as C# subclasses:
- `ModItem`, `ModProjectile`, `ModNPC` for content;
- `ModSystem` for world hooks;
- `ModCommand` for test commands;
- MonoMod detours (`On_Main.DoUpdate += ...`) when you need vanilla internals.

No reason to go lower.

## How the game works (what we had to learn)
- **NPC sheets:** frame height = texture height / `Main.npcFrameCount[type]`, so any consistent frame
  size works. Vertical strips.
- **Orientation:** items are drawn pointing right. NPC sprites face left and the engine flips them.
  Projectile rotation 0 means pointing right, unless you draw it yourself in `PreDraw`.
- **Vanilla AI styles:** aiStyle 3, the "fighter", flees in daylight, so a daytime walker enemy needs custom
  `AI()`. Slimes can reuse aiStyle 1.
- **World edits:** destroying tiles is `WorldGen.KillTile`. For multiplayer, follow vanilla explosives' net
  messages.
- **Camera:** you can steer it through `ModSystem.ModifyScreenPosition`; screen shake via
  `PunchCameraModifier`.
- **Lab mode:**
  - `-tmlsavedirectory <dir>` isolates saves;
  - `-skipselect Player:World` loads straight into a world;
  - `Main.instance.InactiveSleepTime = TimeSpan.Zero` keeps full speed while unfocused.

## Build steps
1. Put `FalArsenal/` in `Documents/My Games/Terraria/tModLoader/ModSources/`.
2. In game: Workshop > Develop Mods > Build + Reload. Or from the command line:
   `dotnet tModLoader.dll -build <ModSources>/FalArsenal`.
3. Get the items with `/arsenal` (or the recipes), and summon the boss with `/mothership`.

## Verification
- **In game:** `client.log` shows the load, and screenshots of the window show sprite scale and orientation.
- **Scripted scene:** a showcase `ModSystem` spawns waves on a timeline and fires the weapons, so a take
  reproduces exactly.
- **Builds:** the example compiles to a `.tmod` with 0 warnings on three command-line routes (`dotnet build`,
  and `tModLoader.dll -build` on the SDK and on the bundled runtime). The in-game Build + Reload wasn't re-run
  for the ported example.
- **Not verified:** multiplayer.

## Gotchas
1. **Recording from inside the game leaked 17 GB of memory in one take.**
   - **Cause:** this FNA3D's D3D11 `ReadBackbuffer` allocates a full-size staging texture per call.
   - **Fix:** capture the window from outside with ffmpeg `gfxcapture=hwnd=...`.
2. **`SDL_AUDIODRIVER=disk` recorded nothing.**
   - **Cause:** FAudio on Windows talks to WASAPI directly.
   - **Fix:** use a process-loopback capture of the game's PID (`um/ps1/ProcLoopback.ps1`).
3. **The recording's tail was lost.**
   - **Cause:** gfxcapture stalls on a frozen window, so ffmpeg never read the 'q'.
   - **Fix:** send 'q', then wait on a background thread. Never block the game's main thread. Write
     `.mkv`, which survives a kill.
4. **Takes stopped matching.**
   - **Cause:** explosions crater the showcase world.
   - **Fix:** restore a pristine copy of the world before every take (`um backup`).
5. **tModLoader refuses to start.**
   - **Cause:** the free tModLoader app isn't in the Steam library.
   - **Fix:** add it. Never patch the check.
6. **The agent killed its own shell.**
   - **Cause:** `pkill -f <pattern>` matched the agent's own command line.
   - **Fix:** kill by exact PID only.
7. **Sprites came out with grey fringes or a floor shadow.**
   - **Cause:** the generated art had soft shadows under objects.
   - **Fix:** flood-fill cutout with a grey tolerance or keep-top (`um sprite cutout --grey 150 --keep-top 0.8`),
     then one nearest-neighbour fit.

## Assets
- **Prompt style:** "16-bit pixel art game sprite in the style of Terraria, crisp dark outline, limited
  palette, centered, plain flat white background, no shadow, no text" plus the object and its orientation
  ("perfectly horizontal side view, muzzle pointing right").
- **Frame sizes:** launcher 64x26, missile 38x16, nuke 40x84, boss 240x150 x2 frames.

## Cost and time
Roughly a day for the weapons and showcase, and another half-day for the boss set (approximate), with one
agent and a human reviewing clips. fal spend was a few dollars.

## Open questions
- Multiplayer sync for the nuke's world edits at scale.
- A proper boss arena and loot table beyond the showcase.

# Super Smash Bros. Melee's decompiled engine inside Terraria: a native DLL under tModLoader, 3D fighters, its engine replayed bit-exact against Slippi Dolphin recordings

> The Melee decompilation's PC port (`melee-pc`) is built as a headless x64 DLL with a small C API and loaded by
> P/Invoke into tModLoader. Melee's own code moves the fighters, one engine frame per Terraria tick, and Terraria
> draws them as 3D models, lit by the world. In a headless bench all 26 fighters replay their real-Melee
> recordings bit for bit (29 recordings, both ports). Inside Terraria, real runs re-run by a second agent cover
> Mario's and Link's movement and 3D drawing for 17 fighters. Since then the coordinator ran 116 scripted beats on
> the then-current build and, on the integrated build, a 27-scenario in-game test suite (whose collision failures
> were mostly the test checker's) and a recorded 5,524-frame CPU-versus-CPU match that Terraria replays identically
> to the headless engine and to the original recording. Attacks against Terraria enemies, the pad path, sound, effects,
> the character select screen, the match modes, terrain collision and the Terraria lockout have second-agent
> verification that is synthetic or by reading IL only; a release and online play are not done.

## Setup
- **Host:** Terraria 1.4.4.9 on tModLoader 2026.08.3.0 (Steam), on the .NET 8.0.0 runtime tModLoader ships. FNA
  23.10.0.0 with SDL2 2.28.2: read from the DLLs, because FNA's folder name `1.0.0` is not its version. Windows
  11 Pro x64, one desktop machine.
- **Guest code:** [melee-pc](https://github.com/999sian/melee-pc) at commit
  `e83383539a4fd06e9bd8b28c270b3d1ecc7d3be3` (2026-09-29), the [doldecomp/melee](https://github.com/doldecomp/melee)
  decompilation plus a PC platform layer. Built in WSL Ubuntu 24.04: gcc 13.3.0 and CMake 3.28.3 for Linux
  probes, `x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc` **13-posix** for the Windows DLL (the port's graphics layer uses
  `std::thread`, which needs the posix variant even though the DLL doesn't link that layer).
- **Guest data:** the game's files (Melee NTSC-U 1.02), extracted with DolphinTool to a folder outside the mod.
  The DLL reads them at runtime; nothing from the game is in the mod or its repository. Every player needs their
  own copy of Melee NTSC-U 1.02, dumped from a disc they own; don't download disc images.
- **Target rules (user's decision):** Melee 1.02 **plus Slippi's `$Required` codes**, the way Melee is played
  online today, **minus UCF** (the community controller fix, which ships inside the same required block).
- **Oracle:** Slippi Dolphin 3.6.4 (the official portable build of
  [Ishiiruka](https://github.com/project-slippi/Ishiiruka)) driven by [libmelee](https://github.com/altf4/libmelee)
  0.47.3 on Python 3.12.10, in a lab copy whose game settings have the 9 UCF 0.84 code blocks removed. The user's
  own Dolphin configuration is untouched (hash checked).
- **Lab:** tModLoader started with `-tmlsavedirectory <lab folder>` and `-skipselect`, saves snapshotted with
  `um backup` first, a flat test floor, daytime forced while the lab flag is set. The DLL lives in a folder
  outside the mod, so it is never packed into the `.tmod`. The lab runs while the player keeps using their own
  tModLoader, so a classifier tells lab processes from the player's and only the lab's can be closed, by exact
  PID; extra labs run from their own copy of the install
  (`running-several-isolated-tmodloader-test-instances-in-parall.md`).
- **Process:** an orchestrator assigned every task to one agent and its verification to a different one, which
  re-ran or re-measured it; up to 12 Claude agents ran in parallel at the peak, plus smaller ones for
  mechanical work and verification. Grok drafted and reviewed designs read-only as a second model.

## Route and why
`decomp-recomp`, embedded as a library: the libsm64 / Elden Ring Mario pattern
(`techniques/rebuilt-guest-engine-inside-a-host.md`). Melee's state and rules cross into Terraria; **nothing of
Melee's renderer crosses** (the port's GX/WebGPU layer, Dawn and SDL are not linked). Terraria draws.

Considered and dropped:
- **A C# reimplementation from the `.dat` data** came first, about 2,500 lines: movement, attacks, defence,
  knockback and generated tables. Against real Melee on the same 116 scripted beats, judged on position only, it
  matched 52; the embedded engine matched 110 (a second agent's comparison). Every special move would have
  needed hand-written logic: about 34 distinct movement specials and 18 projectile moves across the roster.
- **Pre-rendered sprite sheets** of each fighter (Blender, about 90 sheets per fighter): an estimated 1.5 to 20
  hours of unattended rendering for the roster (the estimates differ in how many frames are rendered), lighting
  baked in, and parts whose visibility depends on the action missing. They were replaced by real-time 3D models
  posed by the engine.
- **Running the whole game headless and bridging it** (a passthrough) stayed an unused fallback. Embedding only
  the simulation turned out cheaper than expected: from the first build to Mario moving inside Terraria took
  under a day.

## How the game works (what we had to learn)

### Loading Melee's engine into tModLoader
- melee-pc's CMake already builds the game as a static library separate from the port. The DLL is that library
  plus a small glue layer: generated stubs for console hardware (graphics, audio, memory card, disc, network),
  a 96 MB arena at a fixed address below 4 GB, a crash guard that turns a game panic or an access violation into
  an error code, and a reset that copies the game's statics back from a snapshot. It imports only KERNEL32 and
  msvcrt. Recipe and traps: `techniques/hosting-a-decompiled-console-engine-as-a-native-dll-inside-a.md`.
- The mod binds it with `NativeLibrary.Load` from a configurable path outside the mod and never frees it. A mod
  reload unloads the C# side, but the DLL and its state stay in the process, so every session starts with
  `mtb_reset` and then `mtb_init`.
- **The C API (`mtb_*`).** It is versioned (magic `MTBR`, major version 2 with a handshake, a minor version for
  additive features) and made of fixed-size, pointer-free blocks pinned with `_Static_assert` in C and offset
  checks in C#. Core calls: `init(files_dir)`, `reset`, `load_collision`, `set_slot`, `create_fighters`,
  `step_pads`, `read_state_slot`, `read_items`, RNG seed get/set, `last_error`. Optional, bound by name when
  present: pose, stage points, camera, sub-entity pose (Nana), hitboxes and hit injection, audio, effects.
- **What a fighter needs from the game's files:** `LbRb.dat`, `PlCo.dat` (common fighter data) and its `Pl??.dat`.
  Final Destination's collision, blast zones (−246, 246, 188, −140) and camera bounds come from `GrNLa.dat`.

### How frames cross: one engine frame per Terraria tick
- Both games run at 60 Hz. In `ModPlayer.PreUpdate` the mod builds the pads and calls `mtb_step_pads` once; in
  `PostUpdateRunSpeeds` it writes the engine's position into the `Player` (feet anchored, velocity zeroed,
  Terraria's own movement suppressed for that tick). Two agents' real runs measured 0.031-0.036 ms per step on
  average.
- **Units:** 3.5 px per Melee unit, so Mario's 11.98 units are the Player's 42 px; Melee's Y points up, Terraria's
  down; the origin is local (the tile edge under the fighter's feet when it was created). One conversion
  function owns all of this.
- **Terrain:** Terraria tiles in a window around the fighter (120×68 tiles) become Melee collision lines. A line
  has the solid on its right (floors left to right, right walls top to bottom, ceilings right to left, left
  walls bottom to top), with `0x100` for a pass-through platform and `0x200` for a grabbable ledge. The first
  version treated slopes and half blocks as full blocks and had no ledges. A later version adds slopes, half
  blocks and platforms, ledge stubs at floor ends, one collision joint per connected solid (with a single joint
  the fighter could grab a ledge through a wall), and live reloads that remap every fighter's stored line
  indices. A second agent verified it in three rounds with synthetic tests and fire runs (bench 29/29, no floor
  panic over 26 fighters × 11 buttons, a cap on a loop that also hangs the original port's build); one rare
  recoverable panic is left.
- **When Terraria owns the player** (mount, grappling hook, pulley, bed, death, teleports), the engine doesn't
  step. When it ends, the fighter is recreated at the player's feet: `reset` + `init` + `create`, which replays
  Melee's entry animation (Gotcha 3).
- **What a headless Melee match needs besides fighters** (each found by a divergence or a crash): a stage-class
  object whose only job is to tick the collision counter every frame (airborne floor checks depend on it), the
  crowd-reaction setup the match scene runs, Final Destination's stage points, and Melee's combat camera computed
  without drawing (off-screen logic depends on it).

### How input crosses: XInput → a raw GameCube pad → Melee
- Melee reads pads in two stages. **Stage A** is the controller library: a radial clamp of radius 80 with `s8`
  truncation, direction bits from radius 30, and scaling (sticks /80, triggers /140). **Stage B** runs inside the
  fighter code (`Fighter_procInput`): dead zones from the common fighter data, Z synthesis, and a digital L/R
  press that forces the analog value to 1.0. The DLL's step takes stage-A output; the mod does stage A in C#
  (`EnginePad.FromRaw`, transcribed from the decomp's `controller.c`) and must never apply stage B itself.
- A second agent replayed 6 real recordings through `EnginePad` plus the decomp's `Fighter_procInput`: equal to
  Slippi's recorded processed input in 30,557 of 30,557 frames (4,198 with the stick moving). Real data never
  exercised the clamp beyond radius 80, the C-stick, digital L/R or raw trigger values.
- **The pad.** XInput read directly for 4 pads (the system DLLs only), with no dead zone. FNA's one-argument
  `GamePad.GetState` adds its own dead zone on top of Melee's; `GamePadDeadZone.None` is the fallback path.
  Floats become raw GameCube values with `(int)(axis * 80)` and `(int)(trigger * 140)`, truncated towards zero,
  with no second Y flip.
- **The layout only decides which GameCube button each Xbox button writes**, so everything after it stays
  bit-exact. Default: Nintendo/Switch positional (B = A attack, A = B special, Y/X = jump, RB/LB = Z, triggers =
  analog L/R, a full press = digital L/R); presets for a GameCube/Dolphin layout and a custom one. Start opens
  Terraria's pause menu and never reaches the engine. The implementing agent's synthetic test (94 checks) drove
  the real DLL and saw it react to every button on frame 1. A second agent confirmed the mapping and the path to
  the engine the same way, found that a single pad at XInput index 1 left port 0 dead and a short window in which
  the temporary 16:9 resolution could reach the user's `config.json`, and re-verified the fixes (any single pad
  now drives the fighter; the 2+ pad logic survived 3.38 million fuzzed frames with 0 violations). All synthetic;
  no physical pad has been tested.

### How the animation was matched, frame by frame
The engine publishes joint matrices and mesh visibility; the mod skins the user's converted models on the CPU,
renders them into a render target in `Main.OnPreDraw` and pastes that as a player layer. Four checks, each
re-run by a second agent: the simulation is bit-exact (so the action and frame are Melee's); drawing changes no
engine field; the pose equals the animation tracks decoded straight from the `.dat`; and the pose equals real
Melee's RAM, read from Dolphin every frame. The last one showed that tails, capes and hair in Melee only move
right because the game *draws*: Slippi's `DynamicsFix` code plus a graphics-free "draw-effects" step at the end
of each engine frame reproduce it. Details, numbers and gotchas:
`techniques/skinned-3d-models-inside-tmodloader-posed-by-an-external-eng.md`.

### Melee ↔ Terraria: hits, the lockout and the screen
- **Fighter vs fighter and items stay inside the engine** (exact). The translation happens only at the border,
  the "hit bridge", in both directions. Designed by Grok and reviewed by a separate Grok session over three
  rounds against the decomp and tModLoader; implemented by a Claude agent and verified by second agents in two
  rounds (after a second implementation: bench 29/29 byte-identical, one hit per Terraria tick holds over about
  2.3 million checks, reads pure, launch direction right; integrable together with an engine fix for a hit
  flash). **Synthetic tests only until the first in-game suite (see Verification).**
  - *Melee → Terraria:* each frame a pure read returns the active hitboxes; the mod sweeps each one as a capsule
    from its previous position against `NPC.getRect()`, applies one hit per hitbox group per activation per NPC
    (Melee's own victim-list rule), and turns it into a single `StrikeNPC` through `HitModifiers`. Knockback comes
    from Melee's own knockback function with a fixed weight of 100; the mod never writes `npc.velocity` or
    `npc.immune`.
  - *Terraria → Melee:* NPC contact, projectile, spike and trap hits are queued with a new `mtb_apply_hit` and
    drained inside the step, right before Melee resolves that fighter's hits, as a synthetic item hit through
    the game's own item-hit path. Melee computes percent, knockback, hitstun and hitlag. Damage goes through a
    configurable curve (`25·d/(d+40)` percent, at least 1). On the Terraria side, `ImmuneTo` returning true plus a
    detour on `Player.Hurt` keeps Terraria's dodges, debuffs and life loss away from the fighter.
  - Measured synthetically: a jab gives 3% and a knockback of 33.4 on a weight-100 target, bit-equal to the game
    function; an injected 3.7% hit adds exactly 3.7% with hitstun 15 and hitlag 4; the 29-recording bench stays
    byte-identical with the new reads called every step.
- **The Terraria lockout.** While the player is a Melee fighter, Terraria's player tools are off: items, mounts,
  hooks, every teleport, doors, chests, town-NPC chat, hotbar and quick keys; Esc opens the options menu.
  Enemies, bosses and traps still interact. Rules: block the effect, never the raw input (the engine reads the
  pad in `PreUpdate`, before `TriggersSet.CopyInto` fills the `control*` fields); block entering, not leaving;
  leave world-forced events alone. The first review found seven escapes (the gravity globe flips the screen,
  Esc with Autopause leaves the game paused, right-click on portable banks opens them, the return portal is
  consumed, the step stool, two rare ones), later rounds a few regressions and about fifteen passive ones (a second
  model's review); after the third attempt a second agent's IL sweep of 2,691 methods found none left, with 15
  symmetric detours and a clean exit. **Build and IL reading only; not run in game.**
- **16:9.** Writing `Main.PendingResolutionWidth/Height` does nothing outside the options menu;
  `Main.SetDisplayMode` applies at once. A detour on `Main.SaveSettings` keeps the temporary resolution out of
  the user's `config.json` (a second agent found a window of up to 120 ticks where it could still reach it; fixed
  and re-verified); on a non-16:9 fullscreen monitor the mod draws into a centred 16:9 viewport instead.
  Synthetic tests and the build only.
- **Added since the first version of this note** (second-agent verdicts in brackets): sound through Melee's own
  audio mixer running headless inside the DLL [verified synthetically; hardening against corrupt sound files
  delivered, not yet verified]; Melee's particles and effect models read from the engine and drawn [partly
  verified]; the character select screen with its countdown [verified in three rounds, ending with 2.4 million
  fuzzed frames and corrupted images or music that no longer crash]; Melee's stamina (HP) and 200% modes, stocks,
  and an "arena anchor" with blast zones and 16:9 bars [partly verified, integrable; three narrow carry-over
  gaps]; Melee's camera driving both the view and the model, with a jitter fix [partly verified: the jitter fix
  holds]. Still being worked on: the HUD, the rest of the match flow, and fixes for what the first in-game suite
  found.

## Build steps
1. In WSL Ubuntu 24.04, install CMake, Ninja and `mingw-w64` (posix variant). melee-pc's preflight script lists
   the X11/Wayland headers SDL3's configure step wants. `-DCMAKE_OPTIMIZE_DEPENDENCIES=ON` stops the static
   library from waiting on the whole graphics stack (1,934 → 1,080 build steps). `ninja melee_game` builds the
   library (13.5 MB, 48 s on 16 threads).
2. Build your own core target next to it: the `mtb_*` API, the allocator, a printing `OSPanic`/`OSReport`,
   and **generated** stubs for the remaining hardware symbols, with value-returning ones classified. Repeat the
   game target's forced include (`-include src/pc/compat.h`) on your target.
3. Apply the floating-point and Slippi fixes as build-time patches (on by default):
   `techniques/bit-exact-decomp-ports-reproduce-the-original-compiler-s-and.md`.
4. Link it as a DLL with the C and C++ runtimes static and the guest's panic and abort wrapped
   (`--wrap=OSPanic --wrap=abort`), and copy `melee_core.dll` to a folder outside the mod. Point the mod's config
   at it and at your extracted files; the data path goes in through `mtb_init`, never an environment variable.
5. Convert your fighters' models with your own converter (on HSDRaw) into a folder outside the mod.
6. In the mod: the P/Invoke binding, tiles → collision lines, the pad path, the session lifecycle, the 3D
   renderer, and a config toggle. Note that a normal `dotnet build` of a tModLoader mod also packs the `.tmod`
   into your `Mods` folder (`tMLMod.targets` runs `BuildMod` after `Build`). Check compilation on a private copy
   without the pack target, and pack with tModLoader's own `-build` into a lab folder (hosting note, Gotcha 10).

## Verification
**Oracle.** Melee 1.02 in the lab Slippi Dolphin plays scripted input "beats" (walk, dash, jumps, every attack,
shield, rolls, specials) from the same beat file the mod's lab script plays in Terraria; a comparator diffs the
two per frame. For the engine itself, a headless bench replays each real recording's inputs through the DLL and
compares every state field bitwise. Trace replay is described in `techniques/oracles-how-agents-know-a-mod-works.md`.
- **Recording the truth:** one scripted recording per fighter (26, plus a Link pilot), 2,952 compared frames each,
  plus two earlier Mario recordings: 29 in all. The 27 per-fighter recordings ran unattended in 32.8 minutes with
  no retries (implementing agent's figure; a second agent's re-recording of two fighters took the same 72-73 s
  each). Port 2 is an idle second Mario that walks away from the action.
- **Contamination is marked per frame** (P2 disturbed, P1 past the stage edge, a KO): 10 recordings are clean end
  to end, and 12 contain KOs. Comparisons in Terraria cut at the beat before the first dirty frame.
- **Determinism of the truth** is shown for Mario only (3 runs with 3 seeds identical). Peach's forward smash
  pulls a random item, so her re-recording differs.

**Not verified:**
- 9 fighters never drawn in the lab (Zelda, Sheik, Young Link, Pikachu, Jigglypuff, Mewtwo, Mr. Game & Watch,
  Marth, Roy) and Nana; movement inside Terraria was traced only for Mario and Link and, in the recorded match,
  Fox and Samus;
- the hit bridge in play: the first in-game suite exercised it and found damage-accounting problems (several worm
  segments added into one hit; an arrow's damage not matching what the target lost), which are being repaired;
- physical pads, keyboard play, the lockout and 16:9 in game; live terrain edits only through the first suite;
- sound content (the checks are synthetic), Melee's effects, the HUD, the camera, blast zones and stocks, damage
  modes and the character select screen, beyond the recorded replay and the first suite;
- local multiplayer, online play, rollback with Terraria events;
- coexistence with other mods, hot reload, a second machine.

No release has been attempted.

## Gotchas
1. **The user had been playing the old engine all along.** **Symptom:** "sprite Mario every so often" in the
   user's own game. **Cause:** the engine toggle defaulted to off and the user had never saved the mod's config,
   so their game always ran the C# fallback. **Fix:** check the default a user actually gets, and log which engine
   is running.
2. **No pad button did anything.** **Cause, three parts:** the mod read buttons only through `ModKeybind`s, and a
   keybind's default binding reaches a player's input profile only when they press "reset" in the controls menu,
   so the user's profile had none; Terraria kept reading the pad itself (A mounted, B grappled, which handed the
   player back to Terraria and recreated the fighter 17 times in under half a minute); and FNA's dead zone sat on
   top of Melee's. **Fix:** read XInput directly, detour `PlayerInput.GamePadInput` while the fighter owns the pad
   (not `Main.SettingBlockGamepadsEntirely`, which `Main.SaveSettings` writes to `config.json`), and fall back to a
   keybind's default key. (Implementing agent's diagnosis; a second agent confirmed the button path synthetically
   and found the index-1 pad case.)
3. **On slopes the model squashed and popped back.** **Cause:** slopes were full blocks to the engine, the spawn
   landed inside a solid, the engine and Terraria positions drifted more than 16 px apart, and the fix-up recreated
   the fighter, which replays Melee's entry animation. **Fix:** real slope geometry, lifting the spawn out of
   solids, remapping line indices on reload; recreating without the entry animation is suggested. (Two agents
   explain the same loop differently; neither is proven.)
4. **Fighters landed on Final Destination's ledge vertex instead of being pushed off it.** **Cause:** stage
   objects tick a collision counter every frame, and airborne collision uses the floor routine that extends floors
   into a neighbouring wall only when its per-fighter copy equals that counter. The DLL had no stage object, so
   the counter never moved. **Fix:** a stage-class object whose only job is that tick. A build without it brings
   back the 5 ledge failures (verified causally).
5. **10 of 116 beats (grabs and pushes) diverged in Terraria.** **Cause:** the real recording had an idle second
   Mario nearby (Melee won't start a Vs match with one port), which the grab connected on and which pushed Mario;
   the lab had no rival. Confirmed from the `.slp`. **Fix:** the same idle rival at the same spot gave 2,892/2,892;
   later truths walk the rival far away first.
6. **The first beats of every recording were lost and the whole truth shifted.** **Cause:** Melee spends about
   100 entry frames ignoring the pad. **Fix:** replay nothing until the fighter is standing. A walk-distance "bug"
   with a correct top speed was this shift: fix the instrument before tuning physics.
7. **The truth wasn't vanilla Melee.** **Cause:** Slippi's required code block includes UCF 0.84 (dashback,
   shield drop, SDI, cardinals) and other gameplay codes. **Fix:** a lab copy of Dolphin with exactly the 9 UCF
   blocks cut, the rest reproduced in the engine as switchable tags. Edit the settings file byte-exactly: `sed -i`
   rewrote the line endings of the whole file.
8. **Slippi and libmelee plumbing.**
   - Slippi's Dolphin is based on an older Dolphin and exits silently (code 3) on a `.rvz` image:
     `DolphinTool convert -f iso` first.
   - libmelee raises `Unknown path` unless the Dolphin folder name contains `netplay`.
   - libmelee's `speed_*` fields are twice the per-frame displacement: compare positions.
   - libmelee 0.47.3 can't decode an unfinalised `.slp`; its stick conversion differs from the game's on 29 exact
     tie values; its action-frame convention is one frame off the engine's in looping states.
   - Port 2 must be a human port that picks a fighter and idles: a CPU walks over and attacks.
   - Re-seed the RNG every frame from the `.slp` pre-frame seed; common code and items use it for every fighter.
9. **A special the script pressed never happened.** **Cause:** the beat landed while the fighter was still in a
   grab or another special, so the recording has no such move. **Fix:** wait for an actionable state before
   every special.
10. **A dirty truth compared whole, exit code 0.** **Cause:** the per-recording contamination cut was looked up
    by the fighter named on the command line instead of the truth file's own, and nothing checked that the mod
    played the truth's fighter; later, a lowercase file name missed its key on a case-insensitive file system.
    **Fix:** key the cut by the truth file and check the fighter in the trace against the truth (verified). The
    lowercase case is still open.
11. **A fix looked identical to no fix.** **Cause:** the one-command compare script copied the `.tmod` but never
    rebuilt it. **Fix:** build inside the script and refuse to compare when any `.cs` file is newer than the
    `.tmod`.
12. **The extracted audio was a mix of regions.** **Cause:** a flat extraction keeps the first file-system entry
    for duplicate names (Japanese `.ssm` files next to English ones), and DolphinTool's `-o` once produced *folders*
    named `Pl??.dat`. **Fix:** extract preserving directories, and list duplicate base names before trusting the
    files.
13. **Dolphin took the foreground by itself during an unattended oracle run**, even launched minimized and not
    activated. See `recording-game-footage.md`, Gotcha 10.
14. **Second-model research drafts came back in 80 s with invented citations.** **Cause:** an API key in the
    environment overrode the subscription login and selected a non-reasoning default model. **Fix:** unset the key
    for that child process only, pin the model, and check every quoted code line mechanically against the source.
15. **Terraria → Melee hits planned on `ModifyHurt` would have missed some hits.** **Cause:** Terraria's dodges
    run before it. **Fix (design review, synthetic tests only):** `ImmuneTo` returns true and a detour on
    `Player.Hurt` records the raw damage first.
16. **The workflow's linear phase model blocked new work.** **Symptom:** adding four features reopened phase 1
    of the project's ledger, which modelled Universal Modder's 10-step loop as one global phase counter, and the
    validator rightly refused to close phase 3. **Fix:** per-track phases: a core track plus one per fighter and
    one per component, each with its own steps 1-10.
17. **The first in-game test suite failed 27 of 27, then 13 of 27, and neither was mostly the mod.** **Cause:**
    first, a relative scenario path resolved against the game's install folder, so no scenario loaded; then a test
    checker that did not know the original game's edge grabs, a helper that returned a cell inside a solid mass, and
    one scenario built a row off. **Fix:** absolute paths checked by the launcher
    (`running-several-isolated-tmodloader-test-instances-in-parall.md`, Gotcha 3); a second agent re-derived
    each failure from raw traces and mutated real data to prove the corrected checker still fails real
    fall-throughs (`when-the-first-real-run-fails-suspect-the-oracle-re-deriving.md`).
18. **A recorded match replayed in Terraria agreed with the original for 55 s, then diverged.** **Cause:** the mod's
    own terrain-to-collision streaming replaced the replay's stage collision one tick after it was created.
    **Fix:** a collision lock during replays (hosting note, Gotcha 13).
19. **The bench that gated every engine build had four false greens.** **Cause:** nobody had tried to make it fail.
    **Fix:** twelve fabricated broken builds found the holes, and a diff closed them
    (`prove-your-replay-bench-can-fail-mutant-builds-exposed-four-.md`).

## Assets
None are shipped. The 3D models are converted on the player's machine, from their own copy of the game, with an
own converter built on HSDRaw into a compact format kept outside the mod; the mod contains code only. The earlier
Blender sprite sheets were dropped. No generated (fal) assets were used.

## Cost and time
About three days (2026-10-08 to 2026-10-10) of orchestrated sessions. The embedded-engine route, from the first
library build to Mario moving inside Terraria, took under one day. Per-fighter cost became recording and checking
rather than code: one unattended recording session for all 26, and a replay of all 29 recordings through the DLL in
seconds.

## Open questions
- In-game runs of the hit bridge, pads, lockout, 16:9 and Nana (second-agent verification exists for all of them, but
  only synthetic or by reading IL).
- The hit bridge's rollback case (Terraria hits are lost if the engine re-simulates), players 2-4, shield
  damage, the attacker's hitlag, clanks.
- The remaining Slippi gameplay codes, and new recordings that exercise them.
- In-game checks of sound content, effects, the HUD, the camera, blast zones, damage modes and the character select
  screen, beyond the recorded replay and the first in-game suite.
- The Marth/Roy cape during their neutral special; the camera's remaining jitter (a second agent confirmed that the
  engine-driven camera removed the fighter's jitter, at most 1.02 px for the fighter and 0.5 px for the world
  against 110 px before, but damage numbers and health bars still jump up to 6 px at high zoom).
- Distribution: the DLL contains the decompiled game and is not distributable, and neither are the converted
  models, audio or anything else read from the disc. A source-only release, where each player builds the engine
  and supplies their own copy of Melee NTSC-U 1.02, is the option under study; the licence questions are open.
  The build-time patches (routines transcribed from `main.dol`, such as MSL's trig and `PSMTXConcat`) are
  derived from the game's executable too. Shipping only your own code and having each player bring their own
  disc lowers the risk but doesn't remove it: Nintendo has taken down projects that shipped no Nintendo files.
  Keep Nintendo's names and art off any mod page and its thumbnail, and run `um publish check` on a release
  (`skills/publish-mod/SKILL.md`). The rollback snapshot and determinism suggest online play is feasible; it's
  untested.

# Playing Test Drive Unlimited 2 online with Project Paradise 2

> TDU2's official servers are gone; **Project Paradise 2** (project-paradise2.de) is the community
> revival. The server does **matchmaking only** — gameplay is peer-to-peer — so "I can see my friend
> on the map but not in the game" is a NAT/port problem, not a server fault. Separately, **AMD drivers
> released after February 2025 break the game** (rendering issues, driver timeouts, system freezes),
> and neither dgVoodoo2 nor DXVK fixes it — only a driver downgrade does.

## Setup

- **Retail TDU2** (Atari/Eden Games, 2011) plus the **Project Paradise 2** server and its launcher
  (v3.1.2 at time of writing). Account is created inside the game the first time you start it.
- Community references: TurboDuck TDU2 modding wiki (turboduck.net/forums/topic/28390), `djey47/tdumt2`
  tooling, and the PP2 Discord guides (install, port forwarding, troubleshooting, modding, launcher,
  offline→online migration; last updated 2025-11-09).
- If the game crashes on start on a modern OS, that is a separate compatibility problem — see
  `running-tdu2-on-modern-linux.md` for the NULL-pointer fix and the D3D9→D3D11 route.
- **Ownership:** PP2 requires an owned, activated copy (DVD or Steam), per project-paradise2.de/install.
  DRM and activation workarounds are out of scope for this KB.

## Route and why

Passthrough to the community server — no game files need modifying for the online part. The value of
this note is the failure-mode map: which symptom is a network/NAT issue, which is a GPU driver
regression, and which is a launcher/wrapper problem. Those get misattributed constantly.

## How the game works (what we had to learn)

- **P2P gameplay, server-side matchmaking.** The server only *connects players to each other*. Actual
  gameplay data (positions, cars, movement) is exchanged **directly between peers**, and at least one
  player in a session must accept incoming connections. There is no relay/NAT server — the game is old
  and uses its original networking stack.
- **NAT types** shown in the launcher: **Green = Open:FullCone** (fully open, can host), **Orange =
  RestrictedCone / Moderate**, **Red = Strict:Symmetric / UdpBlocked**. Red or Orange can still play
  online but **cannot host sessions** — you depend on someone else hosting to see other players in
  freeroam. Only *FullCone* counts as fully open; *Open:Symmetric* is not green.
- **Proximity-based multiplayer.** You are placed into a session/lobby with nearby players
  automatically; not seeing others is normal depending on activity.
- **Lobby capacities:** Freeroam 8, Houses 10, Casino hall 26, Casino slots 32.
- **DLC items** via the in-game store: press "buy", OK, confirm the Atari token amount (you always have
  enough); a password prompt can be skipped with OK.
- **Launcher (v3.1.2):** *Profiles* let you keep multiple configs (e.g. vanilla vs modded), each
  pointing at a `TestDrive2.exe` with per-profile toggles — Magic Ram, Magic Cores, Magic Prio,
  Vehicle Dirt, Vehicle Damage, Online Mode. *Service* logs in with your in-game account and can upload
  the savegame to PP2 cloud and/or keep local backups (recommended 3–4 savepoints). *Information*
  shows hardware and copies a system report to the clipboard for support.
- **The original networking is Atari-era.** TDU2 shipped on Xbox 360 and PC; the PC version's online
  play ran on Atari's own servers. It never used the original Xbox Live service (closed April 2010).

## Build steps

### Make NAT fully open (host lobbies)

1. Open your router's admin page (its IP is in network settings).
2. Log in, and **make sure the connection is IPv4** — an IPv6 address can mask the IPv4 one.
3. **Enable UPnP** (lets the game auto-forward), apply, restart router and PC.
4. Check the NAT type **in the launcher** — you may need to reopen it once or twice to refresh.
5. If still not Fully Open: forward **UDP 8889** manually and **disable UPnP** while doing so —
   having both UPnP and a manual rule for the same port causes issues. Apply, restart.

### Convert an offline profile to online

1. Check the name is free: `https://login.project-paradise2.de/ismynamefree` (a taken name can't be
   used online).
2. Copy your profile folder from `Documents\Eden Games\Test Drive Unlimited 2\savegame` to the desktop.
3. Delete everything under `Eden Games` (leave it empty).
4. Start the game and create a profile with the **exact same name** plus account name and password.
5. Play to level 1, then exit.
6. In `savegame`, delete the newly created profile folder — but keep `ProfileList` and `SystemDefault`.
7. Paste the offline profile folder you saved on the desktop back in.
8. Start the game: level, licences, etc. should match, now online.

(Credit: "Ellie from Steam", via the PP2 guide.)

### Unpack the game for mods

1. Finish a **packed** install and run the launcher's **"check gamefiles"** first — do **not** run
   gamefile check on an already-unpacked game, it breaks it.
2. Use the TDU2 Unpacker GUI (turboduck.net/files/file/276-tdu2-unpacker-gui/) to copy/unpack into a
   new folder.
3. Install mods by copying their folders into the matching game folder (e.g. a mod's `bnk` folder →
   `euro/bnk`), replacing files when asked.

## Verification

- Source: Project Paradise 2 Discord FAQ/pinned staff posts (2025-02 through 2026-03) and the official
  PP2 guides PDFs (2025-11-09): port forwarding, troubleshooting, offline→online, modding, launcher.
- **NOT independently verified in-game** by this agent. Treat driver-regression versions and network
  behaviour as community-reported; re-confirm against the current server/FAQ before relying on them.

## Gotchas

1. **See a friend on the map but not in the game.** **Symptom:** their position shows on the map, but
   you never meet in the world. **Cause:** the server knows their position (map works) but the direct
   P2P connection fails — most routers block inbound by default, and there is no relay. **Fix:** get a
   **Fully Open (FullCone) NAT** — enable UPnP, or forward **UDP 8889** (with UPnP off). At least one
   player in the session needs open inbound access; it sometimes works when another lobby member is
   open, which is why it looks intermittent.
2. **AMD GPU: rendering issues, driver timeouts, system freezes.** **Symptom:** visual corruption,
   driver timeouts, or hard freezes on an AMD card. **Cause:** **drivers released after February 2025**
   regress the game. **Fix:** downgrade to a driver from **February 2025 or earlier**. **dgVoodoo2 and
   DXVK do not fix this** — don't burn time on wrappers for this symptom.
3. **NVIDIA GTX 1650/1660 and all RTX: map crashes/freezes.** **Symptom:** the map crashes or freezes.
   **Cause:** known NVIDIA interaction. **Fix:** apply one of the two community fixes (a dgVoodoo2
   D3D12 preset, or the alternative) — they **override each other**, so only the last installed is
   active; try which works best. With the new launcher, move `uplauncher` out of the game folder so the
   launcher starts properly. If using MSI Afterburner or another overlay, close it before launching
   with dgVoodoo2.
4. **"TDU2 has to be launched by Steam".** **Symptom:** the game refuses to start. **Cause:** Steam
   integration mismatch. **Fix:** on a Steam copy, enable **"Steam Build"** in the launcher (keeps
   achievements); on a non-Steam copy, delete `steamapi.dll` from the game folder.
5. **New steering wheel not recognised.** **Symptom:** wheel does nothing. **Cause:** not
   auto-detected. **Fix:** configure the control mapping manually.
6. **Tabbing out crashes the game.** **Symptom:** alt-tab out and back → crash/freeze. **Cause:** older
   game, fullscreen handling. **Fix:** use **ALT+Enter** to toggle fullscreen; be aware of the crash.
7. **Refresh rate above 60 Hz not applying.** **Symptom:** high-refresh monitor stays at 60 Hz.
   **Cause:** >60 Hz only works in **fullscreen**, and only if the monitor supports the mode. **Fix:**
   use fullscreen and check the monitor's supported modes.
8. **Don't combine multiple car packs.** **Symptom:** broken/conflicting cars after adding packs.
   **Cause:** packs replace the same files. **Fix:** pick one car pack; also finish story mode first,
   since modded cars can make races unbeatable.
9. **Gamefile check on an unpacked install breaks it.** **Symptom:** game broken after "check
   gamefiles". **Cause:** the check expects a packed install. **Fix:** only check gamefiles on a packed
   install.
10. **Mod policy (community rules).** Mods allowed if they: don't harm other players, aren't used
    competitively (leaderboards, CRC, ORC), and don't cause server issues or crashes for others. Money
    cheating is at your own risk (no support); cheating is prohibited in competitive races. The C.T.R
    physics mod is explicitly "do not use in multiplayer races".

- Whether the Linux dgVoodoo2 route and the Windows AMD driver regression interact (the regression is
  a Windows driver issue; Linux uses Mesa/amdgpu).
- Exact port ranges beyond UDP 8889 the P2P stack uses, for a minimal port-forward rule.
