  - "https://github.com/blueskythlikesclouds/HavokAnimationExporter"
---

# Havok HKX: the chunked packfile family across game generations (and when you need the SDK)

> Havok ships two very different on-disk shapes: the **classic binary packfile** (one flat object
> graph, FO4/Skyrim era) and the newer **chunked tagfile** (`TAG0/SDKV/...`, 2015.1 onward). Reading a
> modern chunked file is usually just parsing; *converting* between versions, or reading a
> vendor-customized variant, needs the matching `hkCompatFormats.dll` — and that is where most projects
> get stuck. This note records the version→format mapping and the parser set that actually works.

## When to use it

Any time you meet an `.hkx`/`.hkr` and need to know (a) which Havok version wrote it, (b) whether a
public parser can read it, and (c) whether you are looking at a format problem or an SDK problem.

## How

### Identify the version first

| Game / asset | Havok version | Format |
|---|---|---|
| Fallout 4 | **2014.1.0-r1** (v11, 64-bit LE) | classic binary packfile |
| Skyrim SE | **2010.2.0-r1** (v8, 64-bit LE) | classic binary packfile |
| Watch Dogs: Legion — retail assets | **2017.2.0** (`SDKV="20170200"`) | chunked tagfile |
| Watch Dogs: Legion — leak/dev tree assets | **2015.1.0** (`SDKV="20150100"`) | chunked tagfile |
| Watch Dogs: Legion — some vehicle collision | **2014.2.5-r1** | classic binary packfile |
| Starfield — physics/collision | **2019.02** (`SDKV="20190200"`) | chunked tagfile |
| Test Drive Unlimited 2 — vehicle + level/scenario collision | **5.5.0-r1** (v5, 32-bit LE) | classic binary packfile |

**The single most useful check:** the chunked tagfile carries its version in a literal `SDKV` chunk.
Decode that and you know the writer. Do not trust "the wiki says 2017.1" — real WDL retail assets
measured `20170200`, which corrected an earlier documentation error.

### The chunked tagfile shape

Standard chunked files are a sequence of four-byte-magic chunks. The tags seen in the wild:

`TAG0`, `SDKV`, `DATA`, `TYPE` (with sub-tags `TPTR`, `TSTR`, `TNA1`, `FSTR`), `BITS`, `STORAGE`,
`ENUM`, `VALID`, `ITEM`, `PTYPE`, `ITYPE`, `MASK`, `INDX`, `PTCH`.

Starfield's 2019.02 and WDL's 2017.2.0 are the **same structural family** — a parser written for one
reads the other. The `StarfieldMeshConverter` parser is the reference implementation for both.

### Two serialization modes for a vendor-customized Havok

Disrupt-engine titles (Watch Dogs) use a **custom Havok**; a stock commercial SDK cannot render their
files. Two shapes appear:

- a **compact** layout (uses `TCRF`-style packing), and
- a **portable** layout (`TYPE`/`TNA1` self-describing).

Dev-tree SUV collision measured as the portable layout; that is the readable one.

### Parsers that work without an SDK (reading)

- **`hkxpack`** (Java, MIT) — original reader.
- **`hkxpack-plus`** (Java, MIT) — 910 bundled class definitions; the best validation tool.
- **`HKX2-Enhanced-Library`** (C#) — 589 autogenerated classes; most complete.
- **`havoklib`** (C++, GPL), **`blender-hkx`** (MIT), **`hkdump`** (C++, MIT).
- **`hkxcmd`** — "Havok Command Line Tools 1.4", Skyrim `HKX <-> XML/KF`.
- **`StarfieldMeshConverter`** — full chunked parser for 2019.02 (also the WDL 2017.2 reference).
- **`tagtools`** — `TagTools.py` + `TypeDatabase.xml` for tagfile inspection.

### Exporters (writing)

- **`HavokAnimationExporter` (HAE)** (C#, `blueskythlikesclouds`) — generates **skeleton and
  animation HKX** from FBX for Sonic titles; the rare public case of a *writer*, not just a reader.
  Options: `-s/--skl` skeleton HKX,
  `-u/--uncompressed`, `-f/--fps` (default 60), platform `-w/--windows`, `-x/--xbox360`, `-p/--ps3`,
  `--wiiu` (2012.2.0 only), `-t/--tagfile` (2010.2.0 / 2012.2.0 only). Sonic-specific caveats: new
  bones need the `@NEW` tag (Unleashed); root animation unsupported; Sonic Forces needs tagfile output
  plus a TagTools backport of the skeleton.

### When you actually need the SDK

Reading self-describing portable/chunked files needs no SDK. **Converting** between Havok versions —
and reading a compact/vendor variant — goes through `hkCompatFormats.dll`. Empirical result:
the Ubi-shipped Havok Content Tools **2017.2.0-r1** runs, but with a missing/mismatched
`hkCompatFormats.dll` it refuses the very assets it should convert:

- SUV 2017.2.0 chunked → `[s11n.Serialize] The format was not recognized (hkSerialize.cpp:419)`;
- truck 2014.2.5 packfile → access violation `c0000005`.

Building the missing 2017.2 `hkCompatFormats.dll` from a newer SDK **failed**: the conversion
implementation module (`Tools\FileConvert\CompatFormats\compatLoad`) is not shipped, the configure
script is Python-2 only. The conversion source present in the SDK is
a *patch library* only, not a runnable filter.

Havok SDKs are licensed; don't plan on one. The 2015–2017 SDKs in particular are not reachable, so
for WDL-era assets, prefer parsing the self-describing portable form and skip the SDK conversion path
entirely.

### Reading a 5.5.0 classic packfile: the file is self-describing, so parse the reflection

Old packfiles (5.x) are rejected by every public reader, and the matching-era Havok Content Tools
are a licensed build — not something to depend on or redistribute. The good news is you don't need
them: the packfile **carries its own class reflection**, so a parser can be written from the bytes
alone.

Observed layout (TDU2, `fileVersion 5`, 32-bit LE):

- **0x40-byte header** — magic `57 E0 E0 57` / `10 C0 C0 10` at 0 and 4, `userTag` at 8,
  `fileVersion` at 12, a layout byte each for `bytesInPointer` / `littleEndian` / `reusePadding` /
  base-class-optimization at 16 (TDU2: `04 01 00 01` = 4-byte pointers, LE, no padding, base-class
  optimization on), `numSections` at 20, `contentsSectionIndex` at 24, `contentsSectionOffset` at 28,
  the class-name section index at 32 and its offset at 36 (TDU2: 0xE4), the 16-byte contents version
  string (`Havok-5.5.0-r1`) at 40,
  and `flags` / `maxPredicate` (both `0xFFFFFFFF`) at 56 / 60.
- **Section table at 0x40** — one 48-byte entry per section: a 19-byte name tag, a `0xFF`
  separator, then seven `uint32` fields — `absoluteDataStart`, `localFixupsOffset`,
  `globalFixupsOffset`, `virtualFixupsOffset`, `exportsOffset`, `importsOffset`, `endOffset`. The
  offset fields are **relative to that section's `absoluteDataStart`**, and the sections are
  contiguous: for TDU2, `__classnames__` 208+1280, `__types__` 1488+23584, `__data__` 25072+7040 =
  32112 = the whole file. That arithmetic is the cheapest check that a slice has the right length.
- **`__classnames__`** — a pool of records: `uint32 signature` + a constant `0x09` marker byte + a
  null-terminated name. TDU2's 1280-byte pool holds 54 records and consumes exactly its length, e.g.
  `0x1b58f0ef`→`hkpPhysicsSystem`, `0x3224de76`→`hkpRigidBody`, `0x090cd72e`→`hkpListShape`. Every
  class-name offset (the header field, and the virtual fixups) is relative to the start of this
  section — not to the file.
- **`__types__`** — the `hkClass` reflection: every class's name, parent, size, enums and members
  (member name, type, subtype, `cArraySize`, flags, offset). This is what makes a generic reader
  possible — you read the class layout from the file instead of hard-coding a version's registry.
- **`__data__`** — the object graph, laid out per the reflection above. Every pointer is a
  section-relative offset repaired by one of three fixup tables, each reached from its
  `…FixupsOffset` in the section table and each holding offsets relative to its own section:
  - **virtual fixups** — 12-byte records `(uint32 srcOffset, uint32 sectionIndex, uint32 dstOffset)`,
    one per object, i.e. a class-name pointer. Verified on TDU2: the object at `__data__`+0 has
    `(0, 0, 228)`, and `__classnames__`+228 is `hkpPhysicsSystem` (the root object); 40 objects gave
    40 records, mapping the repeat offenders to `hkpBoxShape` / `hkpConvexTransformShape`.
  - **local fixups** — 8-byte `(srcOffset, dstOffset)` pairs within the same section, ended by a
    `0xFFFFFFFF` sentinel.
  - **global fixups** — 12-byte `(srcOffset, dstSectionIndex, dstOffset)` triples, also
    sentinel-ended, for pointers that cross sections.
  Stop at the sentinel or at the table end, not by dividing the span: the tables are 16-byte
  aligned (measured on TDU2 `f430`'s `__data__`: local 5904, global 5968, virtual 6560, exports
  7040), so span ÷ record size can be off by one. In that section the local span is exactly 64
  bytes (8 pairs); the virtual span is exactly 480 (40 × 12, matching the 40 objects) and has
  **no sentinel** at all; and the 592-byte global span is 49 triples plus a 4-byte `0xFFFFFFFF`
  sentinel (592 = 49×12 + 4), with no padding after it.

A minimal reader therefore: parse the header → walk the section table → read `__classnames__` →
decode `__types__` into a class registry → decode `__data__` against that registry, applying the
virtual fixups to bind each object to its class. That is enough to read TDU2's vehicle physics
(a `hkpPhysicsSystem` with 4 rigid bodies, 4 limited-hinge wheel constraints, and a chassis
`hkpListShape` of 13 box/convex child shapes) with no Havok SDK at all.

### Writing one back: match the header's `layoutRules` to the target

At minimum, the four rule bytes at header offset 16 —
`bytesInPointer`, `littleEndian`, `reusePadding`, `emptyBaseClassOptimization` — must be written to
match the target, and the fixup tables are *regenerated from the object graph*, not copied. Havok's
own `AssetCC` demo converter takes the four as one argument (`--rules4101`) and rejects anything
other than `[48][01][01][01]` ("Rules must be of the form [48][01][01][01] e.g. 4101"; first digit 4
or 8, the rest 0 or 1). Getting it wrong for the target is the classic self-inflicted wound: writing
the console rules on a PC packfile produces a file with the right size and the right (palindromic)
magic in which every multi-byte field is byte-swapped. `AssetCC` is cited here only as the SDK's
reference behaviour for the rules argument; it was **not** the tool used for the round trip below.

The round trip below was verified **off-game only**, on TDU2 `5.5.0-r1`, with our own unpublished
local writer (`parse_hkx.py`): XML → binary with `04 01 00 01` → binary → XML — same
32112-byte size as the source, reads back to the same object graph, and the re-extracted XML matches
the original except for `-0.000000` → `0.000000` (negative zero). 357 of 32112 bytes differ, all of
them either those signed zeros or 4-byte slots inside the rigid-body/motion structs that never appear
in the XML — members the format marks as non-serialised (cached motion-state / swept-transform data a
loader recomputes), which the writer leaves at their defaults.

The useful loop that follows: extract from the container → XML → edit a shape transform or a wheel
hinge axis → binary with the source's own rule bytes → back into the container. Off-game round trip
only; the in-game load is still the oracle.

## Gotchas

1. **`SDKV` is the ground truth.** **Symptom:** docs disagree about a game's Havok version.
   **Cause:** old community notes and vendor trees differ from retail. **Fix:** decode `SDKV` from a
   real retail asset; 2017.2.0 for WDL retail, 2015.1.0 for the leak, 2019.02 for Starfield.
2. **"Same chunk tags" ≠ "same version".** **Symptom:** a 2017.2 parser reads a 2019.02 file fine,
   but conversion still fails. **Cause:** the tag *family* is shared; the *version* and the compat
   filter are separate. **Fix:** identify by `SDKV`, not by tag list.
3. **A classic packfile hides among chunked assets.** **Symptom:** a "WDL HKX" won't parse as a
   tagfile. **Cause:** WDL mixes a 2014.2.5 **classic packfile** (vehicle collision) with 2017.2.0
   chunked. **Fix:** check the first bytes — classic packfiles start with magic
   `57 E0 E0 57 10 C0 C0 10` and the version string `hk_2014.2.5-r1`; `1E 0D B0 CA CE FA 11 D0` is the
   pre-2015 binary-tagfile magic, a different animal.
4. **The SDK's prebuilt libs are not enough.** **Symptom:** `hkCompatFormats.dll` present but
   conversion still fails. **Cause:** the shipped `hkCompatFormats.dll` may be for a different version
   (a PDB path showed `D:\Development\2015_1` for one). **Fix:** verify the DLL's own version; a
   2015.1 DLL will not serve 2017.2.
5. **A newer SDK can still support an older target.** **Symptom:** you only have the 2018.1.0 SDK and
   need 2017.2. **Cause:** you assumed you needed the matching SDK. **Fix:** 2018.1.0's
   `hkHavokVersions.h` lists `HK_HAVOK_VERSION_201720r1 = 60`, and `Compat/Patches/2017_2/` contains
   the 2017.2 patch source — but the *conversion tool* still needs its implementation module, which is
   absent. Support in headers ≠ a buildable converter.
6. **The exe's version-registry list is not the game's version.** **Symptom:** `strings` on the
   executable yields `Havok-3.0.0` … `Havok-5.5.0-r1` and you cannot tell which one it runs.
   **Cause:** that list is the *compatibility* registry (every version the serializer can read), and
   the runtime "built with version [x]" message is assembled at run time. **Fix:** read the version
   string out of a real asset instead. For a classic packfile it sits at header offset 40 (see the
   TDU2 recipe below); the last entry of the registry list is a hint, not proof.
7. **Havok data can live inside a vendor container, not a `.hkx`.** **Symptom:** no `.hkx`/`.hkr`
   files anywhere, so you conclude the game has no Havok. **Cause:** the data is embedded in an
   engine archive. **Fix:** grep the archive for the classic packfile magic
   `57 E0 E0 57 10 C0 C0 10`; TDU2 hides its vehicle physics inside `KNAB` `.bnk` containers
   (magic at offset 0x08), stored uncompressed so it is greppable in place. Not every container has
   Havok: TDU2's `__Unknown/` folder (132 files) is only RIFF/WAVE audio, `KNAB` blobs and `IGE2`
   files — zero Havok signatures.
8. **Every public parser rejects old 5.5.0 packfiles — write your own from the reflection.**
   **Symptom:** `hkxpack`/`hkxpack-plus`/`HKX2` all fail on a TDU2 vehicle `.hkx`
   (`hkxpack` prints `[SEVERE] Could not find file for hkpPhysicsSystem.`). **Cause:** these readers
   only bundle class definitions for 2010.2.0-r1 / 2014.x. **Fix:** don't reach for the licensed-era
   SDK; parse the file directly. A 5.x packfile is self-describing — read the `__types__` reflection
   into a class registry, then decode `__data__` against it, so you never hard-code a version.
9. **A byte-exact repack can still be unreadable — check endianness first.** **Symptom:**
   you write the binary back, the size and the magic match, but the reader crashes. **Cause:** the
   rule bytes at header offset 16 were written for the wrong target (console rules flip every `uint32`
   in the file), and the magic `57 E0 E0 57 10 C0 C0 10` is byte-swap-invariant — so a "the magic is
   right" check proves nothing. **Fix:** copy the source header's four rule bytes back unchanged
   (`04 01 00 01` for a 32-bit LE PC packfile), then verify by *reading your own output* and diffing
   the result, not by eye.

**Reading a classic packfile's version by hand:**

```
off=$(grep -abo $'\x57\xe0\xe0\x57\x10\xc0\xc0\x10' <file> | head -1 | cut -d: -f1)
dd if=<file> bs=1 skip=$((off+40)) count=16      # -> "Havok-5.5.0-r1"
dd if=<file> bs=1 skip=$((off+12)) count=4 | od -An -tu4   # -> file version (5)
```

## Seen in

- Watch Dogs: Legion HKX research (unpublished local work; 54,419 real retail `.hkx` sampled, all `SDKV=20170200`)
- Starfield physics/collision (`StarfieldMeshConverter`, `SDKV=20190200`)
- Fallout 4 / Skyrim SE parser compatibility (hkxpack-plus, HKX2-Enhanced-Library)
- Test Drive Unlimited 2 vehicle + level/scenario collision (285 vehicle `.bnk` plus `Islands/**` level `.bnk`, all `Havok-5.5.0-r1`; `__Unknown/` has none)
- Sonic Unleashed / Generations / Lost World / Forces animation (`HavokAnimationExporter`, SDKs 5.5.0, 2010.2.0, 2012.2.0)

kind: technique
title: "Hooking a host engine's post-world render pass so world geometry occludes your overlay"
tags: [rendering, occlusion, depth-buffer, hooking, projection, frustum-parity, overlay, native-hook, d3d9]
date: 2026-10-11
agents: ["OpenCode (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash)"]

links: ["https://github.com/carxt/JohnnyGuitarNVSE/blob/b3521cb0b577632473fa731b7b9f83fe346738bf/JG/internal/Game/Bethesda/BSShaderUtil.cpp"]

# Hooking a host engine's post-world render pass so world geometry occludes your overlay

> You are drawing foreign geometry inside a host game. It shows up, but it is never hidden by the world:
> it floats over terrain, over menus, over everything. The fix is not a shader tweak - it is to draw it
> inside the host's world pass, in the short window where the world depth buffer is still bound. Getting
> there has one prerequisite almost nobody expects (projection parity), and two traps that will waste a
> day each (an address after a call, and your own Z clears).

## When to use it

- You draw foreign geometry (another game's model, a custom overlay, an editor gizmo) into a host engine
  through a hook, and the world must occlude it.
- You are about to choose between a **Present/overlay** draw and a **scene** draw.
- You already have a scene draw and it "does not occlude no matter where I hook".

## How

### 1. Pick the draw style deliberately

| | **Present overlay** | **Scene geometry (in-scene draw)** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| where | after world, imagespace and UI | inside the world pass, pre-imagespace/UI |
| world occlusion | **none** | yes (depth-tested) |
| host lighting | no (you fake it) | yes (host accumulation) |
| drawn over menu UI | **yes** | no |
| projection | you must reconstruct and match it | the host camera is used |

Symptoms that you are on the wrong side: no occlusion; lighting does not match the scene; the object
appears over menu UI; a hard vertical brightness seam (you are after the imagespace/menu-blur composite).

The **most robust** form is to create real host scene nodes (host `NiTriShape`/`BSFadeNode` under the
player/world root) so the host culls, lights, depth-tests and thumbnails them for you. If that is too
much work, the D3D draw-in-scene form below is the next best and is what the worked example shipped.

### 2. Find the frame dispatch, then the scene render function

- Locate the engine's **frame-render dispatcher** and the **gameplay scene-render path** (the normal
  case) as distinct from menu/variant paths. A hook inside the gameplay path is structurally not run by
  the pure menu path - but pause/pipboy-style frames that still render the live world do reach it, so a
  runtime menu guard is still mandatory.
- **Do not assume the scene-render function contains the world render call.** In the worked example the
  plan of record named a `RenderScene` call inside the gameplay render function; a read-only map of its
  81 calls proved there is **none** - the four `RenderScene` sites live in callee functions. Verify the
  premise before building on it.

### 3. Land projection parity FIRST (the prerequisite)

**Build your projection from the host's LIVE camera frustum, not from your own config.** If your near/far
(or the projection's depth mapping) differ from the host's, your Z values cannot compare against the
world depth buffer for any object at any draw point - so occlusion fails **everywhere**, and every hook
candidate you try will falsely "fail".

- Read the live projection from the host camera (worked example: `NiCamera::m_kViewFrustum`; live
  near/far were `5.0 / 353840.0` host units while our config said `0.002 / 100`).
- If the frustum is asymmetric (`l != -r`, `t != -b`), build an **off-centre** projection - recomputing a
  symmetric one from FOV/aspect loses a viewport shift (scopes/dialogue/VATS) and biases the object
  horizontally.
- Keep your own FOV for framing if you like; take only the **depth mapping** from the live frustum.
- Log it as an oracle: `pov: frustum n=.. f=.. cfg=(..) live=1 s=..`.

### 4. Find the main-target scene render call, and hook its return

- Among the host's scene-render calls, only the one **not bracketed by an offscreen render-target
  begin/end** is the main-bound (backbuffer) world pass. The bracketed ones are aux/offscreen passes
  (water/VATS/rendered menu) - instrument them, **never draw there**.
- **Hook the call's return, not an address after the call.** An address after a call is not a semantic
  point: in the worked example the address after the world render call turned out to be a **shared
  stack-object destructor called after all four render sites**. It patched cleanly, executed, and never
  drew.
- The working shape: detour every call site so your thunk **`call`s** the original (do not tail-`jmp`),
  and run your draw after the original returns. At that instant the world is in the backbuffer and the
  **world depth buffer is bound, pre-imagespace/UI**.
- Before drawing there: verify the site's **calling convention** (worked example: every site is cdecl,
  `add esp,0C`) and use a **stack-transparent** thunk (`popl`/`call`/`pushl`/`ret`). A bare `call` shifts
  the callee's arguments by 4 and breaks the frame.

### 5. Do not clear Z in that window

The host's world depth must survive so your geometry is depth-tested against it. Suppress your own Z
clears while in the post-world window. A leftover "clear Z" is a classic reason a correct hook still
shows through walls.

### 6. Avoid double-drawing

If you also draw from a Present path, gate it: the in-scene draw sets an "already drew this frame" flag
and the Present-path draw keeps skipping while the in-scene pass drew.

### 7. Prove it with a Z-tested test quad (or walk behind a hill)

- Verify the bound target identity at draw time (render target 0 / depth-stencil surface).
- The decisive test: put the object behind a hill and record at 60 fps. In the worked example, at t=20 s
  the vehicle's wheels and lower chassis were hidden behind a terrain ridge (only the cage above it) and
  at t=23 s it was gone entirely, with the view direction unchanged.
- **Describe each side's pixels before reading any log line**, and note honestly if you have no guest /
  reference frame for the same shot - then the comparison is UNVERIFIED, not MATCH.

### 8. Add the telemetry in the same build

Log the hook install (found/hooked/skipped/notcdecl), the post-draw enable flag, the live frustum vs your
config, and a throttled frame-time line. In the worked example:
`camera: render-scene ownership found=4 hooked=4 skipped=0 notcdecl=0 postDraw=1` and
`render: post-world draw third=0 seated=0 veh=1`.

## Gotchas

1. **No occlusion at any hook point.** **Cause:** your projection used your own near/far while the host
   camera had a different one, so your Z could not compare against the world depth buffer. **Fix:** land
   frustum parity from the live camera first.
2. **The detour patches, executes, and never draws.** **Cause:** the hooked address after a call was a
   shared destructor used by several render sites. **Fix:** hook the render call's **return**.
3. **Drawing in an aux pass does nothing (or corrupts it).** **Cause:** you picked a `RenderScene` call
   inside an offscreen render-target begin/end (water/VATS/rendered menu), not the main-target pass.
   **Fix:** pick the call with no RT bracket; instrument the others only.
4. **Your geometry shows through walls even though the hook is right.** **Cause:** you cleared Z inside
   the post-world window, destroying the host's world depth. **Fix:** suppress your Z clears there.
5. **The frame breaks when the hook fires.** **Cause:** a **bare `call`** shifts the callee's arguments
   by 4, or the site's calling convention was not checked. **Fix:** verify cdecl/`stdcall` per site and
   use the transparent `popl`/`call`/`pushl`/`ret` thunk.
6. **It draws twice (or flickers).** **Cause:** both the in-scene and the Present path drew the same
   frame. **Fix:** the in-scene pass sets the "drew this frame" flag; Present skips when set.
7. **It draws over the pause/main menu.** **Cause:** world-rendering menu frames still reach the
   gameplay render path. **Fix:** a runtime menu guard, and prefer a point inside the gameplay path
   (which the pure menu path does not run).
8. **Wrong framing or no occlusion on VATS/killcam/dialogue frames.** **Cause:** a different camera or
   frustum may be live on those frames while your draw suppresses Z clears. **Fix:** log the POV/menu/VATS
   flags at the post-draw and test one such frame explicitly.
9. **A cheap test quad "occludes" and the real object does not.** **Cause:** the quad's Z came from your
   config, not the live frustum (see 1). **Fix:** re-derive and re-test after parity lands.
10. **Matrix-convention guess rolls the world.** **Cause:** a guessed convention: the camera transform's
    memory order (row- or column-major) and the multiply order the code assumed (`M*p` with column vectors,
    `p*M` with row vectors) didn't agree. **Fix:** prove the convention from the live engine - read the
    engine's own matrix and check a known direction.

## Seen in

- Halo 3's Warthog, Chief and weapons inside Fallout: New Vegas (the author's project; no field note
  or public repository yet)
  - `BSShaderUtil::RenderScene` (`0x00B6C0D0`, cdecl, taking the `NiCamera` and the `BSShaderAccumulator`,
    as JohnnyGuitarNVSE's `BSShaderUtil.cpp` also names it) hooked at its four call sites; live frustum
    `5.0 / 353840.0`; the shared-destructor dead end; the 60 fps occlusion clip.

## Related

- `geometry-transfer-host-draws-guest-meshes.md`: the route this hook serves (the host draws the guest's
  meshes), and restoring the host's render state after your draw.
- `frame-compositing-depth-and-pose-sync.md`: the other route, where the guest's colour and depth are
  composited into the host frame instead.
- `porting-a-vehicle-semantic-traps.md`: the live near/far as one of several guessed meanings (gotcha 4).

## What a future agent should try first

1. **Instrument the host's frame dispatch and count the scene-render call sites** with a read-only pass
   (log, or Cheat Engine read-only - never breakpoints). Confirm which call is the main-target pass
   before touching anything.
2. **Read the live camera frustum and build the projection from it**, then log `live=1` and your config
   side by side. Do not evaluate hook candidates before this.
3. **Hook the main-target scene render call's return** with a transparent thunk, and draw immediately
   after, with your own Z clears suppressed.
4. **Prove occlusion with a walk-behind-a-hill clip at 60 fps**, and state plainly if you have no
   reference frame for the same shot on the other side.

  - https://www.mingw-w64.org/
tags: [decomp, native-dll, pinvoke, tmodloader, dotnet, c-api, abi, stubs, arena, crash-guard, snapshot, rollback, determinism, versioning, mashup, gamecube]

# Hosting a decompiled console engine as a native DLL inside a .NET game mod

> Once a decompilation has a PC port, the game can be built as a headless x64 library and loaded into
> another game's .NET mod loader by P/Invoke. The host calls one function per frame and reads the guest's
> state back, so the guest's own code (every move, every special) runs unchanged while the host draws and owns
> the world. This note is the recipe and its traps, from putting Super Smash Bros. Melee's decompiled engine
> inside Terraria through tModLoader.

## When to use it
- A decompilation (or a decomp-based PC port) of the guest exists, and you need *its* behaviour, not an
  approximation. The alternative is rewriting the mechanics in the host's language. In this project a
  2,500-line C# rewrite matched walking within a few pixels, but drifted up to about 127 px elsewhere (against a
  truth that included the community controller fix) and needed hand-written logic for every special move (about
  34 distinct movement specials and 18 projectile moves across the roster).
- The host runs mods as .NET assemblies (tModLoader, BepInEx, SMAPI, MelonLoader...) and can call native code.
- You want rollback, replays or a "1:1" claim later. A library with an explicit snapshot and a fixed frame
  step makes that possible; a rewrite rarely does.
- Not for guests whose decomp still has non-matching functions in the parts you need (they behave
  differently), or for hosts with anti-cheat: loading native code is a client modification.

## Setup (where this was measured)
- Host: Terraria 1.4.4.9 on tModLoader 2026.08.3.0, its bundled .NET 8.0.0 runtime, FNA 23.10, Windows 11 x64.
- Guest: [melee-pc](https://github.com/999sian/melee-pc) at commit `e83383539a4fd06e9bd8b28c270b3d1ecc7d3be3`,
  the PC port built on the [doldecomp/melee](https://github.com/doldecomp/melee) decompilation. Built in WSL
  Ubuntu 24.04 with `x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc` 13 (the **posix** threads variant), CMake 3.28 and Ninja.
- The guest reads its data files (`.dat` archives) at runtime from a folder outside the mod; every player needs
  their own copy of the game. Neither the DLL nor any game data goes into the `.tmod`.

## How

### 1. Cut the game library out of the port, without its renderer
- A decomp-based port usually already separates "the game" from "the platform layer". melee-pc's CMake builds
  the game as a static library (`melee_game`) and links it with a graphics and audio layer (aurora,
  Dawn/WebGPU, SDL3). Build only the library: here `ninja melee_game` took 48 s on 16 threads.
- **Don't link the guest's renderer.** The host draws. Linking aurora pulled in Dawn, SDL and abseil, and
  abseil resolved against a Windows DLL that CMake found through the WSL `PATH`. Leaving graphics out removed
  the problem.
- Link an empty probe against the library and look at what is undefined. Here it was 418 symbols, and every
  one belonged to console hardware or online services: graphics (GX) 117, audio (AX/AI/AR) about 45, OS 32,
  netplay/ranking/replay 80, memory card 20, video 12, disc 7, pad 5. No fighter, stage-collision, stage, item
  or scene-graph symbol was missing (implementing agent's count). That list is the size of the job.

### 2. Generate the stubs, and classify what returns a value
- A script links, collects the undefined symbols, writes stubs and repeats until the link converges (at most
  4 rounds). It reads already-provided symbols with `nm` from the objects, not from a hand list.
- Each stub returns a **typed zero**, counts its calls and warns once. A `void X(void){}` stub for a function
  that returns a value hands back whatever is left in RAX/XMM0, which is garbage (Gotcha 3).
- Port symbols that return a value make the generator **fail** unless a table classifies them:
  - `zero`: zero really is the right answer offline (no network, no memory card, unlock-all off);
  - `trap`: zero would be wrong, but only code the host never runs calls it (online mode, menus, music). The
    stub panics, and the crash guard turns that into an error code: it fails loudly instead of lying.
- Symbols the game declares as **data** need data definitions; the generator stops if one is missing.
- **Some "hardware" is arithmetic.** Vector normalisation, a screen projection (`GXProject`) and the port's own
  trig wrappers were among the generated no-ops. Link the math libraries, transcribe what is left from the
  original executable, and blank only real I/O (Gotcha 4).
- Make the guest's panic and log functions (`OSPanic`, `OSReport`) print before anything else. While they were
  stubbed, failures were silent segfaults; once they printed, each failure named its missing piece (the file
  system, the archive symbol table). Read the messages critically: a "heap is full" panic was really a missing
  archive, because the stubbed disc layer reported every file as size 0 (found by a second agent).

### 3. Give the guest an address space it believes in
- The port stores disc pointers in 32-bit slots and treats any value below 16 MB as an audio-RAM offset. So the
  guest's heap (the "arena", 96 MB here) must lie entirely inside `[16 MB, 4 GB)` of the 64-bit process.
- The DLL reserves it at a fixed address with `VirtualAlloc`, falling back to `VirtualAlloc2` with an address
  ceiling. `0x80000000` was free both in a plain `dotnet.exe` and inside tModLoader with FNA, SDL2 and Steam
  loaded.
- The guest's heap calls go to the DLL's own allocator over that arena: 32-byte aligned and zeroed, because the
  decompiled code assumes both.
- At startup the DLL checks that a test `malloc` from the C runtime lands above 16 MB, and refuses to start
  otherwise (Gotcha 2).

### 4. Guard every call
- Every exported call that runs game code sits between a `setjmp` and its return. The guest's panic and `abort`
  are wrapped at link time (`--wrap`), and a vectored exception handler catches access violations, illegal
  instructions and divisions by zero **on the calling thread, only during the call**.
- The call then returns an error code (`-6` panic, `-7` hardware exception) with the message in a last-error
  buffer, and the engine stays faulted (`-8` on any later call) until the host resets it.
- Without this, one guest panic ended the whole host process (measured: exit code 3 in a .NET test host).
- What a guard can't cover: a hang (a call that never returns can't be cut from its own thread), a stack
  overflow, silent memory corruption. The escape hatch for those is the same contract in a worker process:
  the ABI stays, only the transport changes.

### 5. Make "reset" a memory copy
- melee-pc already groups the decomp's statics for its netplay rollback: a build step renames `.data` and
  `.bss` into named PE sections between start and end markers. The DLL build adds to the same range the 10
  objects the port leaves out (audio, video and memory-card code), the port's own C objects, the DLL's glue and
  the stubs. Then it checks with `nm` that the key globals are inside and the DLL's own guard state is outside.
- The first `init` copies both ranges before any game code runs (about 0.34 MB of data and 2.3 MB of bss).
  `reset` clears the file cache, zeroes the used arena, copies the ranges back and bumps a **generation**
  counter. The DLL is then as freshly loaded, even after a fault mid-call.
- The same snapshot is what makes rollback possible later. Anything new that persists between frames (a draw
  mode, a camera block) must live inside it, or rollback breaks silently.

### 6. A small fixed contract (the "MTB" C API)
- Every block that crosses is fixed-size, pointer-free and little-endian, with 4-byte fields. `_Static_assert`
  pins every offset in C, and the C# side checks `Marshal.SizeOf` and `OffsetOf` of every field at load.
  Big-endian game data never crosses: the C side converts field by field when it copies host data in.
- The first call any host can make returns a 32-byte ABI block (magic `MTBR`, version, unit system, block sizes,
  limits). A host that disagrees **refuses and changes nothing**. From v2, `init` also fails (`-14`) until the
  host calls `handshake(2)`, so an old host that ignores the version still fails cleanly.
- Version rule: the major version moves with any change of meaning. Additive features that no published host
  uses yet get a **minor version** in a reserved field of the ABI block instead (pose channel, stage points,
  camera, Slippi's off-screen rule, and so on), so v2 hosts keep their handshake.
- The core calls are `abi`, `handshake`, `init(files_dir)`, `reset`, `load_collision`, `set_slot`,
  `create_fighters`, `step_pads` (one 60 Hz frame for up to 4 pads), `read_state_slot`, `read_items`,
  `set/get_rng_seed` and `last_error`. Later, optional: pose, camera, stage points, sub-entity pose, hit
  bridge, audio, effects.
- **Asking never consumes.** `last_error(NULL, 0)` returns the length; `read_items(NULL, 0)` returns the count.
- Errors are numbered, and the host treats any of them as "engine off, say why".

### 7. Bind it from .NET
- `NativeLibrary.Load` from a configurable path **outside the mod folder**, then
  `Marshal.GetDelegateForFunctionPointer` with `Cdecl` delegates. No `unsafe` is needed: blittable structs and
  arrays are pinned for the call.
- Required exports bind with `GetExport`, and a missing one rejects the DLL before any game code runs.
  **Optional features bind with `TryGetExport`**, plus a check of the minor version: an older DLL still loads
  and the feature is just off. Each feature lives in its own partial class file (`Native.Audio.cs`,
  `Native.HitBridge.cs`, ...), which also let parallel agents work without sharing a file.
- **The DLL is never freed.** A tModLoader mod reload unloads the managed assembly, but a native library loaded
  this way stays in the process with its arena and state. So every session starts with `reset` (idempotent)
  and then `init`, and the generation counter tells the host when to re-send collision and recreate fighters.
- One thread: every call comes from the game thread, never concurrently. No seqlock is needed while nothing
  else reads the blocks; if a worker thread or process ever does, the state snapshot needs one.

### 8. Step it once per host tick
- In tModLoader, `ModPlayer.PreUpdate` builds the pad and calls `step_pads`. `PostUpdateRunSpeeds` then writes
  the engine's position into the `Player` (feet anchored, velocity zeroed, Terraria's own movement suppressed
  for that frame). Both games run at 60 Hz, so one Terraria tick is one guest frame.
- Measured in two independent real runs inside tModLoader (3,065 steps each): mean 0.031-0.036 ms per step,
  max 0.21-0.23 ms. A full `reset` + `init` + `create` cost about 7.6 ms extra in the frame it happened
  (implementing agent's measurement).

### 9. Reads must be pure; prove it
- A read that runs guest code can change guest state. Here the first pose read ran the scene graph's matrix
  setup, and for one item kind it allocated 64 bytes in the arena: the simulation diverged only because the
  host *looked*.
- Make reads compute into a private buffer and return `-15` if the arena changed anyway. Test it by
  **write-protecting the guest's memory** (`VirtualProtect`) around every read. A second agent's harness found
  0 writes in 349,450 reads over 29 recordings and 50 item kinds, and its self-test tripped on the old DLL.
- When the original game *does* change state while drawing, model that as an explicit, deterministic step at
  the end of the frame, not as a side effect of the host's reads. The skinned-models note has the case.

### 10. Change it in pieces, in parallel, without breaking the oracle
- Never edit the upstream sources. Every behaviour change is a **build-time patch script**: it copies the
  upstream file, rewrites the exact statements, **fails if the anchor statement appears 0 or 2 times**
  (upstream moved), compiles with the exact line from `compile_commands.json`, and swaps the object in a copy
  of the library. Each patch is a named tag that can be switched off (`=0`) for causal experiments.
- For parallel work, each agent gets its own copy of the core and delivers a `patch -p1` file with an assigned
  minor version. New C code goes in new files and header additions in a delimited block. Patches merge in
  order of minor version, followed by one official build.
- The gate for every merge is the replay bench: all real recordings still bit-exact, with CSVs byte-identical
  to the previous build. A function-by-function disassembly diff with addresses stripped shows exactly which
  functions a patch changed (a second agent's rebuild of one patch: 0 of 23,563 functions different).

## Gotchas
1. **The data path set from C# never reached the DLL.** **Symptom:** the guest couldn't find its first archive
   and panicked. **Cause:** `msvcrt.dll` copies the process environment when it loads, so
   `Environment.SetEnvironmentVariable` in .NET changes a different copy from the one the C code's `getenv`
   reads. **Fix:** pass paths through the API (`init(files_dir)`), or export a setter that calls `_putenv`
   inside the DLL.
2. **An archive loaded as zeros, with exit code 0.** **Cause:** a test exe linked without ASLR got a C-runtime
   heap below 16 MB; the port's file cache took those buffers for audio-RAM offsets and cached zeros. The
   first load was still correct (the copy into the arena happened first); the second load of the same file
   panicked. **Fix:** link host exes with `--dynamicbase --high-entropy-va`. The DLL inherits a high heap from
   the .NET host, and refuses to start if a test `malloc` lands low.
3. **A stub that returned "something".** **Cause:** a `void` stub for the audio-RAM base pointer, whose caller
   copied from `data + RAX`. **Fix:** typed zeros, a value table with a source for each entry, and trap stubs
   that panic.
4. **Stubs that compile and lie.** **Symptom:** nothing aborts, but the floor normal comes out (0, 160), every
   fighter is "on screen" and every angle is wrong. **Cause:** vector normalisation, the graphics SDK's
   projection and the port's trig wrappers were blanked as "hardware". **Fix:** link every pure-math library.
   A lying stub is worse than an unresolved symbol, which at least gets reported.
5. **Six different compile errors, one cause.** **Cause:** the game target exports its include paths and
   defines as PUBLIC but its compile options as PRIVATE, among them a forced include (`-include src/pc/compat.h`)
   that defines the disc types. **Fix:** repeat the forced include on your own target.
6. **The link stopped on four symbols.** **Cause:** they are variables the game writes to; a function stub
   would put that write into `.text`. **Fix:** define them as data.
7. **Access violations deep into a match** (one fighter's recovery special ending at frame 2926, another
   fighter at 3025). **Cause:** a crowd-reaction pointer that the match scene initialises and a headless host
   never set. **Fix:** call the game's own setup function where the scene does. Look for everything else a
   headless loop skips: here also a stage object whose only job is to increment a collision counter every
   frame, which the airborne floor checks depend on (see the game note).
8. **A possible hang no time budget can catch.** **Cause:** a `while` loop in the scene code is controlled by a
   network stub; a garbage `true` would loop forever on the host's game thread. **Fix:** fixed values for every
   stub that controls flow, and a worker process as the fallback if a hang ever shows up.
9. **The arena ran out after about 990 terrain reloads.** **Cause:** the collision loader allocates fresh
   tables on every call, and the arena only shrinks on reset (about 94 KB per reload, 190 KB for a 1,482-line
   mesh). **Fix:** the DLL's allocator records the first tables and hands the same blocks back on later loads
   of the same size: 2,000 reloads left the arena unchanged. A later multi-joint loader found per-island blocks
   still leaking (about 822 KB over 200 reloads) and replays those too (implementing agent's report).
   Swapping the guest's data under it has a second trap: fighters keep *indices* into the old line table, and
   an index past the new count made a line walk spin forever. Remap every stored index to the matching new
   line, or to -1 so the fighter falls (implementing agent's report, synthetic tests only).
10. **A build overwrote the player's installed mod, twice.** **Cause:** `dotnet build` of a tModLoader mod also
    packs the `.tmod` into the player's `Mods` folder (`tMLMod.targets` runs `BuildMod` after `Build`), whether it
    builds the live source folder or a copy. It happened during a verification, and again later from a different
    agent that built in place; the installed file was restored from a backup eight minutes after the second one.
    **Fix:** compile checks on a private copy with the pack target removed; build the packed `.tmod` with tModLoader's own `-build` command and a `-tmlsavedirectory` that points
    into a lab folder, so the file lands there (the outputs confirmed it); keep the installed `.tmod` read-only
    while that runs; hash it, and note its modification time, before and after every build; back it up before the
    first build; and write the rule in the project's rules file and in every agent's brief.
11. **A configuration the API accepted ran NaN on every frame.** **Cause:** the camera block's validation missed
    a zero field of view, in a field everyone had read as a tilt angle. A second model's review and a boundary
    fuzzer found more holes of the same kind. **Fix:** derive every rule from the guest's own asserts and
    divisions, then fuzz boundary blocks. After the fix, a second agent's own search accepted 2,258 blocks with
    0 failures, while 213 of its 292 control blocks broke the earlier DLL.
12. **A meaning changed without a version bump.** **Cause:** bumping the major version would break every
    existing host's handshake. **Fix:** a minor version in a reserved ABI field for additive changes, and the
    rule written in the header.
13. **The host's own terrain streaming silently replaced the guest's stage collision one tick after a replay
    started.** **Symptom:** a recorded match replayed inside the host game agreed with the original for about 55 s
    of match time and then diverged: the first differing frame was before the match began (the floor line index
    was 1 in the headless replay and 0 in the host), and later a dash grab that missed in the original connected in
    the host. The headless replay of the same inputs was exact. **Cause:** the mod's terrain-to-collision streaming
    runs every tick for any session that has a fighter. The replay builds its stage mesh itself, so the streaming did
    not consider it its own: on the next tick it sampled the host world's tiles (where the stage had been stamped
    as visual blocks), rebuilt collision from them and reloaded it into the engine. The log said so 0.1 s after the
    creation. The new mesh had another line order, another load mode, and walls on tile edges instead of the
    stage's real edge, shifted by under one unit, which was enough to let one attack reach a frame earlier.
    **Fix:** a collision lock in the engine session (every reload request is refused, counted, and answered "ok"
    as for an identical mesh), switched on right after the replay creates its fighters; the streaming idles during a
    replay; and a watchdog that checks every step that the installed mesh and the load counter are the ones from
    creation and writes `COLLISION REPLACED` into the result file if not. **Proof:** a synthetic console that
    repeated the host's reload path produced a trace identical to the host's in every column except the line
    indices; the same path with the lock was identical to the headless replay. In the real game the replay then
    matched the headless engine across the whole match and the original recording on all 5,524 frames. **Lesson:**
    in a host, find everything that talks to the guest every tick, not only what you call yourself.

## Verification
- Real run inside tModLoader: the DLL loads from outside the mod, the arena reservation succeeds, and the
  engine drives the fighter on every traced frame (2,892/2,892, no fallback), at the step cost above. A second
  agent re-ran it with its own comparator.
- Synthetic (a .NET 8 test host, not the game): layout checks on both sides, idempotent reset, runs after a
  reset bit-identical to the first run, and a panic, an access violation and an `abort` each returned as codes
  and recovered by reset. A second agent with its own host reproduced 181 frames bit for bit against a real
  recording and ran 58 API abuse calls; another ran 1,017 abuse probes of the pose API with 0 failures.
- The replay bench (29 real recordings, both ports) is the regression gate for every patch; see the bit-exact
  technique note.
- Integration: seven patches written in parallel, each in its own copy of the core, were merged in minor-version
  order into one DLL (53 exports). The bench stayed 29/29 identical, and a combined soak with everything switched
  on ran 8.3 million steps with 0 failures and clean rollback and determinism (implementing agent). A different
  agent's 10-minute soak of the same DLL also passed: 268 matches (about 89 hours of Melee), 0 crashes, 15,186
  rollback checks without differences. Two hidden clashes were caught on the way: one pose id used by two features,
  and a version number defined twice.
- The bench itself was checked with twelve deliberately broken builds, which found four false greens
  (`prove-your-replay-bench-can-fail-mutant-builds-exposed-four-.md`).
- **Not verified:** unloading and reloading the DLL in one process (unsupported by design), a guest hang, the
  worker-process variant, any machine but one.

# How multiplayer mods sync the world, AI and interactions

> A cross-game survey of the routes multiplayer mods take to keep player worlds, NPC/AI and interactions in
> sync. Compiled from public netcode references and the code and design docs of four public multiplayer mods,
> and matched against the co-op mods in this knowledge base (TUNIC, Dishonored, AC4 Black Flag). This is a
> method map, not a built-and-verified mod: what was actually run in a game is in the `Seen in` notes, not
> here.

## When to use it

Read this *before* designing any feature that has to be shared between two or more players in a game that
was not built (or was built only partly) for multiplayer: free-roam co-op, synced NPCs, shared world edits,
trading, PvP on a server the user hosts. It tells you which synchronization model to commit to and which
primitives to layer, and it is the shortcut to the answers you would otherwise derive from scratch.

Pick a game route only after deciding these, because the model dictates the simulation:

- **Can the game be made bit-deterministic?** If yes → deterministic lockstep is cheap and small. If no
  (most engines; and always true for a mod you cannot rewrite) → state transfer.
- **What is authoritative?** For a mod, the host (or a server you run) owns the shared world, and each player
  usually owns their own character (see the co-op default below).
- **What has to cross the wire?** Inputs (lockstep), or state (client-server), or both (hybrid).

The rules from `skills/mod-any-game/references/safety.md` still hold. In a co-op mod, each player runs their own
copy and the mod's traffic goes over its own transport (direct UDP, a VPN, a relay you run). It never goes
through the game's official online services, and it never touches a client protected by anti-cheat. PvP mods
are for servers the user runs.

## How

### The two fundamental models

A game is a pure function `(state, inputs) -> new_state`. Two ways to share it (Mikola Lysenko's framing in
[Replication in networked games](https://0fps.net/2014/02/10/replication-in-networked-games-overview-part-1/)):

| | Determinism / lockstep | State transfer / client-server |
|---|---|---|
| On the wire | **inputs only**, peers | **state**, one authority |
| Runs the sim | every peer, whole world | server, then broadcasts |
| Needs determinism | yes (bit-exact) | no |
| Bandwidth | tiny (inputs) | grows with world/entities (mitigated by deltas) |
| Cheat resistance | tampered state desyncs, but every peer holds the whole world (map hacks) | high if server-authoritative |
| Cost | none (or a cheap relay) | server CPU + bandwidth |
| Fits | RTS, turn-based, 4–8 player | FPS, co-op, MMO, large worlds |
| Variants | delay-based; **rollback (GGPO)** | snapshot interpolation; **state-sync** (hybrid) |

- **Rollback (GGPO)** = lockstep + predict the remote input ("carry the last one forward") + on a wrong
  guess restore the state saved at that frame and re-simulate to the present, inside one render frame.
  Needs cheap whole-state save/restore.
- **State-sync (hybrid)** = run the sim on both sides, exchange inputs *and* state, let state correct drift.
  No perfect determinism needed; highest implementation effort.

For a **co-op mod**, the practical default is **distributed authority** on top of state transfer. Each player
owns and simulates their own character with the game's own code, sends its state, and shows the other players
as puppets with snapshot interpolation. The host owns the shared world (flags, pickups, doors) and arbitrates
claims on it, and either owns the AI or hands each enemy to the player fighting it. Glenn Fiedler's
[network-model guide](https://mas-bandwidth.com/choosing-the-right-network-model-for-your-multiplayer-game/)
names this as the model to consider when converting an existing single-player game, and the co-op mods under
`Seen in` all work this way. Full server authority with client prediction and reconciliation needs the host to
simulate every player's movement from their inputs, which a mod can rarely make the game do. Keep it for games
that already ship a server simulation (tModLoader, a server you run).

### Topologies

| Topology | What it is | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| P2P | peers exchange inputs/state directly | lockstep RTS, rollback fighters; needs NAT punch; lag-switch exposed |
| Client-server (dedicated or host) | one instance owns the real sim | FPS/co-op/MMO; cheat-resistant; needs prediction to feel good |
| Relay | dumb forwarder, no simulation | NAT fix + hides IPs (Steam Datagram Relay); fighters over relay |
| Distributed authority | each client owns some objects | Unity NGO; cheap, spreads sim cost, weaker security, flaky late-join |

### Core techniques (authoritative client-server)

The server runs a fixed-timestep loop; clients predict and interpolate.

```text
while running:
    tick += 1
    for client in clients:
        inputs = buffer.pop_for_tick(tick)      # buffered, maybe late
        simulate_player(client.player, inputs)  # server is physics authority
    run_game_logic(tick)                        # combat, scoring, pickups
    history.record(tick, world.snapshot())      # for lag compensation
    for client in clients:
        send(client, delta(relevant_state(client)), ack=client.last_input_seq)
```

- **Client-side prediction.** Apply your own input immediately, tag it with a sequence number, keep
  unacked inputs + predicted state in a ring buffer, then send it. Without this, every press costs a full
  RTT.
- **Reconciliation.** When a snapshot acks input `n`: snap the local state to the authoritative state and
  **replay every input after `n`**. Snapping without replaying stutters every packet. Blend small
  corrections over a few frames (Source `cl_smoothtime`).
- **Interpolation.** Remote players/AI cannot be predicted; buffer 2+ snapshots and render them ~100 ms in
  the past (Source `cl_interp 0.1` at 20 snapshots/s).
- **Lag compensation.** Server keeps ~1 s of hitbox history; on a fire command it rewinds candidates to
  when the shooter saw them (`now − one-way latency − shooter's interp delay`), tests, restores.
- **Snapshots + delta compression.** Send each client the diff vs the last snapshot it **acknowledged**;
  bitmask of changed fields + values, compact binary. A lost ack self-heals (next delta uses an older
  baseline). Resend recent snapshots redundantly so loss doesn't stall.
- **Interest management.** Send only entities near/visible to each client (spatial index + range query).
  Entering entities get a full spawn snapshot; leaving get a despawn.
- **RPC vs replicated state.** State = "what is" (unreliable, latest-wins). RPC = "what happened"
  ("play impact", "you died") on a reliable channel. Client→server RPCs are always validated.
- **Transport.** UDP with your own sequencing/acks (never TCP for the hot loop — head-of-line blocking
  stalls the stream). ENet, GameNetworkingSockets, Unreal/Unity transports, QUIC/WebTransport.

### AI / NPC sync

Rule: **the server/host owns the AI; never trust the client** (same reason as movement). The host computes
decisions and replicates resulting state; clients render it. If the AI is deterministic and clients run the
same code they can predict and correct only on disagreement — small deltas left alone, medium interpolated
back, large snapped.

In co-op between friends, trust matters less than latency and the game's own AI assumptions. TUNIC's co-op
mod gives each enemy to the nearest player (handoff with about 4 m of hysteresis): the unmodified AI then
chases its local player, and the owner streams its state to the others.

### Interaction sync

1. Client detects an interaction → sends a **request** (event object / RPC).
2. Host **validates** it (type whitelist, ownership, distance, NaN/inf guards, rate limits).
3. Host mutates authoritative state.
4. Host broadcasts/replicates the result, or sets a dirty flag the next sync cycle picks up.

Late-join/reconnect always does a **full snapshot**; steady state sends increments. Design the join path
explicitly.

### What the mods actually do (patterns worth copying)

- **Tiered bands** (KCD2-MP): FAST ~20 Hz transforms/velocity/anim (unreliable, latest-wins); SLOW ~2 Hz
  vitals/equipment; RARE on-change appearance/role + join snapshot (reliable).
- **Periodic complete snapshot + validated action** (FS25 NPCFavor): `NPCStateSyncEvent` sends the whole NPC
  roster every 5 s, on state changes and on join, in pages of at most 50 records with a sequence number, so an
  older snapshot never replaces a newer one. Client→server interaction events are validated server-side.
- **Change-only serialization** (King Arthur's Gold Sync): objects implement serialize/deserialize; the
  framework syncs an object only when its bytes change, 16-bit id overhead, auto-assigns free ids.
- **Server owns NPCs + extra-AI payload** (Terraria/tModLoader): `npc.netUpdate` syncs the NPC; extra AI
  fields ride along; projectiles are owner-authoritative; player data is diffed against a snapshot.
- **Own avatar + puppets + owner-arbitrated claims** (the co-op mods under `Seen in`): each player sends their
  own character's state (Dishonored: 30 Hz snapshots, 100 ms interpolation) or actions (AC4Coop replicates
  actions so the puppet animates itself). Shared pickups are credited once through a claim the owner arbitrates
  (TUNIC: first claim wins).

### Choosing a model

| Game | Model |
|---|---|
| RTS, thousands of units | deterministic lockstep (+ relay) |
| Fighting, twitch 1v1 | GGPO rollback |
| FPS / co-op / open world / MMO | client-server + prediction/interpolation/lag-comp |
| Turn-based / board | every-frame or global timestamp (latency irrelevant) |
| Casual co-op mod, no dedicated server | distributed authority: each player owns their character, the host owns the world, AI owned by the host or per enemy |

## Gotchas

1. **Player rubber-bands on every packet. Cause:** reconciliation snaps to the server state but does not
   replay the still-unacked inputs. **Fix:** on ack, snap and replay inputs `n+1..present`; blend the
   visual correction over a few frames.
2. **Two machines desync in lockstep. Cause:** float non-determinism across compilers/SIMD (FMA,
   transcendentals, x87 vs SSE, `-ffast-math`), seeded-RNG call-count mismatch, or iteration order over
   pointer-keyed containers. **Fix:** fixed-point math (or tightly controlled float), fixed timestep,
   synchronized RNG with an identical number of calls, sorted iteration, per-frame state checksum.
3. **Game slows to the worst connection / stutters when a packet is late. Cause:** lockstep waits for the
   slowest peer's input. **Fix:** local input delay, a relay with a notion of time, or rollback instead of
   waiting.
4. **One lost packet freezes the whole stream for ~1 RTT. Cause:** running the realtime stream over TCP
   (head-of-line blocking). **Fix:** UDP with a partial-reliability layer (ack bitfield, re-send only what
   matters); keep TCP for login/matchmaking/chat.
5. **A late joiner sees an empty or wrong world. Cause:** no explicit full-state path; only steady-state
   deltas exist. **Fix:** a dedicated bulk-snapshot-on-join path (NPCFavor's paged `NPCStateSyncEvent`, KAG
   full serialize), and test it — this is the thing that "works most of the time but not always".
6. **NPCs disagree between players / teleport. Cause:** AI was client-authoritative or non-deterministic
   while clients also simulated it. **Fix:** make the host own the AI and replicate its state, or make the
   AI fully deterministic with synced inputs; only correct clients when the host disagrees.
7. **Constant NPC jitter. Cause:** snapping small corrective deltas. **Fix:** threshold corrections —
   ignore tiny deltas, interpolate medium ones, snap only large ones (tune by playtesting under bad nets).
8. **"I hit them on my screen but the server says miss." Cause:** no lag compensation, and the shooter's
   interpolation delay wasn't accounted for. **Fix:** server rewinds targets by `latency + interp delay`
   before the hit test.
9. **Bandwidth explodes with many entities. Cause:** full snapshots to every client. **Fix:** delta vs the
   last acked snapshot + interest management (send only what's near/visible).
10. **Cheaters teleport / one-shot through walls. Cause:** trusting the client's position or damage.
    **Fix:** server-authoritative; clients send intent, the server simulates and validates every
    interaction.
11. **Rollback spikes into a "spiral of death". Cause:** re-simulating a large state for many frames each
    render frame on a CPU-bound game. **Fix:** add 2–3 frames of input delay, cap the rollback window, and
    do not attempt full-state rollback for large multiplayer states (it fits small 2-player P2P).
12. **Everything is fine in the lab, breaks on the internet. Cause:** testing on LAN/no jitter.
    **Fix:** simulate latency, jitter and packet loss during development; checksum state to catch desyncs
    early.

# Installers, load order and loaded-code checks for multi-part mods

> Mashups ship several moving parts (a host plugin, a loader, a guest mod, sometimes a worker or a converted
> asset set), and their install scripts are where users lose settings or end up with half an install. These
> are the patterns and pitfalls found in projects' installers and loaders.

## When to use it
Before writing an install/uninstall script, a launcher, or a startup check for a mod that hooks a native
game, and when a mod "doesn't load" for some users.

## How
1. **Check the loaded code, not just the file.** Steam-wrapped executables are decrypted in memory, so the
   file on disk doesn't show the real code. [BullySkate](https://github.com/Faiqie/BullySkate) launches Bully through Steam, then its native plugin
   requires all 203 code fingerprints and 19 data locations before installing hooks. [Touhou HFR](https://github.com/vittorioromeo/th12_hfr) also
   requires Steam versions to be launched through Steam and checks expected instructions.
2. **Load early enough.** PipeLink found `dinput8.dll` loaded too late for GTA SA's mod loader and its own
   plugin; it installed the same loader payload under the name of a DLL imported at startup, keeping the
   original under a new name.
3. **Pin and verify downloads.** [SkateGM](https://github.com/the-schwilliam/SkateGM)'s fetch script pins SDL2 2.32.10 and a mapping-database commit and
   checks SHA-256. Counter-examples: the [Minecraft × Half-Life](https://github.com/SawyerTheNerd/Minecraft-X-HalfLife) tools fetch Java from a mutable "latest"
   endpoint; [NewVegasCraft](https://github.com/Davozh/new-vegascraft)'s first script pinned versions without hashes and pulled shader headers from a
   moving branch. A download "stamp" is not a content digest.
4. **Record ownership so uninstall can be exact.** BullySkate validates prepared asset sets by hash, keeps
   timestamped backups and refuses an unknown existing loader. NewVegasCraft's early installer kept existing
   configuration on install but deleted those paths on removal; the GTA V example's `--remove` deleted
   `ReShade.ini` even if the user had one before, until install began leaving a marker when it creates the
   file. Keep a manifest of what you created vs replaced.
5. **Replace loaded DLLs safely.** NewVegasCraft switched to copy-then-rename so an already-mapped DLL isn't
   rewritten in place (under its Proton setup).
6. **Divide responsibilities with other mods.** Touhou HFR with a popular rotation wrapper: the wrapper owns render targets,
   rotation and presentation; HFR owns timing, input and replay and turns off its own scaling. HFR re-takes
   its graphics imports after a translation patch loads, then chains them, after older imports had been
   silently removed. Document the exact combinations tested.
7. **Separate "installed", "loaded", "connected" and "plays".** Each is its own check; a successful
   install is not gameplay acceptance.

## Gotchas
1. **Name checks pass on the wrong build.** **Cause:** the installer checks only file or process names
   (e.g. a batch-file installer). **Fix:** hash or fingerprint the target.
2. **Half an install.** **Cause:** copies are not transactional (BullySkate and SkateGM both copy in
   steps). **Fix:** stage to a temp folder, verify, then swap; detect a partial previous run on start.
3. **A backup marker that lies.** One installer uses the backup DLL as the only "backup complete" marker, and copies
   DLL and launcher in separate steps. **Fix:** write the marker last, after verifying every file.
4. **Version parsing.** BullySkate's loader check compares decimal versions, so 15.10 would read as 15.1.
   **Fix:** compare version components as integers.
5. **Duplicate loaders.** PipeLink's early return when a loader already exists happens before cleaning
   obsolete copies. **Fix:** inventory every loader before deciding.
6. **Tests that print instead of fail.** SkateGM's disc-image fixture and several Lua checkers print
   failure without a failing exit status. **Fix:** make every check affect the exit code.
7. **A build that skips the meaningful checks.** One project's default build skips asset-dependent smoke
   tests and reuses an existing library without validating its revision. **Fix:** report skipped checks.

## Verification
Versions are in `skills/mashup-mods/references/mashup-cases.md`. Creator results are reports.

kind: technique
title: 'Loading Pre-Sequel assets in Borderlands 2: header-only package surgery, mesh conversion and what still fails'
status: in-progress
agents:
- Claude Code (Opus 5.5)
humans: ["@Pherdee-boi"]

# Loading Pre-Sequel assets in Borderlands 2: header-only package surgery, mesh conversion and what still fails

> Borderlands 2 and The Pre-Sequel (TPS) are the same UE3 branch: both cook packages as version 832,
> licensee 46. This note is how an agent got TPS's laser beam particle systems and TPS's tether mesh to load
> and render inside BL2, from the user's own TPS install, by patching a copy of TPS's `Startup.upk` header
> and converting one native format. TPS's shader cache still crashes BL2, so materials come from BL2.
> Nothing from either game is shipped: the user runs the converter on their own files.

## When to use it
- You want an asset from TPS (or another cooked UE3 game of the same version) inside BL2, loaded by an SDK
  mod, without a GUI tool.
- You need to know which parts of a cooked TPS package BL2 can read as-is and which crash it.

## How
**1. Find the assets.** TPS keeps all laser content in `Startup.upk`: `GD_Cork_Weap_Lasers` (types,
balances, firing modes), `FX_CO_Wep_Laser` (particles, meshes, materials, textures), `Weap_Co_Lasers`
(models), `Ake_Cork_Wep_Lasers` (audio). Decompress a copy (see `reading-ue3-gearbox-games-offline.md`).
The OpenBLCMM-Data TPS pack has the property dumps.

**2. How BL2 loads a foreign package.**
- Put the file in `WillowGame/CookedPCConsole/` and restart (the package list is read at startup). Name it
  after the root package you want to address, e.g. `FX_CO_Wep_Laser.upk`.
- `DynamicLoadObject("Pkg.Obj", Class)` on an object of a package that isn't loaded returned None. What
  works is `unrealsdk.load_package("Pkg")`, which loads the **whole** package; then `find_object`.
- Loading the same package a second time crashed the game. Load once, keep a flag.
- Root what you keep (`ObjectFlags |= 0x4000`, RF_RootSet).

**3. Make the copy loadable by patching only header bytes** (export data keeps its offsets):
- **Summary:** BL2 silently refuses a cooked package from another cooker. Set `CookerVersion` to BL2's
  (134; TPS had 0x80086) and `EngineVersion` to BL2's (1712575; TPS 2630070). Clear
  `PKG_StoreFullyCompressed` (0x04000000) in the package flags when you store the file decompressed.
- **Root:** in a seek-free `Startup.upk` each original package is a top-level export flagged
  `EF_ForcedExport` (0x1). Re-parent the children of the package you want (outer → 0, the file's root) and
  clear `EF_ForcedExport` on that subtree.
- **Only load what you need:** compute the closure of the objects you want (tagged object references from
  the dumps and the binary, plus a material's native `UniformExpressionTextures`). Clear
  `RF_LoadForClient | RF_LoadForServer | RF_LoadForEdit` (0x0007000000000000 in the 64-bit object flags) on
  every other export: `load_package` then never creates them (52,000 of 52,600 exports here).
- **Imports:** point every import nothing in the closure needs at the `Core` package, so TPS-only classes
  and missing assets are never looked up. Retarget a TPS-only class used by the closure to a BL2 class with
  a compatible role (here `Engine.OzParticleModuleLocationLine` → `Engine.ParticleModuleLocation`, whose
  unknown properties are skipped on load).
- **Shared content both games have** (e.g. `FX_Shared_Sparks`): leave it out and assign BL2's copy at
  runtime.

**4. Streamed textures.** A texture's top mips may live in a `.tfc` (here TPS `CharTextures.tfc`); BL2 has a
file with the same name but different contents. Copy just those LZO blocks into a new `.tfc`, set the
texture's `TextureFileCacheName` to an existing name entry, and rewrite the mips' offsets in place.

**5. Static meshes need converting** (they crashed BL2's loader as-is). Diffing meshes that ship in both
games' Startup showed one real difference:
- TPS packs vertex positions: stride 8, two extra bytes, a bias and scale (3 floats each), then int16 x, y,
  z, w per vertex, position = bias + scale × v / 32767. BL2 stores stride 12 and three floats.
- BL2 has one more byte (zero in every shared mesh) 44 bytes before the end of the native data, right before
  the lighting GUID.
- Inline bulk-data headers store the absolute file offset of their payload. After converting, append the
  export at the end of the file, update its serial offset and size, and rewrite those offsets.
- Converted TPS copies of shared meshes match BL2's bytes except for the material reference and position
  rounding.

**6. Drive what TPS's engine drove.** The TPS beam is a local-space mesh emitter. TPS's firing mode has
fields BL2 lacks (`BeamLengthScaleName`, `BeamMeshRestSize`, `BeamContinuousDamage*Name`), so in BL2:
- put the TPS particle system into BL2's beam firing mode (`PartSysTemplate`); BL2 spawns it and feeds
  `SourceLocation`, `TargetLocation` and `Direction` (same parameter names);
- each frame, find the component BL2 spawned and set `BeamLengthScale` (length / rest size), the damage-ramp
  parameter, its translation and its rotation toward the target.

## Gotchas
1. **Silent "None" from `load_package`.** **Cause:** cooker/engine version mismatch in the summary.
   **Fix:** BL2's values (step 3).
2. **Crash while loading.** **Cause:** a native format BL2 reads differently. Find it by staging: build
   one test package per piece (texture, mesh, shaders, material), load them in order, and append a progress
   line to a file with `fsync` before each load (the SDK log loses its tail in a crash). Here the texture was
   fine, the mesh and the shader cache crashed.
3. **TPS `SeekFreeShaderCache` crashes BL2.** BL2 keeps all material shaders in
   `RefShaderCache-PC-D3D-SM3.upk` (chunk-compressed); TPS embeds a shader cache per package. Without
   shaders a TPS material can't render, and BL2 can't rebuild it (cooked materials keep only their parameter
   expressions). **Fix (for now):** a BL2 material, or a runtime `MaterialInstanceConstant` of a BL2 master
   with the TPS texture.
4. **Python traces don't work in BL2's SDK** (see the BL2 game note), so you can't find where a beam hits
   from the mod. **Fix:** let BL2's beam code compute the ends and read them back from the component's
   parameters.
5. **Crash dumps** (`WillowGame/Logs/*.dmp`) showed exception code 0x1 raised from KERNELBASE, which is
   the engine's fatal-error path. The text of the last mod log line was still in the dump's memory when the
   log file didn't have it.

## Open questions
- Port TPS shaders: decode BL2's shader cache format (per shader type) and translate the TPS entries, or
  accept BL2 materials.
- Check the remaining native formats (skeletal meshes, AkEvents) the same way before porting whole guns.

# Madness/Chameleon binary containers: .bml (binary XML) and .sgb/.sgx (track scenes)

> Slightly Mad Studios' Madness/Chameleon engine stores object hierarchies two ways: a compact binary
> `.bml`/`.sgb` and a plain-XML `.xml`/`.sgx` sibling built from a **reflection schema**. The container
> is simple — a magic, a chunk table, then per-chunk payloads — but the payload is a typed attribute
> stream that references separate number/bool/string sections. This note records the byte layout and the
> attribute IDs you need, so a tool can read the containers without re-deriving them. Mesh payloads
> (`.meb`/`.imb`) and the car transform file (`.vhf`) are covered separately.

## When to use it

- You have a `.bml` (car/setup), `.sgb` (track scene) or `.sgx` (XML track scene) from NFS Shift / Shift 2 /
  Project CARS / Test Drive: Ferrari Racing Legends and need the object list, transforms, and mesh
  references.
- You are extending/replacing the 3ds Max **SMS Importer** (`SMS_import.mcr`) or the Blender
  `meb_import`/`vhf_import` addons, and need a documented container instead of reverse-engineering the
  MaxScript.
- Related prior note: car meshes `.meb`/`.imb` and transforms `.vhf` are documented in
  `games/need-for-speed-shift-2/chameleon-mesh-formats-meb-vhf.md`; this note is the *container* layer only.

## How

Authoritative source: `SMS_import_v3.1c.mzp` → `SMS_import.mcr` by vagos21 & Chipicao. Function anchors:
`readBLMY` (line 60), `readCarBML` (line 1107), `readNODE` (line 1208), `readTrackSGB` (line 1259),
`readTrackSGX` (line 1376), `recurXML` (line 1148).

### `.bml` — binary XML (`readBLMY`, line 60; struct comment at line 28)

- Magic **`BLMY`** at `0x00`.
- Header: `u32 numChunks`, `u32 filesize`, `u32 zero`.
- Chunk table, one entry per chunk: 4-char name + `u32 size` + `u32 offset` + `u32 zero`. Seek to `offset`.
- Known chunks: **`HEAD`, `ELMT`, `ATTR` (typo'd `ATT R` in some dumps), `COLL`, `NUMB`, `BOOL`, `STRS`** —
  i.e. `struct BLMY(ELMT, ATTR, COLL, NUMB, BOOL, STRS)` (line 28). A real sample also showed a `STRSL`
  string-list chunk.
- `HEAD` yields `num_elmt`, `num_attr` (lines 88–89).
- `ATTR` entries are `struct attr(ID, type, val, num_values, nextAttr)` (line 29). An attribute is a
  **typed reference into another section**: numeric values come from `NUMB` (indexed by `val`), booleans
  from `BOOL`, collections from `COLL`, and strings from `STRS`/`STRSL` relative to a base offset
  (`STRSoffset`).
- Attribute IDs that matter for cars (`readCarBML`, lines 1119–1132):
  - `773578924` = **OBJpos** — 3 consecutive `NUMB` floats (`val+1..val+3`).
  - `-351767367` = **OBJorient** — a quaternion, 4 `NUMB` floats.
  - `1933617737` = **OBJscale** — 1 `NUMB` float.
  - `1259803821` = **mesh filename** — a string at `ATTR.val + STRSoffset` (import the referenced `.meb`).
  - `-263649155` = **modelName** — the same, used to rename the paired `.vhf`.
- The `.bml` has a human-readable sibling `.xml` (e.g. `t01_01_03_setup.xml` next to
  `t01_01_03_setup.xml.bml`). That XML is the **reflection schema**: `<class name="..." base="...">` with
  `<prop name="..." type="String|U32|F32|Bool|Fct"/>`, defining classes such as `BRTTIRefCount`,
  `BPersistent`, `CMissionSettings`, `CCareerEventSettings`. The `.bml` is the serialised instance of that
  schema — same data, compact form.

### `.sgb` — binary track scene (`readTrackSGB`, line 1259)

- Start by seeking to **16** (the magic/header word).
- Then a sequence of chunks to EOF: 4-char `CHname` + `u32 CHsize` + `u32 CHcount`.
- **`TALF`**: `fseek(CHsize - 12)` — a section to skip.
- **`MMUS`**: `CHcount` object records, each with `OBJsize, OBJid, STRstart, vhfOffset, v2, v3, v4`.
  `OBJsize` selects the node shape:
  - **108** → a single node: three strings (`NODEtype`, `NODEname`, `mebpath`) then sphere
    (`offset` vec3 + radius), transform (`pos` vec3, `orient` quat, `scale`), `matrixNumber`, instance count.
  - **152 / 204 / 256** → a `readNODE` chain of 1/2/3 nested nodes.
  - default → three stacked transforms followed by two nested `readNODE`s.
- `readNODE` (line 1208) reads `NODEtype`/`NODEname` via an offset-based `getSTR`, a bounding sphere, a
  transform, then discovers how many object offsets follow by a heuristic loop (comment in the source:
  *"assumption is the mother of all fuckups"*), then per object reads `NODEtype`, `NODEname`, `mebpath`.
  A path containing `_data` is rewritten to the shared track-assets directory.
- Any unrecognised chunk is skipped with `fseek(CHsize - 12)`.

### `.sgx` — XML track scene (`readTrackSGX`, line 1376)

Plain XML with root **`SCENE`**, loaded via .NET `System.Xml`. `recurXML` (line 1148) walks
`OBJ_ID`/`NODE` (recurse), `MATRIX` (attributes `Offset` vec3, `Orientation` quat, `Scale`), and `RESOURCE`
(attribute `Filename` → a `.meb` to import). It is the XML twin of `.sgb`.

## Gotchas

1. **Chunk names look misspelled.** **Cause:** the binary chunk tags are `ATTR`/`STRS` etc. and some tools
   render them with stray bytes. **Fix:** compare on the first three chars or use the known 4-char list.
2. **Wrong number of objects in `.sgb`.** **Cause:** the `readNODE` object-count discovery is a heuristic
   loop, not a stored count. **Fix:** follow `OBJsize` (108/152/204/256) and re-derive; treat the default
   branch as "unknown, needs the MaxScript logic".
3. **Strings read as garbage.** **Cause:** `ATTR` string values are **offsets into the `STRS` section**, not
   inline strings. **Fix:** seek `val + STRSoffset`, then `readstring`.
4. **Transforms accumulate unexpectedly.** **Cause:** `readNODE`/default branches compose `OBJpos +=` and
   `OBJorient *=` across successive nodes. **Fix:** mirror the MaxScript's parent/child composition order,
   or import each node with a dummy parent rather than assuming a single transform.
5. **`.bml` vs `.xml` disagree.** **Cause:** the `.xml` is the *schema* (class/prop definitions), not the
   data instance; the data is in the `.bml`. **Fix:** use the `.xml` to name/type the attributes, and the
   `.bml` to read values.

## Seen in

- **NFS Shift / Shift 2 Unleashed, Project CARS, Test Drive: Ferrari Racing Legends** (Madness/Chameleon
  engine) — `.bml`+`.vhf` cars, `.sgb`+`.sgx` tracks, `.meb`/`.imb` meshes.
- SMS Importer 3.1c by **vagos21 & Chipicao** (`SMS_import_v3.1c.mzp` → `SMS_import.mcr`); the Blender
  `meb_import`/`vhf_import` addons handle meshes/transforms but not these containers.
- Forum attachment sample pair `t01_01_03_setup.xml` + `t01_01_03_setup.xml.bml` (NFS Shift era) was used to
  confirm the `BLMY` header and chunk list.

```
